## Bracebridge Dinner and Vintners' Holidays: Yosemite's Christmas Season, Honestly

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/bracebridge-dinner-and-vintners-holidays
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-08-27. Last updated: 2026-08-27.
Summary: Bracebridge Dinner and Vintners' Holidays, explained: what they cost, what's included, when tickets sell out, and whether they're worth it.

Two names turn up every year in the same searches: the Bracebridge Dinner and Vintners' Holidays. Both happen at the Ahwahnee. Both get described online in the same breathless language, "iconic," "legendary," "bucket list." Neither description tells you what the evening actually is, what it costs, or whether the tickets you want are still there to be had. They are two different events, on two different calendars, sold two different ways, and conflating them is the fastest way to book the wrong one or miss the window on both. Here is what each one is, what it costs, when it sells out, and an honest read on whether it is worth the trip.

### Two events, not one

Vintners' Holidays runs in November: four multi-day sessions built around California winemakers, each ending in a five-course paired dinner. A session includes a "Meet the Vintners" opening reception, four tasting seminars led by the visiting winemakers, and the closing gala dinner, sold as a package with a room at the Ahwahnee, Yosemite Valley Lodge, or Curry Village. You cannot buy just the tastings; the room is part of what you are booking.

The Bracebridge Dinner runs in December: a single, several-hours-long dinner theater pageant, staged repeatedly through the month in the Ahwahnee's Great Lounge and dining hall. It is Tudor-costumed, live-sung, built around a seven-course feast, and involves a cast and crew that runs past a hundred people. Unlike Vintners' Holidays, a Bracebridge ticket buys the performance and the meal only. A room at the Ahwahnee is a separate booking, and plenty of guests drive in for the evening and drive home after.

The overlap that confuses people: both are staged in the same building by the same concessioner, both are the kind of thing a magazine calls "a Yosemite Christmas tradition," and both get lumped into vague web copy that never says which one has a wine list and which one has a knight in it. They don't compete for the same night. They compete for the same kind of trip, the one built around a single expensive evening rather than a week of trails.

What the Bracebridge Dinner actually contains, if the name means nothing to you: a cast of characters (a pious parson, a French chef, a wild Scottish cousin, a lusty widow of several husbands, and a Lord of Misrule who runs the room) leads guests through a procession of courses, including a boar's head and a baron of beef carried in by costumed servants, some of the props original to the 1920s production. A professional chorale sings carols between courses, there's a wassail bowl, and the whole thing runs about four hours. It reads as more theater than dinner, because it is: you are watching a play while it feeds you, not attending a meal with background music.

### Where both of these came from

The Bracebridge Dinner is nearly a century old. The Ahwahnee opened in 1927, and the hotel's then-president, Donald Tresidder, wanted an opening-season holiday spectacle to match it. He hired pageant director Garnet Holme to build one around Washington Irving's Old Christmas at Bracebridge Hall, and the first dinner ran that December. Holme died in 1929; the hotel handed the rewrite to a young photographer who had been playing the production's "Lord of Misrule," and Ansel Adams's version of the script is substantially the one still performed. For decades the dinner was one of the hardest tickets in California: through 2002, roughly 2,000 seats a year were allotted by lottery against as many as 60,000 applications. The concessioner has since added performances and moved to first-come, first-served sales, which makes the tickets easier to get and no less expensive.

Vintners' Holidays is younger and started smaller: a 1982 idea from the Ahwahnee's then-beverage manager and chief concierge to fill the hotel's slow weeks between the fall shoulder season and the December rush, built around a handful of visiting winemakers. It grew into a recurring, sponsor-driven program that now runs four sessions every November.

One historical wrinkle worth knowing if you read anything written between roughly 2016 and 2019: during that window, a trademark dispute with the park's former concessioner forced Yosemite Hospitality to rename the Ahwahnee "The Majestic Yosemite Hotel" and rebrand several of its programs. The dispute was resolved and the original names, including the Ahwahnee and the Bracebridge Dinner itself, came back into official use afterward. If you find an older review or brochure using the "Majestic" branding, it is describing the same place and the same dinner.

Photo: Chris Dunstan / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### What each one costs, and what the money buys

Vintners' Holidays packages, room included, have started somewhere north of $450 per person based on double occupancy in recent years; the exact number moves with which room category and which session you pick, and rises from there for the Ahwahnee's better rooms. That price covers the reception, all four seminars, the closing gala dinner, and the room itself for the length of the session. Measured against a standalone hotel stay plus a nice dinner out, it is not an outlandish add, since you are paying for a room you would have booked anyway plus a genuinely unusual set of wine programming.

The Bracebridge Dinner is the pricier evening on a per-hour basis, because you are buying only the performance and the meal. Tickets have run into the several hundreds of dollars per adult for years, and after the dinner's return in December 2024 following a five-year pause, reporting on that season put prices over $500 a person, with lower-priced passes for children. That is dinner-and-a-show money at a scale most restaurants don't approach, and it buys exactly that: a few hours, not a room, not a second night, not a discount if you're already staying at the hotel.

Both events run through the same channel, travelyosemite.com or 888-413-8869, which is also the number the Field Guide's own Park Bulletin lists for park lodging generally. Neither ticket type shows up on the general lodging-availability tools that cover the gateway towns; they are inventory the concessioner controls directly.

### What books out first

This is the practical question, and the two events answer it differently. Bracebridge Dinner tickets typically go on sale eight to nine months before the December performances, which for a given year lands around March or April, and they have sold out every year since the dinner's return. If you are reading this in late summer hoping to walk into a December seat, the honest answer is that the good dates, and often all of them, are usually gone by the time the leaves turn. The dinner also runs on a fixed schedule of specific performance nights across the month, roughly every other day from early to late December, so there is no such thing as "just show up on a slow Tuesday": every night is its own sold ticket allotment.

Vintners' Holidays lodging books on the same 366-day window as any other Ahwahnee, Lodge, or Curry Village reservation, one year and a day ahead, rolling. That means the November session dates open to booking roughly a year before each one runs, and the same logic the Field Guide has laid out for in-park lodging generally applies here without modification: set a reminder for the morning that window opens if your dates are fixed, and if you miss it, check back regularly. Cancellations happen continuously, with a real wave in the final weeks before any date, and a Vintners' Holidays package that shows sold out in July can have space again in September.

Put simply: if you want this December's Bracebridge Dinner and you haven't already booked it, you are likely working the cancellation list, not the original sale. If you want next December's, the move is to watch for tickets to go on sale in the spring and buy immediately. Vintners' Holidays gives you more runway either way, since it rides the same rolling booking window as a normal room, and the same patience-rewards-persistence rule applies.

Photo: Ahmed Radwan / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

### What the park is actually like that week

Neither event happens in isolation from the season around it. Tioga Road and the upper stretch of Glacier Point Road are typically closed by November, chain requirements on the Valley approach roads are a real possibility on any given night, and the days are short: the sun is down well before five in December, and the drive out after a late Bracebridge performance is a dark, possibly icy, mountain drive. The winter guide covers what's open, what's closed, and how the chain rules actually work, and it is worth reading before you commit to a same-day drive-in-drive-out Bracebridge trip rather than staying the night. If dinner is the whole point of the visit, a room removes the single biggest risk in the plan, which is not the pageant, it's the road afterward.

### Is it worth it

For the right trip, yes, with conditions attached. Both events are genuinely unusual, not manufactured hotel programming: Vintners' Holidays is real access to working winemakers in small-group seminars, and the Bracebridge Dinner is a nearly century-old theatrical production that exists nowhere else, with production values and a cast size that a $500 restaurant tasting menu cannot buy you. If the occasion justifies the spend, an anniversary, a milestone birthday, a family tradition you're starting, both deliver something a normal trip to this park does not.

They are not the way to introduce a family to Yosemite for the first time, and they are not a budget trip by any definition; a standard visit here costs a fraction of either package. The Bracebridge Dinner in particular is not built for young children: the performance runs about four hours, the dress code is genuinely formal (a dark suit or cocktail dress at a minimum, tuxedos and gowns are common, and costumes on guests are discouraged since the cast is already wearing them), and most guidance around the event treats it as unsuited to kids under ten. Vintners' Holidays, being a room package built around wine seminars, is even less of a kids' event by design. They also are not primarily hiking trips: both happen in the shortest, darkest weeks of the year, with most of the high country locked behind winter road closures, so the days around the event are for the Valley floor, not the granite above it. If what you actually want is a normal winter visit to this park, at a normal winter price, the season itself is the better article to read, and a standard room at any of the Valley's lodges gets you the empty trails and the clearing-storm photographs without the four-figure evening.

If the Ahwahnee itself is sold out for the dates you want, whether for a Vintners' Holidays package or simply a room to pair with a Bracebridge ticket, the gateway towns are the fallback, though none of them replicate the point of either event, which is being inside the building where it happens. A live availability search around the park is the fastest way to see what's actually left on your dates before you decide the trip doesn't work this year. For a bite that doesn't require a costume or a wine glass, the Ahwahnee's dining room also runs its regular seasonal menu on nights neither event is happening, covered along with the rest of the Valley's kitchens in the Field Guide's restaurant guide.

#### Before you write off this season

The Ahwahnee itself books through the concessioner, not here. But if it's full for your dates and a gateway-town stay would still make the trip work, this is a two-minute way to see what's actually open nearby.

## Yosemite fire restrictions, explained: what's banned, what still works, and how to check before you go

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-fire-restrictions-explained
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-24. Last updated: 2026-08-24.
Summary: Yosemite's Stage 1 fire restrictions, explained: what's banned below 8,000 feet, what still works, and how to check before your trip.

You bought a bundle of firewood at the gas station in Mariposa, because that is what you do before a Yosemite camping trip. You get to the site, unload the cooler, and find a ranger notice zip-tied to the fire ring: no wood fires. Not tonight, not this week, not until further notice. The bundle rides home unopened. This is not a hypothetical. Yosemite is under Stage 1 fire restrictions right now, and every summer a fresh set of visitors arrives not knowing that the rules changed since the last time they camped here, or that they ever change at all.

The restrictions are not complicated once someone lays them out, but nobody hands you the list at the entrance station. Here is what is actually banned, what still works, why the line sits where it does, and how to check whether any of this has changed by the time your trip starts.

### What is in effect right now

Yosemite implemented Stage 1 fire restrictions at 12:01 a.m. on Friday, August 7, 2026, parkwide below 8,000 feet in elevation. The park cited hot, dry weather, low fuel moisture, and windy conditions raising the potential for fast wildfire growth, on the recommendation of the Yosemite Fire Program. The restrictions apply until further notice, which in practice means until conditions improve enough for the park to lift them, not on a fixed calendar date.

This is separate from, and layered on top of, the small lightning-caused fires that made news partway through August. An early-morning storm on August 12 started eight fires in the park, including ones near Aspen Valley, Dewey Point, and Wawona Road; the largest reported was a couple of acres. None triggered evacuations or site closures. Those fires are not why your campfire is banned. They are one symptom of the same dry conditions that triggered the restrictions a few days before the storm, and they are worth knowing about mainly because they explain why the park is not in a hurry to lift the ban.

### What is actually banned

Below 8,000 feet, parkwide: no building, maintaining, attending, or using a wood or charcoal fire, including twig stoves, the small backpacking stoves that burn sticks instead of fuel. That covers a campfire at your site, a charcoal grill, a hibachi, anything that burns solid fuel.

Smoking is restricted too. Below 8,000 feet, smoking is prohibited except inside an enclosed vehicle, inside a campground or picnic area where wood and charcoal fires are otherwise permitted, or in a posted designated smoking area. That is a real change from ordinary conditions, and it catches people who assume the fire rules and the smoking rules are the same thing. They are related, but the smoking rule is broader.

### What still works

You can still cook, and you can still have light and heat at your site. Portable stoves that burn pressurized gas, liquid fuel, or propane are permitted, and so are alcohol stoves, including the small tablet or cube stoves backpackers carry. If your plan for the trip was a camp stove for dinner and a headlamp for light, none of that changes.

Established fire rings in developed areas keep working, with one exception. Designated frontcountry campgrounds and picnic areas below 8,000 feet are exempt from the wood and charcoal ban, so a ring at Upper Pines or Wawona Campground can still hold a fire. Residential areas in the park's developed communities are exempt too, with one carve-out: in El Portal and Foresta, only charcoal fires are allowed, not wood, because those two communities carry the highest structure-fire exposure in the park. Everywhere else the exemption for residential and developed areas covers both.

Above 8,000 feet, in the wilderness, campfires are allowed in existing fire rings, up to 9,600 feet. That upper bound is not a fire-danger rule, it is a standing, year-round wilderness regulation: above 9,600 feet, wood is scarce and slow to regenerate at that elevation, so fires are prohibited there regardless of fire restrictions. The 8,000-to-9,600-foot band is the one place in the park right now where a genuine wood campfire, built in a ring that already exists, is legal. That is most of the high country above Tuolumne Meadows and along the Sierra crest, and almost none of the Valley, Wawona, or the areas most visitors camp in.

Photo: Cory Goehring

### Two rules, not one, and they are not the same rule

Even outside fire restrictions, Yosemite Valley and Hodgdon Meadow run a standing seasonal rule: from May through September, wood fires there are allowed only in the evening, roughly 5 to 10 p.m. That rule exists for air quality, not fire danger. The Valley is a granite trough that traps cold air and smoke overnight, and a hundred and fifty morning campfires produce a haze the whole floor has to breathe. The campground guide covers that rule for a normal summer.

Stage 1 restrictions do not adjust that evening window. They cancel it. Right now, in the Valley and at Hodgdon Meadow, there is no evening exception, because the wood-fire ban is total below 8,000 feet regardless of the hour. When the restrictions lift, the standing evening-only rule comes back into force for whatever remains of the summer season. Two different rules, two different reasons, and only one of them is active on any given week.

### Why the line sits at 8,000 feet, and why it moves

Fuel moisture, the amount of water held in dead grass, brush, and duff, drops fastest at lower, hotter, drier elevations. The Valley floor and the foothill approaches dry out first and stay driest longest. The high country holds moisture later into the season, sees fewer visitors overall, and has a shorter, cooler fire season by nature. Drawing the restriction line by elevation targets the terrain that is actually dangerous rather than banning fires park-wide when only part of the park is at risk.

The number itself is not fixed. It reflects that year's conditions and gets set, and can be reset, by the park's fire managers as the season develops. In some past seasons the working elevation line has sat lower, closer to 6,000 feet, when conditions were more severe or a fire was actively burning nearby. In 2026 it is 8,000 feet. The mechanism is what stays constant: check the current line before you assume last year's trip rules still apply.

### How to check before you drive up

Three places, and check them close to your trip rather than when you booked it, because restrictions can tighten, loosen, or shift elevation with a week's notice.

The park's own fire restrictions page (nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/firerestrictions.htm) states whatever is currently in effect, in the same terms used here. The current conditions page (nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/conditions.htm) rolls fire restrictions in with road and trail status, so it is worth a look regardless. And the Park Bulletin on this site tracks what the current NPS Yosemite Guide edition says is happening, updated roughly every five weeks, alongside the day-to-day alerts that move faster than that. None of these substitute for the others; the fire restrictions page is the one with the actual rule text.

### What this means for your specific trip

Car camping in a Valley or Wawona campground. Bring a camp stove. The bundle of firewood you were going to buy at the gate is not usable right now except as fuel for nothing. Marshmallows are not off the table, they just need a canister stove instead of a fire, and a lot of campers do this anyway once they realize a stove is faster and does not leave you smelling like smoke in the tent.

Backpacking above 8,000 feet. You can build a fire in an existing ring, below 9,600 feet, if your route takes you that high. Most first and second nights out of trailheads at Tuolumne, Glacier Point Road, or the Valley rim start below that line, so plan on your stove for at least the early part of most routes. The backpacking guide covers permits, bear canisters, and the rest of what the paperwork does not tell you.

A day trip with a picnic. Grills in designated picnic areas are exempt, so a charcoal grill at a developed picnic site still works. A campfire ring you find along a trail or a beach that is not in a designated campground or picnic area does not count as an exemption, restrictions or not.

Smoking anywhere in the park below 8,000 feet. Car, permitted campground, or posted smoking area. Nowhere else, restrictions or not, and the fine-print addition during restrictions is that "permitted campground" now specifically means one where fires are still allowed under the current rules, which narrows the list.

### This is a different question from whether your trip will be smoky

The two get conflated constantly, and they are answered by different pages and solved by different packing lists. Fire restrictions are about ignition: whether you personally can start a flame. Smoke is about air quality: whether a fire burning somewhere else, in the park or upwind of it, is putting particulate into the air you are breathing. You can have a trip under full fire restrictions with perfectly clear skies, and you can have a trip with no restrictions at all where the Valley is gray from a fire three counties away. Neither condition predicts the other.

The smoke season guide covers the second question in full: how to read an AQI number, where in the park the air tends to be cleanest on a bad day, and when to flex your itinerary uphill. This piece only answers the first one. If you are checking one page before a late-summer trip, check both; a clean-air day can still be a no-campfire day, and a smoky day does not excuse a fire that restrictions do not allow.

### Violating the ban is not a technicality

Fire restriction violations are enforceable federal citations, and if an unattended or illegal fire escapes and requires a suppression response, the person responsible can be held liable for the cost of putting it out, which is a categorically larger number than any fine. Every fall, Yosemite's fire crews run planned burns specifically because prescribed fire keeps the forest from becoming the kind of fuel load that turns an escaped campfire into the summer's news story. A ranger who finds an unattended fire during Stage 1 restrictions is not treating it as a judgment call.

### When restrictions usually lift

Restrictions like this one typically go into effect in July, after a stretch of hot, dry weather has pushed fuel moisture down, and they come off when temperatures drop and real rain falls, not on a schedule. Historically, Yosemite has close to a 90 percent chance of a season-ending precipitation event, defined as two or more inches of rain, by October 31. Recent examples: fire restrictions were rescinded in September 2022 after a cooling, wetter pattern moved in, and again in late October 2021 after a combination of rain, snow, and cooler temperatures reduced the danger enough for the park to lift them. Most years land somewhere in that window: sometime after Labor Day, before Halloween, tied to whichever storm actually delivers.

That overlaps almost exactly with the shoulder season this site already covers in detail. The fall guide walks through the sequence of closures that follows Labor Day, and the smoke season guide covers the separate, related question of air quality when a fire is actually burning nearby. Fire restrictions, smoke, and the shoulder-season calendar are three different systems that happen to move on roughly the same clock, and a September or early-October trip can run into any combination of the three.

### The practical version

Check the fire restrictions page in the days before you leave, not when you booked. Pack a camp stove regardless of what the restrictions say on the day you check, because conditions can tighten between booking and arrival. If a wood fire at 9 p.m. under the stars was the whole point of the trip for you, that experience is currently available only above 8,000 feet, in an existing ring, and it comes back everywhere else the week the park says the conditions allow it. Until then, the granite, the water, and the trails are exactly as available as they always are. Just cook on a stove.

#### Sources

- Fire Restrictions, NPS Yosemite
- Current Conditions, NPS Yosemite
- Yosemite Fire Information and Updates, NPS Yosemite

## Yosemite in three to five days: one park per day

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-three-to-five-days
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-23. Last updated: 2026-08-23.
Summary: A Yosemite itinerary for 3, 4, or 5 days: the Valley, Glacier Point, the Tioga high country, and Hetch Hetchy, one park per day, plus the winter version.

The third day is where a Yosemite trip changes species. A one-day visit is triage, and we have argued at length that triage done early and done well is a great trip. A two-day visit is triage plus one earned view from above the Valley floor. The third day is the first one you do not have to defend. Nothing on it is the only chance you will get. You can wait out a morning of weather, take the wrong turn, stay an extra hour at the place that turned out to be the point, and the trip absorbs it. Most of the bad advice about Yosemite itineraries comes from people planning day three the way you have to plan day one, as a checklist against a clock. This is the other way.

The organizing idea is simple, and it comes from the shape of the park rather than from any theory of travel. Yosemite is four parks wearing one name. The Valley is a canyon: you stand at the bottom of it and look up. The rim, the Glacier Point country, is the same canyon from the top edge, looking down. The high country along Tioga Road is a third landscape entirely, open granite and meadow at 8,600 feet where you are on top of everything and under nothing. And the far corners, Wawona with its sequoias in the south and Hetch Hetchy in the northwest, are each most of a day by themselves because of where the roads go. These four are separated by an hour or two of mountain driving in directions that point away from each other. A trip of three to five days works when you give each one its own day and stop trying to splice them. One park per day. That is the whole system.

### The roads decide the menu

Before the days, the constraint that outranks them. Two of the four parks hang off seasonal roads. Glacier Point Road typically opens in mid-to-late May; in 2026 it opened on May 9, and it closes again on September 8 for another season of construction, so this year the rim is a spring-and-summer proposition even by its own standards. Tioga Road opened May 15 in 2026, unusually early, and closes with the first serious snow, typically in November. From roughly November into May, in a normal year, the menu is shorter: the Valley, Wawona, and Hetch Hetchy, which are exactly the plowed roads. The winter version of this itinerary is at the bottom of the piece, and it is a real trip, not a consolation.

So the first act of planning a three-to-five-day visit is not choosing hikes. It is checking which of the four parks your dates can reach. The trip selector does this arithmetic for you month by month, the Park Bulletin carries the current road status, and the Park Service's road line is the last word in the shoulder weeks. Every plan below assumes you have done that check.

### Day one: the Valley, exactly as if it were your only day

Day one does not change because you have more days behind it. Arrive before 8 a.m., park once, and work the floor: Tunnel View at first light, Bridalveil, the Lower Yosemite Fall loop, Cook's Meadow, then a slow hour on a rock by the Merced. That sequence, the reasoning behind it, and the things to refuse are the whole subject of the one-and-two-day guide, and I am not going to shorten it here into something worse. Do that day as written.

The reason the Valley goes first is not that it is the best day. It is that it is the best orientation. The Valley teaches you the park's scale, its shuttle, its parking, and its light in one pass, at the bottom of the elevation ladder, on the day your legs are freshest and your alarm discipline is still intact. Every later day gets easier because this one went first. It is also the day most protected from weather: the floor is walkable in rain that would waste the rim. If your parking goes wrong or the day runs long, nothing downstream breaks, which is not true in the other direction.

One addition earns its place on a multi-day trip: end the day at Valley View or back at Tunnel View for last light. On a one-day visit that is a luxury against the drive home. On day one of four it is fifteen minutes, and it is the first time you will have seen the same stone in two different lights, which is quietly the thing this trip is for.

Photo: Joshua Earle / Unsplash

### Day two: the rim

Day two climbs to the top of the wall you spent yesterday underneath. Glacier Point Road leaves Wawona Road at Chinquapin and runs about seventeen miles to a paved overlook at 7,200 feet that puts you at eye level with Half Dome, with yesterday's entire itinerary laid out three thousand feet below you like a map of itself. This is the single most efficient day-two in American parks, and the order of operations matters less than the two rules: bring water, because there is no drinking water at Glacier Point this season, and get up the road in the morning, because the point and its parking are a zoo by midday in summer.

The shape of the day: stop at Washburn Point first, the overlook a bend before Glacier Point that most cars skip, which trades the Valley view for the best roadside look at Vernal and Nevada Falls stacked in their granite staircase. Then Glacier Point itself, a 0.3-mile paved walk from the lot. Then back down the road a mile and a half to the shared trailhead for Sentinel Dome and Taft Point: about 2.2 miles round trip each, around five miles if you do both, one an open granite cap with a 360-degree horizon and the other a fissured ledge hanging straight over the Valley. Do both if the legs agree. Eat lunch on the rim. The long version of this day, including the sunrise variant, is in the Glacier Point Road guide.

Strong hikers have a second way to spend this day, and it is the best hard day in the park: up the Four Mile Trail from the Valley floor to Glacier Point and down the Panorama Trail past Illilouette and Nevada Falls, about thirteen miles and 3,200 feet of climbing, no car shuffle required. That is its own article, and on a five-day trip it arguably belongs on day four instead, with the driving version of the rim on day two. Either order works. Doing both versions is the kind of thing this trip finally has room for.

### Day three: the high country

Day three goes up, properly up. Tuolumne Meadows sits on Tioga Road roughly 55 to 60 miles from the Valley, call it an hour and a half each way without traffic and closer to two in July, and the drive itself is half the day's content: out of the forest, past Olmsted Point's straight look down Tenaya Canyon at the back of Half Dome, along the shore of Tenaya Lake, and out into a meadow system at 8,600 feet with granite domes standing around it like furniture. If the Valley is the park's cathedral, this is the roof.

The high country rewards modesty. The marquee walks are short and flat because at this elevation you are already standing in the view: Pothole Dome at the meadow's west end, a mile round trip; Olmsted Point's half-mile nature trail; Soda Springs and Parsons Memorial Lodge, a flat mile and a half to naturally carbonated springs that children refuse to believe. Lembert Dome, 2.8 miles and 850 feet, is the earned view if you want one. The altitude is real and it is the thing that ruins high-country days: drink water, expect to move slower than the mileage suggests, and be off the open granite when the afternoon thunderheads build. The full day, including what is actually open up there this year, is in the Tuolumne guide, with Cathedral Lakes as the serious-hike upgrade.

When Tioga Road is closed, day three points south instead: the Mariposa Grove, an hour-plus from the Valley, where the parking sits two miles below the trees at the Welcome Plaza and a free shuttle covers the gap in season. The Grizzly Giant Loop, about two miles among trees that predate the Roman Empire, plus the Wawona Meadow Loop's flat 3.5 miles and a look at the covered bridge, is a full and unhurried day. In winter you walk the closed grove road itself, two quiet miles up, and usually have the Grizzly Giant to yourself.

Photo: Michael Hogarth / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### Day four: one far corner, or one serious hike

By day four the famous list is done, which is precisely what the day is for. Spend it on one thing. Two candidates, and the right answer is whichever one you have been glancing at sideways all trip.

The far corner: Hetch Hetchy. The park's second glacial valley, an hour and three quarters from Yosemite Valley in the northwest corner, dammed in 1923 and still one of the best days in the park: across O'Shaughnessy Dam, through the tunnel, and along the north wall to the base of Wapama Falls, about five miles round trip of rolling trail with almost nobody on it. In spring the waterfalls are the equal of anything in the Valley; in July the crowds you will not see are the entire point. Two logistics rule the day: the access road runs on posted gate hours, roughly sunrise to sunset, and there is no food or fuel out there, so the day travels on what is in the car. The Hetch Hetchy piece carries the history and the trail detail.

The serious hike. If day two stayed on pavement, day four is the day to spend your legs: the Four Mile and Panorama loop above, or the Mist Trail corridor to the top of Vernal or Nevada Fall, three to seven miles of granite stairs and spray. Half Dome belongs to this day too, but only on its own terms: it is permit-only whenever the cables are up, the permits run through a preseason lottery in March and a daily lottery two days out, and a multi-day trip in cable season should play the daily lottery for its middle days rather than promise anyone the summit. Plan day four so that winning the lottery upgrades it and losing it costs nothing. In winter, the serious-hike slot has its own answer, and it is a shorter list worth reading before you commit.

### Day five: the day you stop collecting

Day five has no new territory in it, on purpose. Four parks, four days; the fifth is the first day you are in Yosemite with nothing left to get. Spend it at the pace the place actually runs at. Rent bikes and ride the Valley's twelve miles of paved path, which is the best transportation in the park pretending to be recreation, rentals running roughly April through October. Walk into a ranger program, which is the cheapest expertise you will ever stand next to. Go back to whichever hour of the trip was the best one and have it again: the same rock on the Merced, the same meadow at last light. Fish, sketch, read in a camp chair, watch the climbers on El Capitan from a meadow with your coffee.

I am aware of how this sounds. It sounds like the writer telling you to spend a vacation day doing nothing, in a place you paid a great deal to reach. What I can report, from twenty seasons of watching visitors from the inside, is that the people who come back every year are not the ones who saw the most things. They are the ones who, at some point, stopped. Day five is where that happens on schedule. If you genuinely cannot sit still, the honest alternative is to make day five the second far corner, Hetch Hetchy if day four was a hike, and demote the slack to the afternoons. But try the empty day once.

Photo: KatieRound / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

### Three days, four days, five: what each length buys

The frame above is five days. Compressing it is subtraction, not redesign.

- Three days is the Valley, the rim, and the high country, the three road-connected parks, one per day. This is the shortest trip that sees Yosemite's actual range, canyon floor to alpine meadow, and it is the length I recommend to first-time visitors who ask what enough means. When a seasonal road is closed, its slot goes to Wawona and the grove, or to Hetch Hetchy.
- Four days adds the choice you were forced to skip: the far corner or the serious hike. This is the length where the trip stops being a survey and starts having a center of gravity.
- Five days adds the empty day, which is to say it adds the margin that makes the other four calm. Five is also the first length where basing in two places can beat one, on which more below.

Past five days you are into a different kind of trip: a night in the wilderness, a second lap of the high country, the repeat-visit rhythm where you stop needing articles like this one. A three-day version of this plan is also wired into the itineraries page, where you can open it on the map, reorder it, and carry it with you.

### The winter version

From roughly November into May the rim and the high country are under snow and their roads are closed, and the four-parks frame compresses honestly into this: day one is the Valley as above, colder, emptier, and better-looking under fresh snow. Day two goes up to Badger Pass, where the closed stretch of Glacier Point Road becomes a groomed track and the winter rim is reached on snowshoes, most famously at Dewey Point, about seven miles round trip to the Valley's edge. Day three is the Mariposa Grove on foot up the closed road, or Hetch Hetchy, which sits below four thousand feet and is the corner of the park most likely to be snow-free all winter, gate hours and storm closures permitting. Days four and five, if you have them, are the ice rink, the clearing storms, and the deep quiet that is the season's actual product. Chains ride in the car all winter, no exceptions worth planning around. The winter guide is the season's logistics; the winter hiking guide is the trail inventory that survives the snow.

### Where to sleep, and whether to move

The base question changes with length. For three or four nights, pick one bed and keep it: the hour you save on a clever mid-trip move is paid back double in packing, checkout, and the parking you gave up. Base as close to the Valley as the budget allows, because every day but one starts there: in-park if you can land it, which means booking when the 366-day window opens or camping via the five-month release, otherwise El Portal for proximity or Mariposa for a real town, with the full comparison in the gateway towns piece.

Five days in summer is the one case where splitting the base earns its friction: three nights Valley-side for days one, two, and the far corner, then two nights east at Lee Vining, at the eastern foot of Tioga Pass, so the high-country day ends near the high country instead of two hours from it. That order also points your departure east toward Mono Lake and 395 if that is the way home. If it is not, keep the single base and eat the Tioga drive twice; it is a good drive.

### Common questions

Is three days enough for Yosemite? Yes, and it is the shortest visit that is. Three days covers the Valley, the Glacier Point rim, and the Tioga high country, one per day, without hurry. One or two days is a good trip too, but it is a different kind of trip, covered in its own guide.

How many days is ideal? Four or five. Four adds Hetch Hetchy or one serious hike to the three-day core. Five adds a day with nothing scheduled, which sounds like padding and is actually the best day of the trip.

Can you do Glacier Point and Tioga Road on the same day? You can drive it; you should not. They point in opposite directions from the Valley, each is two to four hours of driving round trip, and combining them turns both into windshield scenery. One park per day.

What order should the days go in? Valley first, rim second, high country third, the far corner or the big hike fourth. The Valley teaches you the park; the rim reuses that knowledge from above; the high country needs the earliest start and the most settled weather, so it benefits from a day of acclimation before it.

Does this work in winter? The compressed version does: the Valley, Badger Pass and the snowshoe rim, the grove on foot or Hetch Hetchy. Tioga Road and Glacier Point Road are closed in winter, typically November into May, so the summer version of days two and three does not exist then.

Do I need a reservation to enter Yosemite in 2026? No. There is no day-use or peak-hours reservation in 2026. You need the $35 seven-day vehicle pass, and international visitors age 16 and up pay the $100 per-person surcharge in effect since January 1.

Should I plan Half Dome into a three-to-five-day trip? Only as an upgrade, never as the spine. Permits are a lottery, preseason in March or daily two days ahead, so build day four to be good without the summit and let a winning application improve it.

### The honest pitch

Three to five days is the first Yosemite trip where the constraint is not the clock, and the discipline is different: not doing less, but refusing to blend. The Valley, the rim, the high country, the far corners. Each is a full day, each is a different park, and the trip that treats them that way comes home feeling twice as long as it was. Give each one its day, hold the fifth one empty, and somewhere in the middle of it, probably on a rock by the river, you will stop planning and notice where you are. That is the product. The rest of this site is just the packaging.

#### One bed, four days of alarms

Every day of this plan but one starts near the Valley, which makes the base the biggest single decision in it. A search on your dates shows what is still holding rooms, in the park and in the gateways, before you commit the itinerary to a bed that is an hour further from day one than it needs to be.

## Winter hiking in Yosemite: the trails that stay open

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-winter-hikes
Section: Trails and Hikes. Published: 2026-08-23. Last updated: 2026-08-23.
Summary: What you can actually hike in Yosemite in winter: Valley floor trails, Columbia Rock, the Vernal Fall winter route, Hetch Hetchy, Wawona, and what is closed.

The email arrives every year around the first week of December, from somebody with a booked room and a creeping suspicion: is there anything to actually hike in Yosemite in winter, or is it all snowshoes and postcards? The suspicion is half right. The park's trail inventory shrinks by something like two thirds when the snow settles in, the famous names on the closed list are exactly the ones people came for, and nothing at the entrance gate explains which is which. But the half that stays open is real hiking, on real trails, through the emptiest and best-looking version of this park, and most of it needs nothing more exotic than boots, traction cleats, and a respect for the clock. This is the inventory: what closes, what stays open underfoot, and the one honest climb of the season. The winter guide covers the rest of the season, chains, Badger Pass, the rink; this piece is only about the trails.

The season this article describes runs from the first lasting snow, usually late November, into April: the Valley floor melts out first after each storm, the shaded corners hold their ice longest, and the Four Mile Trail stays gated into May. Where you fall inside that window matters less than the day's actual conditions, which is the whole discipline of the thing.

### How winter hiking works here: elevation, aspect, ice

Three facts organize everything below. First, elevation. The Valley floor sits at about 4,000 feet, low enough that snow falls, sticks for a while, and usually melts back off the flat ground within days; the rim above it sits at 7,000-plus and holds a snowpack all season. That two-thousand-foot difference is the entire difference between a trail on this list and a trail on the closed list.

Second, aspect. The Valley runs east to west, so its north side, the Yosemite Falls side, faces south and takes sun all day, while the south side and every shaded recess hold their snow and ice for weeks after a storm. A south-facing trail can be bare and dry three days after a foot of snow while a shaded stretch of the same valley is a luge run. This is why the season's one reliable climb is on the sunny wall, and why the Mist Trail's shaded stair is closed.

Third, ice. The thing that ends winter hikes in Yosemite is almost never an avalanche or a storm. It is a paved path that glazed overnight, or a shaded switchback polished by a hundred boots. Traction cleats, the strap-on spikes sold under a dozen names, cost little, weigh nothing, and convert most of the Valley's winter hazards back into walking; carry them and trekking poles on anything that climbs, and put the cleats on before the ice gets interesting rather than after. Add the short days, with the sun down before five in December and off the shaded floor well before that, and the rules of the season write themselves: start mid-morning after the night's ice softens, set a turnaround time, and be off the trail by the time the light leaves it. Check the Park Bulletin and the Park Service conditions page the morning you walk; every entry below is subject to the current storm.

### Closed, so you can stop wondering

The famous absences first, because knowing them is what makes the rest of the list trustworthy.

- The Four Mile Trail closes for the winter, typically from the first lasting snow into May. In lean stretches the Park Service sometimes opens the lower three miles to a gate below Union Point, and that lower section still carries ice in the shade; the switchbacks above stay shut. The loop it anchors is a May-through-fall project.
- The Mist Trail's granite stair beside Vernal Fall closes in winter, along with the John Muir Trail between Clark Point and the top of Nevada Fall. This is not bureaucratic caution: icicles the size of furniture form on the overhanging rock above both stretches and fall onto the trail, and the spray that makes the stair famous in June makes it a sheet of ice in January. A winter route survives, covered below.
- Half Dome is out of season: the cables typically come down the day after Columbus Day and do not go back up until the Friday before Memorial Day, and in between the summit is a mountaineering objective, not a hike. The Half Dome piece explains the system.
- Everything on Tioga Road and upper Glacier Point Road, Cathedral Lakes, Tuolumne, Sentinel Dome, Taft Point, is behind closed gates and under feet of snow. The rim can be reached in winter, but on snowshoes or skis from Badger Pass, which is a different sport and a different article.

Photo: Ahmed Radwan / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

### The Valley floor, which stays yours

The floor is the winter park's main stage, and its flat trails stay open all season, snow or not. The difference from summer is not access. It is that you will be nearly alone on them.

The Lower Yosemite Fall loop, about a mile, paved and flat, changes character completely in winter. The fall itself is modest until the late-winter melt begins, but the amphitheater compensates with the season's own set pieces: on cold mornings the spray builds a frost apron over the talus, and after storms the whole recess hangs with ice that booms when it cuts loose. The paved loop is exactly where the black-ice warning applies; this is a cleats-in-pocket walk, not a sneakers walk.

Cook's Meadow and Sentinel Meadow, a mile of boardwalk, are the winter photograph you already know: Half Dome and Yosemite Falls over frosted grass, at their best in the hour after a clearing storm and in the fog the Merced breathes on cold mornings. The boardwalk glazes overnight; short steps, and cleats if it shines.

Mirror Lake, about two miles round trip on pavement to the lake and roughly five as the Tenaya Creek loop when conditions allow, is a better winter walk than a summer one, for a simple hydrological reason: winter is when the lake starts being a lake again. The seasonal pool that shrinks to a meadow by August refills with the first storms, and the reflections that named the place come back while the crowds are elsewhere. Tenaya Canyon keeps the sun late and loses it early; expect ice in both directions and give the loop away on icy days rather than forcing it.

The Valley Loop Trail is the sleeper of the season. The full circuit runs about 13 miles and the half loop about 7.2, but nobody owes it a lap: it is a chain of flat segments along the base of the walls, and in winter the western reaches toward Bridalveil and El Capitan are as close to having Yosemite Valley to yourself as daylight gets. Pick a stretch, walk it out and back, and add Bridalveil Fall, a half-mile round trip that in winter trades its spring violence for rime and quiet.

### The one real climb: Columbia Rock, and sometimes the top

The season's honest answer to "one serious hike" lives on the sunny wall. The Yosemite Falls Trail from Camp 4 climbs south-facing switchbacks that melt out fast between storms, which makes it the most reliably hikeable ascent in the winter park. Columbia Rock, about two miles round trip and 1,000 feet up several dozen switchbacks, is the destination that fits most winter days: a railed perch with the Valley laid out below, Half Dome and Sentinel Rock across the way, earned before lunch. Another half mile, some of it downhill, reaches the full frontal view of Upper Yosemite Fall, which in cold snaps runs past a growing cone of frozen spray at its base, the season's most underrated sight.

The continuation to the top of the fall, about 7.2 miles round trip with 2,700 feet of gain, is a conditions call, not a default. The upper third holds snow and ice long after Columbia Rock is dry, the final traverses are shaded and exposed, and the overlook's granite is no place for glazed boot soles. In a lean January it goes with cleats, poles, and an early turnaround honestly held; in a deep one it does not go at all. If you make the top, you will likely share one of the park's great summit views with single digits of people. Decide at Columbia Rock, not at the trailhead, and let the mountain overrule the plan.

Photo: KatieRound / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

### The Merced corridor, by its winter route

The trail most first-time winter visitors ask about is the Mist Trail, and the winter version is a different, gentler, still worthwhile animal. The Vernal Fall footbridge stays open all season: about 1.6 miles round trip from Happy Isles with 400 feet of gain on a paved grade whose shaded stretches ice hard, cleats again. The footbridge view of Vernal Fall over a low, clear, green winter Merced is quieter than the spring spectacle and better composed.

Above the bridge, the winter route follows the John Muir Trail toward Clark Point: at the fork, the gate on the upper John Muir Trail is closed, and the left fork drops to rejoin the Mist Trail just upstream of Vernal Fall, so the top of Vernal remains reachable when conditions cooperate. Nevada Fall does not: with the stair and the upper John Muir Trail both closed, there is no winter walking route to its brink, and the corridor's winter ambitions should end at Vernal. Go for the moving water and the empty canyon, keep expectations at that altitude, and read the Mist Trail guide for the rest of the year's version.

### Hetch Hetchy, the winter secret

The best pure winter hiking in Yosemite is in its lowest corner. Hetch Hetchy sits below four thousand feet in the park's northwest, low enough that most winter weeks its trails are simply dry, or briefly white and then dry again. Lookout Point, about 2.8 miles round trip with 500 feet of gain from near the entrance station, buys a panorama of the reservoir and Wapama Falls for an hour and a half of walking. The main event, the Wapama Falls trail from O'Shaughnessy Dam, about five miles round trip of rolling granite ledge along the north shore, is a legitimate all-winter day hike: the falls begin returning with the first big rains, the south-facing trail takes what sun exists, and the valley that holds a hundred quiet visitors in July holds a dozen in January.

Two winter caveats. The access road is gated on posted hours, roughly sunrise to sunset, so the day has a hard frame; and snow can close the road entirely for days after a storm, so check conditions before making the drive. It is an hour and three quarters from Yosemite Valley, which is exactly why it is empty.

### Wawona and the sequoias on foot

The south end of the park keeps two winter walks. The Wawona Meadow Loop, a flat 3.5 miles around the old meadow and golf course, stays walkable nearly all winter at Wawona's 4,000 feet, collecting snow just often enough to be worth timing. And the Mariposa Grove becomes, in my view, a better trip in winter than in July: the grove road closes to vehicles at the end of November, the shuttle stops, and the grove goes quiet. You walk up the closed road or the Washburn Trail, about two miles and a few hundred feet either way, then the Grizzly Giant Loop's two miles among snow-loaded sequoias, and you will meet more coyote tracks than people. Firm snow is boots-and-cleats; fresh snow is snowshoes; the grove guide has the winter section. Sequoias under snow are the best thing this park does in the cold months, and almost nobody sees it.

### When the boots stop working

Above the Valley rim the season belongs to snowshoes and skis, and the line between that world and this article is the snow line itself. The marked winter routes out of Badger Pass, most famously the roughly seven-mile round trip to Dewey Point on the Valley's edge, are the way to stand on the winter rim, and the ranger-led snowshoe walks are the gentlest possible introduction. All of it, along with the chain rules that govern every drive in this piece, lives in the winter guide. The one crossover worth repeating here: snowshoes are for deep fresh snow, and on the packed, icy trails of the Valley floor they are worse than boots with cleats. Match the tool to the surface, not to the season.

### Common questions

Can you actually hike in Yosemite in winter? Yes. The Valley floor's trails stay open all season, Columbia Rock is a real 1,000-foot climb that melts out between storms, the Vernal Fall footbridge stays reachable by its winter route, and Hetch Hetchy and Wawona hike nearly all winter at their lower elevations.

Is the Mist Trail open in winter? The granite stair beside Vernal Fall closes, along with the John Muir Trail between Clark Point and the top of Nevada Fall, because of falling ice. The winter route runs to the Vernal Fall footbridge and, conditions allowing, to the top of Vernal via Clark Point. Nevada Fall has no winter walking route.

Is the Four Mile Trail open in winter? No. It closes with the first lasting snow, typically into May, occasionally reopening its lowest miles to a gate below Union Point in lean spells.

Do you need snowshoes or just boots? On the Valley floor, Hetch Hetchy, and Wawona: boots, with traction cleats in your pocket for ice. Snowshoes earn their weight above the rim, out of Badger Pass, and in the Mariposa Grove after fresh snow.

What is the best winter hike in Yosemite? For effort against reward: Columbia Rock. For solitude and open trail: Wapama Falls at Hetch Hetchy. For the sight nobody expects: the walk up the closed road to the sequoias of the Mariposa Grove.

When does winter hiking season end? Gradually, from below. The floor is spring by April while the Mist Trail stair and the high trails shed their closures with the ice, and the Four Mile Trail waits for May. In between, this list and the March guide overlap on purpose.

### The honest pitch

Winter subtracts most of the trail map and every crowd, and the trade is better than it reads. Walk the floor with cleats in your pocket, climb to Columbia Rock on the sunny wall, take the winter route to Vernal's footbridge, spend one day at Hetch Hetchy and one among snowbound sequoias, and you will have done five hikes that July cannot offer at any price. Watch the conditions page like a local, turn around when the ice says so, and be out of the shade by four. The park does the rest.

#### The trailheads are short; the daylight is shorter

Every walk on this list is governed by a winter sun that quits before five, which makes sleeping close the difference between hiking and commuting. Winter is also the season the rooms actually exist: a search on your dates will show in-park and gateway beds at prices July does not believe in.

Search winter lodging around Yosemite →
Where to stay: every option compared

## Yosemite in March: A Tale of Two Seasons

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-march
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-08-20. Last updated: 2026-08-20.
Summary: Yosemite in March: weather, what is open and closed, chain rules, waterfalls and frazil ice, the foothill bloom, spring break crowds, and planning for both.

March is the month I have stopped trying to predict. I live in El Portal, down the Merced River canyon from Yosemite Valley, and in the span of four recent Marches I have watched this park buried and closed for weeks under record snow, watched a blizzard shut every road into it on the first weekend of the month, watched five feet of new snow land on Tuolumne Meadows in two weeks, and watched a March so hot and dry it erased roughly half the winter's snowpack in thirty days. Same month. Same park. Nobody planning a trip gets to know in advance which of those Marches they have booked.

That is the honest frame for this month: a tale of two seasons, running on the same calendar page. One March is spring. The afternoon touches 70 degrees in the Valley, the waterfalls are audibly coming back to life, the redbud is blooming along the highway, and you have the place at a fraction of its summer crowds. The other March is the biggest winter month of the year, the one the Sierra has an actual name for. You cannot choose between them. What you can do is plan a trip that works in either, and that is a solvable problem. Here is how.

### The month that cannot pick a season

Start with the record, because the ranking guides will tell you March is a mild shoulder month and the last few years say otherwise. In 2023, back-to-back winter storms buried the park under as much as fifteen feet of snow at the upper elevations; the Valley floor took 40 inches in a single day, breaking a daily record that had stood since 1969, and Yosemite closed at the end of February and did not reopen until March 18, its longest weather closure in decades. That snowpack held Tioga Road shut until July 22, the latest opening on record. In 2024, a blizzard closed the park again on March 1; it reopened in stages over the following days. In 2025, the winter rangers measured 61 inches of new snow at the Tuolumne Meadows weather plot in the first half of March alone. And in 2026, the opposite: an unusually hot, dry March cut the park's snowpack roughly in half, from about 65 percent of average at the start of the month to 37 percent by April 1, and pulled the whole waterfall season weeks ahead of schedule.

The swing is not new. Sierra forecasters have called a big late save "Miracle March" since 1991, when the Tahoe-area snowpack went from about 15 percent of normal on the first of the month to nearly 75 percent by its last week, and the name has been earned again several times since. In March 2018 the Tuolumne rangers logged 51 inches in the month's opening storm and 123 inches for the month. What is new, in my time here, is how hard the pattern has leaned on this month lately: the storms that defined each of the last several winters landed in March or within a day of it, while the quiet Marches have been quieter and warmer than they used to be. The month is not averaging out. It is splitting into its two extremes.

March is not a compromise between winter and spring. It is a coin flip between them, and you plan for the coin, not the season you are hoping for.

### The weather, in numbers

The long-term normals for Yosemite Valley, which sits near 4,000 feet, put March at an average high of 57 and an average low of 34, with about five and a half inches of precipitation, which keeps it among the wettest months of the year. Both halves of the coin live inside those averages. A dry, sunny stretch will run Valley afternoons into the 60s and sometimes to 70, with nights still dropping to freezing; a storm cycle will drop snow to the Valley floor one day and turn it to rain the next, because March storms play games with the snow line that January storms do not. The high country is a different world entirely: Tuolumne Meadows at 8,600 feet is under a deep snowpack all month, every year, no matter what the Valley is doing.

The practical translation: pack for both seasons, whatever the ten-day forecast says when you leave. Sun protection and a t-shirt layer for the warm afternoon, real insulation and waterproofs for the storm, and a car packed for winter even if you never open the trunk kit. The forecast at ten days is a mood, not a plan.

### What's open, what's closed

Yosemite Valley is open, along with Wawona and the Hetch Hetchy road, on the same year-round basis as the rest of the winter season. The closures that shape a March trip are the same ones that shape a January trip, and it is worth being blunt about them, because several of the guides ranking for this month get them wrong.

Tioga Road is closed. All of March, every year. Plowing does not usually even begin until mid-April, and in the last several years the road has opened as early as May 15 in a dry year and as late as July 22 in a big one. If a March guide tells you to take a scenic drive through Tuolumne Meadows, close the tab; the writer has not been here. Glacier Point Road is plowed only as far as the Badger Pass ski area, and only while the ski area is operating; when Badger closes for the season, the road closes entirely at Chinquapin until its spring opening in late May or June. The drive-up view from Glacier Point does not exist in March. Mariposa Grove Road is closed for the season too, but the grove itself stays open the same way it does all winter: you park at the South Entrance and walk the closed road, about two miles each way, to sequoias that may still be holding snow.

The two winter amenities are the honest fine print of a March trip, because both of them end as the month begins. The Curry Village ice rink skates its final sessions in the first days of March; in 2026 the season ended on March 2. Badger Pass traditionally runs into late March or early April, but that tradition is wobbling: in 2026 it closed for the season on March 18, and the winter before that it never opened at all. If skiing or the Dewey Point snowshoe is the point of your trip, come early in the month and check the operating status before you drive up, because when Badger is done, so is your trailhead.

### Driving in: assume chains until the forecast proves otherwise

Chain control is a normal part of March. The park's own guidance is to expect chain requirements on any road from November through March, and the rule that catches visitors is not the mounting, it is the carrying: when controls are posted, every vehicle must carry chains, including four-wheel drives and rentals, whether or not they end up on the tires. The full R1/R2/R3 system is explained in the winter guide, and the road-conditions line, 209/372-0200, is the thing to call the morning you drive in.

Route choice matters more in March than almost any other planning decision. Highway 140 through the Merced River canyon is the lowest approach to the park, low enough that it usually takes rain while the higher entrances take snow, which is why it carries the old name "All-Weather Highway." Highway 41 from Oakhurst and Highway 120 from Groveland both climb well over 5,000 feet and see chain control far more often. The full comparison is in the entrances guide; the March summary is the same as the January one. Take 140 if you can.

### The waterfalls are waking up

Here is the spring half of the month, and it is real. The falls that spent the autumn as stains on granite are waterfalls again by March: winter rain and the first warm-spell melt have rebuilt Yosemite Falls to the point that you can hear it across the Valley, and every storm that lands as rain sends it up another notch. It is not peak flow. The main melt pulse arrives with sustained warm weather, usually in May or June, though a dry winter like 2026 can pull the peak weeks earlier. What March offers instead is the sound of the system turning back on, with almost nobody standing at the viewpoints. The month-by-month schedule is in the waterfalls guide.

March also sits inside the season of the park's strangest small phenomenon. On cold mornings after clear nights, the mist from the waterfalls freezes into frazil ice, a slush of crystals that flows down Yosemite Creek like slow wet concrete and piles into white banks along the channel. The Park Service says it happens in spring, especially April but sometimes March and May, on mornings before about 9 a.m. when overnight lows freeze and the falls are running hard; the footbridge area below Lower Yosemite Fall is the classic place to look. There is a whole Yosemite Nature Notes film about it, and a cold March morning after a storm is one of your better chances all year of seeing it yourself.

One expectation to manage: the firefall is a February event. The alignment that lights Horsetail Fall runs roughly mid-to-late February, and while a faint version can still fire in the first evenings of March when the fall has water and the western sky is clean, that is a consolation prize for people already here, not a reason to book the first week of March. If the firefall is the trip, come in February.

### The bloom is in the canyon, not the Valley

The other thing March has that no other month quite matches is on the drive in, not in the park. The Merced River canyon along Highway 140 sits low enough that its spring arrives while the Valley is still flipping its coin, and by the middle of the month the canyon is usually in full color: redbud flaring magenta along the river, and the Hite Cove Trail, whose trailhead is on 140 at Savage's Trading Post, about eight miles west of El Portal, carrying one of the best poppy blooms in the Sierra foothills. The bloom there typically peaks around mid-March. Two cautions that the wildflower photos never carry: the trail is narrow across steep slopes with a poison oak understory, and parking is a handful of shoulder pullouts, so arrive early and check the trail's current status before you count on it. The Valley's own famous bloom, the dogwoods, holds until late April. The full elevation-by-elevation calendar is in the wildflowers guide.

### Crowds, spring break, and the reservation question

Averaged across 2010 to 2024, March brings roughly 160,000 visits to Yosemite against about 625,000 in July, which makes the crowd math simple: on a typical March weekday you are visiting a park running at about a quarter of its summer load. Parking exists. Viewpoints are quiet. Lodging can be booked weeks out instead of a year out. The exception is spring break: the weekends of mid and late March, and Easter week when it lands in the month, concentrate most of the month's traffic into a handful of days, and a warm, sunny spring-break Saturday can produce entrance lines that feel like June. If you have any flexibility, midweek March is one of the emptiest good-weather windows of the whole year.

As of the 2026 season there is no entry reservation to think about: the park dropped its timed-entry system, so entry is first come, first served with the standard entrance fee, in March and every other month. Day-of conditions, closures, and webcams are collected on the conditions page.

### The March homework for a summer trip

Two calendar items live in March even if your trip does not. The Half Dome preseason lottery takes applications during March, which means the month you are reading about is also the month to apply for a cables permit for the summer. And the park's bears begin emerging from their dens in March and April, males first, sows with cubs last, each of them down as much as a third of its body weight and single-minded about food. Spring bears are their own subject, but the March translation is simple: food storage rules are already in full effect, and the animals moving at dusk are one more reason to drive the park roads slowly. Daylight helps you here. The clocks change on the second Sunday of March and Valley sunsets jump from about six to about seven in a single night, with the days stretching noticeably longer by the week.

### How I would build a March trip

Base in or below the Valley, and keep a flexible day. The Ahwahnee and Yosemite Valley Lodge run year-round, Curry Village on a limited early-season schedule, and the gateway towns down 140 put you under the snow line most nights. Give the trip three nights if you can, and treat one day as the swing day you rearrange around the forecast.

If you get the winter March, you have won something, whatever it does to your plans. A clearing storm is the best photographic condition this park offers, and March delivers the last reliable ones of the season: fog tearing off the walls, fresh snow outlining every ledge on El Capitan, and viewpoints that in summer hold a hundred people holding six. Be at Tunnel View when the storm breaks, then walk the Valley loop while the snow is still on the oaks; it rarely survives the next warm afternoon. The photography guide covers where to stand.

If you get the spring March, work the water and the low country. Lower Yosemite Fall and the Valley loop in the morning, with a detour to the creek below the fall if the night was cold and clear, on the chance the frazil is running. The canyon bloom on the drive in or out. A walk up the closed Mariposa Grove road to the sequoias. And an afternoon doing the thing March is quietly best at, which is standing at famous viewpoints without waiting for them.

Camping in March is real but specific: Upper Pines takes reservations year-round, and Camp 4, Wawona, and Hodgdon Meadow run on winter first-come procedures, with nights at or below freezing as the working assumption. Check the current campground status before you commit a March night to canvas.

### The takeaway

March is the last month of winter and the first month of spring, and it refuses to tell you in advance which one you are getting. Come with chains in the trunk and sunscreen in the same bag. Book a base that works in both seasons, keep one day loose, and let the forecast, not the itinerary, decide whether your best day is spent photographing a clearing storm or standing in a canyon full of poppies. Either version is the quiet park, running at a quarter of its summer volume, a few weeks before the crowds return for the year. Both are worth the drive. That's the trip.

#### March rooms exist, except when school lets out

This is still the season when lodging can be booked weeks ahead instead of a year, with one exception: the spring-break weekends of mid and late March fill first, and Easter week behaves like summer. A search on your dates shows quickly which March you are dealing with.
