## Mariposa Grove: how to visit

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/mariposa-grove-how-to-visit
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-07. Last updated: 2026-08-07.
Summary: How to visit Yosemite's Mariposa Grove: the free shuttle, where to park, the four trails, accessible access, winter on foot, and the rules that surprise people.

The Mariposa Grove is the one place in Yosemite where visitors arrive with the same wrong plan, every time. They intend to drive to the trees. You cannot, not in summer, and not since 2018. The parking is two miles down the hill by the South Entrance and a free shuttle covers the gap. Nearly everything else that goes wrong on a grove day follows from not knowing that one fact, so this piece starts there and works outward.

### The geography, which is the whole problem

The grove sits in the park's southern corner, immediately inside the South Entrance on Highway 41. It is not near Yosemite Valley. From the Valley floor it is about an hour of driving each way, which is the single most underestimated number in this article.

Once you are through the entrance station you reach a roundabout almost at once, and the Mariposa Grove Welcome Plaza is the first right, less than a quarter mile in. That is where you park. The grove itself, what the Park Service calls the Arrival Area, is another two miles up Mariposa Grove Road, and in season that road is closed to private vehicles. A free shuttle covers the two miles. This is not a crowd-control measure that gets relaxed on a quiet Tuesday. It is the permanent arrangement the 2018 restoration created, and the reason for it is in the ground under the trees.

### The shuttle

It is free, there is no ticket, and individual riders need no reservation. Buses run roughly every fifteen minutes and take about ten minutes to cover the two miles. They are wheelchair accessible, with lifts and tie-downs, and chair users board first.

The season is the part worth reading carefully, because the Park Service deliberately does not publish a hard date for it. Its standing language is that the shuttle begins no earlier than April 15 and ends on or before November 30. That is a commitment to a window, not a promise about a day, and it exists because the opening depends on when the road is clear of snow.

There is one firm 2026 date available, and it is worth knowing about even though it is not addressed to you. Buses and vehicles over about twenty-one feet must reserve grove parking through recreation.gov, and that reservation window this year runs May 3 through November 30. It is a reasonable proxy for the operating season, because the reservations exist to manage a road the shuttle is running on. Treat it as an inference, not a timetable. Secondary sites publish confident hour-by-hour tables that disagree with each other, and I am not going to launder one of them into a fact here. Check the posted hours at the plaza when you arrive, and note the last downhill departure before you walk away from the stop. People miss it, and the walk down is two miles.

Photo: Nieves / Pexels

### If you hold a disability placard

The road closure has an exception. A vehicle displaying a disability placard or plate may drive Mariposa Grove Road to the Arrival Area, and there is accessible parking at the top. The spaces are described by the Park Service as very limited, which in practice means a handful, so this is a privilege that works best early in the day. The Big Trees Loop at the top is paved and genuinely flat, which makes the grove one of the more rewarding accessible destinations in the park. The accessibility guide covers what the placard does and does not get you elsewhere in Yosemite.

### Walking up instead

You can also walk from the plaza to the grove on the Washburn Trail, which climbs roughly two miles and a few hundred feet through mixed conifer forest before the first sequoias appear. There are two good reasons to do it. One is that the shuttle queue on an August afternoon can be long enough that walking is competitive. The other is that arriving on foot is a better introduction to the grove than arriving on a bus, because you watch the forest change around you rather than stepping off into the middle of the result.

### The four walks, in order of ambition

The Big Trees Loop. Three tenths of a mile, paved and boardwalked, flat, wheelchair accessible, starting from the Arrival Area. It passes the Fallen Monarch, the toppled sequoia whose upturned root mass appears in one of the most reproduced photographs in the park's history, a US Cavalry troop and their horses drawn up along the trunk. If someone in your group cannot walk far, this is the loop that still gives them the grove.

The Grizzly Giant Loop. About two miles with a few hundred feet of climbing, and the one to do if you are only doing one. It takes in the Bachelor and Three Graces, the Grizzly Giant itself, and the California Tunnel Tree. Two hours is a comfortable allowance including the standing around, which there will be a lot of.

The Guardians Loop. Six and a half miles or so into the upper grove, with something over a thousand feet of gain. This is where the crowds thin to almost nothing, and where the Faithful Couple, the Clothespin Tree, and the Telescope Tree are. Give it however long you would normally give a six-mile hike, then add an hour, because the upper grove is not a place anyone walks through quickly.

The Mariposa Grove Trail to Wawona Point. Roughly seven miles round trip from the Arrival Area with a similar amount of climbing, ending at an overlook above the Wawona basin. It is the full day, and the only one of the four that ends with a view instead of a tree.

Distances and gains published for the upper-grove trails vary between sources by enough to matter on a hot afternoon, and some trail-aggregator sites use loop names that do not appear on Park Service signage. Read the map at the Arrival Area before you commit to the long options.

### The trees worth knowing by name

The Grizzly Giant is the one people come for, and it earns it. The Park Service calls it the largest sequoia in Yosemite and puts its age at roughly 2,900 years. Other published estimates run a little higher, which is the normal state of affairs for a tree nobody is going to cut down and count. Look at the first big limb rather than the trunk: it is thicker than the whole of most mature trees you have ever stood under, and it is the detail that finally makes the scale land.

The California Tunnel Tree stands a short way past it, cut through in 1895 so that stagecoaches could be photographed driving through it. It is the only living tree in Yosemite you can still walk through. The more famous one, the Wawona Tunnel Tree, was cut in 1881 and fell in 1969 under a heavy snow load, and its stump is up in this same grove. The tunnel trees piece is the longer version of that story, which is less about vandalism than about what nineteenth-century Americans thought a national park was for.

The Bachelor and Three Graces are four trees growing so close that their root systems are effectively one, which is the practical argument for staying on the trail. Sequoia roots are shallow and wide, running out in a plate rather than down in a taproot, and the thing that kills a mature sequoia is almost never fire or disease. It is losing its footing.

### Winter, when the road closes

Mariposa Grove Road closes to vehicles for the winter at the end of November and reopens when the snow allows, which has meant anywhere from early April onward in recent years. The reopening date moves with the snowpack and is not worth planning around more than a week out.

The grove itself does not close. The road and the trails stay open to foot travel, and walking, snowshoeing, or skiing the two miles up from the South Entrance is one of the quietest good days available in Yosemite in February. You will likely have the Grizzly Giant to yourself. Note that this is not a sanctioned snow-play area; the park's designated sledding hill is at Crane Flat, on the other side of the park. The winter guide has the rest of the cold-season picture.

### What the 2018 restoration changed, and why

For three years the grove was closed entirely. It reopened on June 15, 2018, and what came out is as interesting as what went in: the lower-grove parking lot, the gift shop, the pit toilets, and the commercial tram tours that had run through the trees for decades. Roughly four acres of habitat were restored, boardwalks went in over the wet ground, and the wetland hydrology the roads had interrupted was reconnected. The bill came to about forty million dollars, split evenly between the Park Service and the Yosemite Conservancy.

The reason is a single finding from the park's own survey work. The overwhelming majority of young sequoias in this grove, juveniles and saplings both, were growing within about a hundred feet of wetlands. The seeds need bare, wet mineral soil to take. Paving the wet ground and routing traffic across it did not kill the big trees, which is why the damage went unnoticed for a century. It quietly removed the next generation. The piece on sequoias and fire is the natural history behind that, and the two failures are related: a grove can look magnificent and be reproducing at zero.

The trams are not coming back. That is not a scheduling problem or a budget problem. It is the point of the project.

### The rules that catch people out

Dogs are not allowed on any trail in the Mariposa Grove, including the paved ones. This is the rule that surprises people most, because Yosemite's general policy does allow leashed dogs on paved trails, and the Tuolumne Grove up on Highway 120 permits them on its paved section. The Mariposa Grove is an explicit exception. Dogs are fine in the parking lot and are not allowed on the shuttle, which means one adult stays with the car. The pets guide lays out where a dog can and cannot go in this park, and the answer is narrower than most owners expect.

Food stays within arm's reach. The picnic area at the plaza is a well-known bear spot. A daypack left on a table for three minutes is a daypack a bear has learned to check. The bear guide explains why a food-conditioned bear is usually a dead bear, which is the part that should change behavior.

Stay on the trail and off the root plates. See the Bachelor and Three Graces, above. Compacted soil over a sequoia's roots is a slow injury that nobody watches happen.

Bikes are allowed on Mariposa Grove Road but never on the trails, and only while the road is open to vehicles.

Buses and vehicles over about twenty-one feet need their own reservation. They book Mariposa Grove parking separately through recreation.gov; private cars do not. There is no separate fee for the grove beyond park entrance, and there is no park-wide vehicle reservation in effect for 2026.

### Timing, and the parking lot

The Welcome Plaza lot holds a few hundred vehicles and fills on busy days. It is a smaller number than it sounds, because grove visits are long and the turnover is slow: a lot that holds three hundred cars and empties every three hours serves far fewer people than one that turns over every forty minutes. Various sites will tell you it fills by eight, or by nine, or that you must be there by seven thirty. None of those are Park Service figures. The honest version is the same as everywhere else in this park: early morning and late afternoon work, the middle of the day on a summer weekend does not.

For the day itself, allow two hours as an absolute floor, and that only buys the shuttle both ways and the Big Trees Loop. Half a day is right for the Grizzly Giant Loop with time to stand around. A full day is the upper grove. Add the hour each way from the Valley if that is where you are staying, and consider whether the grove wants to be paired with Wawona rather than squeezed onto a Valley day. The one or two day guide takes a position on that trade.

### The short version

- You cannot drive to the trees in season. Park at the Welcome Plaza by the South Entrance and take the free shuttle two miles up.
- The shuttle needs no reservation, runs about every fifteen minutes, and is wheelchair accessible. Its season runs roughly mid-April to the end of November, with no fixed dates published.
- A disability placard lets you drive the road. Accessible parking at the top is very limited.
- Big Trees Loop, three tenths of a mile and wheelchair accessible, is the everyone-can-do-it option. The Grizzly Giant Loop, about two miles, is the one to do if you do one.
- No dogs on any grove trail, paved included. This is an exception to the park's usual rule.
- In winter the road closes to cars and the grove stays open on foot. Snowshoe it.
- Allow two hours minimum, half a day to do it properly, plus an hour each way from the Valley.

The thing worth holding onto is that the inconvenience is the restoration. The two-mile shuttle ride exists because the parking lot was sitting on the wet ground where the next thousand years of this grove was supposed to start. You are being asked to give up fifteen minutes and a parking space in exchange for sequoias that are not yet born. On the list of things this park asks of visitors, that is close to the cheapest.

### Sources

- Mariposa Grove of Giant Sequoias, NPS Yosemite
- Mariposa Grove Welcome Plaza, NPS Yosemite
- Pets, NPS Yosemite
- Accessibility, NPS Yosemite
- Bears and Food Storage, NPS Yosemite
- Mariposa Grove Restoration, Yosemite Conservancy

---

## Parking in Yosemite Valley: Where the Lots Are, When They Fill, and What to Do at Eleven

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-valley-parking-guide
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-06. Last updated: 2026-08-06.
Summary: Where to park in Yosemite Valley: the three day-use lots, when parking fills, what to do when the lots are full, accessible and RV parking, and the 2026 rules.

The most-asked question I get in Yosemite Valley is not about waterfalls or bears. It is asked at about eleven in the morning, through a rolled-down window, by someone on their third slow lap of the same one-way road: where do I park? It is a fair question and it has a real answer, but the answer is not a secret lot. It is a different plan for the day, and the earlier you make it the cheaper it is. This is the whole picture: which lots exist, what they are actually for, when they fill, and what to do when you have already lost that race.

### The three lots that matter

Yosemite Valley is seven miles long and it has three real day-use parking areas. Everything else is a trailhead pullout, a picnic turnout, or a lot reserved for people who are sleeping there. The Park Service's own advice names the three and then tells you what to do next: park at Yosemite Village, Yosemite Falls, or Curry Village, and see the Valley by shuttle, bike path, and trail. That is the entire official strategy, and it is correct.

Yosemite Village parking. The big one, and the default. It sits in the middle of the Valley next to the Welcome Center, the store, the food, and the museum, and it is the hub the free shuttle radiates from. If you have no particular plan, this is the lot to aim at, because everything else in the Valley is reachable from it without moving the car again.

Yosemite Falls parking. On Northside Drive by Yosemite Valley Lodge, and the closest legal parking to the Lower Yosemite Fall trail, which is the single most-walked path in the park. It is a shuttle stop, and it has a bank of Level 2 electric-vehicle chargers, which is worth knowing because there is not much charging in the Valley and what exists gets occupied early.

Curry Village parking. The east-Valley lot, closest to the Mist Trail corridor, Mirror Lake, and the Pines campgrounds. Some Park Service pages and a certain amount of surviving signage still call this Half Dome Village, a name the concessioner used for a few years in the middle of the last decade; it is the same place. Two practical notes: there are no restrooms in the lot itself, and sleeping in a vehicle or camper there is not allowed, which people discover at two in the morning more often than you would think.

A thing the Park Service does not publish, and which I will therefore not invent: space counts. You will find confident numbers for each of these lots on the wider internet. None of them come from NPS, they disagree with each other, and the capacity that matters on any given morning is not the striped total anyway. It is how many people got there before you.

### The trailheads, and why most of them have no parking

The single most common parking mistake in the Valley is driving to a trailhead. Most of the famous ones have no lot at all. Happy Isles, where the Mist Trail begins, is a shuttle stop, not a parking area; there is no drive-up spot at the footbridge and there never was. Mirror Lake is the same. The Valley's trailhead parking is a small, specific inventory documented on the Park Service's trailhead parking page, and a good part of it exists to serve wilderness permit holders leaving a car for several days rather than day hikers arriving at ten.

So the sequence for a Valley hike is: park in one of the three day lots, ride to the trailhead, walk. Not: find the trailhead, then find parking. The Mist Trail piece assumes this and so does every ranger you will ask.

Photo: Cory Goehring

### When they fill

The Park Service's language is careful and worth reading literally: during the busy summer season, especially on weekends, parking fills early and heavy traffic is common in Yosemite Valley. It does not name an hour, because the hour moves. What it does name is a window. Most vehicle congestion happens between ten in the morning and six in the evening, and the official recommendation is to be inside the park before nine, or to wait and come in after five.

Treat that as the outer bound rather than the target. The advice on this site is an hour stricter in both directions, and it is stricter for a reason: on a busy day the lots fill before the congestion window opens, so nine o'clock is already a gamble. Be through the gate by eight, and before seven on a summer weekend. Coming in the other way, four in the afternoon works as well as five. The crowd forecast makes the same case from a decade of visitation data.

In practice, from twenty seasons of watching it: on a July or August Saturday the Valley lots are effectively gone by mid-morning and the ones nearest the trailheads go first. On a Tuesday in October you can arrive at noon and park at Curry Village without drama. Between those two extremes is every other day of the year, and the variable that predicts it best is not the season, it is the day of the week. The Park Service says this too, in its own dry way, by recommending Monday through Thursday.

You do not have to guess on the day. Text YNPTRAFFIC to 333111 to get park traffic alerts on your phone, and check the conditions page before you leave your room, which is where the live entrance-station waits live. Spring through fall, the park's own typical figures run to an hour or two at the South Entrance on Highway 41 and about half an hour at Arch Rock, Big Oak Flat, and Tioga Pass. Those are ordinary days, not the worst ones; a summer holiday weekend can put a queue miles back from the gate. And all of it is time spent before you have parked anything.

### What to do at eleven o'clock

Say the plan already failed. You are in the Valley, it is late morning, the lots are full, and you are on your second lap. Here is the order I would work through, best option first.

- Stop circling and take the next legal space you see, even the wrong one. A space at Curry Village when you wanted Yosemite Falls costs you one shuttle ride. A third lap costs you most of an hour and may end in the same place. The lots do turn over; midday is when the dawn hikers come out.
- Leave and come back at five. This sounds like a defeat and it is the best move on the list. Drive out to a gateway town, eat lunch somewhere with a table, and return in the late afternoon when the day-trippers are leaving and the light is doing the thing you came for. The Valley between five and sunset is a substantially better park than the Valley at noon.
- Go somewhere that is not the Valley. This is now official park guidance and not just local advice: the 2026 congestion strategy explicitly includes promoting recreation outside Yosemite Valley. If Tioga Road is open, the high country has parking when the Valley has none. So does Wawona, so does Hetch Hetchy, and the Mariposa Grove has its own lot at the Welcome Plaza with its own shuttle.
- Park once, then stay out of the car. Whatever space you end up in, treat it as final. The Valley has more than twelve miles of paved bike path, a seasonal bike share that Yosemite Conservancy makes free for short trips, and a shuttle system that reaches everything. The shuttle and YARTS guide covers how that actually works.
- Next time, do not bring the car in at all. YARTS runs into the Valley on Highway 140 year-round and seasonally from Fresno, Sonora, and Mammoth. A bus rider has no parking problem to solve, which is a strange and pleasant way to spend a day in a park where everyone else is solving one.

The reason there is no secret lot is that the Valley is a seven-mile room with granite on both sides. There is no more floor to give.

### Where you may not park

Park in a designated space, or in a paved turnout with the vehicle completely off the road. That is the whole rule, and the two ways people break it are both common. Driving or parking on vegetation is prohibited, which includes the meadow edges that look like they have been driven on before, because they have, and that is the damage. Blocking a travel lane on a road with no shoulder is the other one, and on the Valley loop it is worse than rude: the road is one lane in each direction for much of its length and an emergency vehicle has nowhere to go around you. Rangers cite and tow. In midsummer they do it constantly.

### Accessible parking

Designated accessible spaces exist at each of the main lots and at several of the picnic areas. Two things are worth knowing beyond that. A disability placard is not just a parking credential in Yosemite: it also permits driving on a couple of roads otherwise closed to private vehicles, specifically the Happy Isles Loop Road and Mirror Lake Road, which converts two of the Valley's shuttle-dependent destinations into drive-up ones. And if you arrive without your placard, or your need is temporary, entrance stations and visitor centers issue temporary ones. Our accessibility guide goes through the rest of it, including who to call before you come.

### RVs, trailers, and the vehicles that do not fit

Length limits are enforced by geometry, not by policy, which is why they are absolute. Vehicles over 45 feet are not permitted on the roads into Yosemite Valley at all. Highway 140 through the Merced canyon is the forgiving approach, with no tunnels and roughly 60 feet of combined length allowed; the tunnels on Highways 41 and 120 drop to about 10 feet 2 inches of clearance at the curb, which is where the roof damage happens. Beyond the Sentinel Dome and Taft Point trailhead, Glacier Point Road caps single vehicles at 30 feet and bans trailers outright.

In the Valley itself, the practical answer for a large rig is Curry Village, which has RV parking near its eastbound shuttle stop. The better answer is to leave the rig at the campground and take the shuttle, because a 32-foot motorhome looking for a space in a full lot at noon is the single least happy vehicle in Yosemite.

### One more thing about the loop

The Valley road system is a loop and much of it is one-way. Southside Drive runs eastbound, into the Valley; Northside Drive runs westbound, out of it. This is why the "just circle back" instinct is so expensive here: you cannot turn around and retry a lot you just passed. You commit to the loop and get another look in twenty minutes. Knowing that in advance changes how you drive it. Pick your lot before you enter the Valley, not as you pass it.

### 2026: no reservation, and what replaced it

There is no day-use or peak-hours vehicle reservation for Yosemite in 2026. The systems that ran in most years between 2020 and 2025 are gone, including the February weekend reservations for Horsetail Fall. The park's stated reasoning is that its own 2025 analysis found most weekdays held available parking, stable traffic flow, and visitation inside operational capacity, so a season-wide requirement was not the most effective tool.

What replaced it is a set of operational measures rather than a gate: real-time traffic monitoring, active parking management in the Valley, more staff at key intersections during peak periods, road-condition alerts, and an explicit push toward weekday visits and toward parts of the park that are not Yosemite Valley. The practical translation for a visitor is simple and slightly uncomfortable. Nothing is now rationing the number of cars that arrive at the Valley on a Saturday in July except the number of spaces, and the spaces run out. The reservation system used to make your parking decision for you. Now you make it yourself, at seven in the morning or at five in the afternoon.

### The short version

- Three day lots: Yosemite Village, Yosemite Falls, Curry Village. Aim at Yosemite Village if you have no plan.
- Be through the gate by eight, and before seven on a summer weekend. The official line is nine; the lots do not wait that long.
- Monday through Thursday is a different park from Saturday.
- Do not drive to a trailhead. Park once, then shuttle, bike, or walk.
- Southside Drive is one-way in, Northside is one-way out. Choose the lot before you commit.
- If it is eleven and everything is full, leave and come back at five. It is the best move, not the consolation prize.

The Valley holds what it holds. Every visitor who accepts that at the entrance station has a better day than the one still looking for a space at noon, and the difference between them is not luck. It is an hour.

---

## The Valley Shuttle and YARTS: Yosemite's Two Buses, and When Each One Beats Driving

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-shuttle-and-yarts
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-05. Last updated: 2026-08-07.
Summary: Yosemite Valley shuttle routes, hours and frequency, plus YARTS bus routes and fares from Merced, Fresno, Sonora and Mammoth, and when the bus beats driving.

Yosemite runs two completely different bus systems and most visitors confuse them, which is a shame, because they solve two completely different problems. One is free, green, and only exists inside Yosemite Valley: it moves you between the places you would otherwise drive between, and it is the reason "park once" is sound advice rather than a slogan. The other is a regional coach service that will carry you from a train platform in Merced or a hotel in Mammoth Lakes to a curb in front of Yosemite Valley Lodge, and it is the only way to visit this park without solving the parking problem at all. Here is what each one is, what it costs, and the honest case for when it beats driving.

### The free Valley shuttle

The in-park shuttle is free. There is no ticket, no pass, no tap, and no reservation. You stand at a marked stop, a bus comes, you get on, and you get off wherever you like. This surprises people every summer and I have watched more than one visitor try to hand the driver a card.

It runs daily from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., which is a longer day than most park transit anywhere, and it is split into two routes that both start from Yosemite Village.

The Valleywide Shuttle is the full loop: roughly nineteen stops covering the visitor center, the lodges, the campgrounds, Yosemite Falls, Curry Village, the El Capitan end of the Valley, and the eastern trailheads. Expect a bus about every 22 to 32 minutes. It is the one to take if you are going somewhere west of Yosemite Village or you do not know exactly where you are going yet.

The East Valley Shuttle is the short loop: Yosemite Village, Curry Village, the Pines campgrounds, and the east-Valley trailheads. Fewer stops, so it comes more often, about every 18 to 22 minutes. This is the workhorse for anyone hiking the Mist Trail, walking to Mirror Lake, or camped in the Pines, and it is the bus most visitors actually need.

The practical read on those headways: the shuttle is excellent transportation and mediocre timekeeping. Half an hour is a long time to stand at a stop with a hungry child, and the buses bunch in midsummer when traffic slows them down. Build the wait into the plan rather than treating it as a delay, and check the posted schedule at the stop rather than assuming a bus is two minutes out.

Every bus in the fleet carries a wheelchair lift and tie-downs. Service animals meeting the legal definition ride; pets do not, which is the constraint that shapes a dog-owner's day in the Valley more than any other. Bikes do not go on board either. There are racks at the stops instead, and in season Yosemite Conservancy underwrites a bike share that is free for short trips, which pairs well with the twelve-plus miles of paved bike path on the Valley floor. On a warm afternoon the bike is genuinely faster than the bus.

Photo: Cory Goehring

### The other in-park buses

The Mariposa Grove shuttle is free and, for most visitors, mandatory. When it is running, the grove road above the Welcome Plaza near the South Entrance is closed to private cars, so you park at the plaza and ride about two miles up to the arrival area. Buses come roughly every fifteen minutes, and the season runs roughly mid-April into late November depending on snow. The exception is the one worth knowing: a vehicle displaying a disability placard may drive the grove road, which turns a shuttle-dependent visit into a drive-up one.

The Glacier Point tour bus is not free and not a shuttle. It is a narrated round trip of about four hours from Yosemite Valley Lodge, generally running from early summer into September, and it is bookable through the park concessioner. It is also the standard trick for hiking down the Four Mile or Panorama trails without arranging a car shuttle: ride up, walk down. The loop piece explains why most people should do that in the other direction.

The Badger Pass shuttle runs twice a day between the Valley and the ski area, free, and only while the ski area is open, so roughly mid-December through March.

The Tuolumne Meadows buses are the ones to check rather than assume. The high-country area shuttle and the hikers' bus have both had interrupted service in recent seasons, and the schedules have not been reliably published in advance. Tioga Road opening is not the constraint; it opened on May 15 this year, unusually early. Do not build a Tuolumne day around a bus without confirming it is running that week.

### YARTS: the bus that gets you into the park

YARTS is the Yosemite Area Regional Transportation System, a public transit agency rather than a tour operator, and it runs full-size coaches on four corridors into Yosemite Valley.

Highway 140, from Merced. The backbone, and the only route that runs year-round, seven days a week. It leaves from the Amtrak station in Merced and calls at Mariposa, Midpines, and El Portal on its way up the Merced canyon. Figure about two and a half hours end to end. Because it connects to a train, this is the route that makes a genuinely car-free Yosemite trip possible from San Francisco, Sacramento, or Los Angeles.

Highway 41, from Fresno. Seasonal, roughly late May into late September, calling at Oakhurst, Fish Camp, the Mariposa Grove, and Wawona. This is the route for anyone flying into Fresno, which is the closest major airport.

Highway 120 west, from Sonora. Seasonal, roughly late May into September, through Jamestown, Groveland, and Big Oak Flat.

Highway 395 and Tioga, from Mammoth Lakes. The shortest season of the four, roughly July into September, because it depends on Tioga Pass being open. It calls at Lee Vining and Tuolumne Meadows on the way over, which makes it the only scheduled transit across the crest of the Sierra.

In the Valley, YARTS sets down at Yosemite Valley Lodge, Yosemite Village, Curry Village, and the visitor center stop, all of which are on the free shuttle, so the handoff between the two systems is seamless. You can pay onboard with a card or exact cash, or reserve ahead at the YARTS ticketing site; walk-ons are accepted as space allows, but a reservation a day out is cheap insurance on a summer weekend. Buses are air-conditioned, have a restroom on board, are wheelchair accessible, and will take a bike in the underfloor compartment if there is room and it is bagged. Children under five ride free, one child aged six to twelve rides free with each full-fare adult, and there are reduced fares for seniors, riders with disabilities, and veterans.

### The entrance fee question, which is genuinely unresolved

For years the headline argument for YARTS was that the fare included your park entrance fee, and the Park Service's own pages still say that riders arriving by YARTS do not pay it. YARTS' own fares page currently says the opposite: that applicable Yosemite entrance and non-resident fees are not included in the fare and remain the responsibility of each passenger.

Those are two official sources contradicting each other, and I am not going to pretend to resolve it from a keyboard. The useful advice is the conservative one: budget as though you will pay the entrance fee, and treat it as a bonus if you are waved through. If you hold an America the Beautiful pass the question is moot. This also matters for the $100 per-person non-resident surcharge introduced at the start of 2026, which technically applies to bus riders as well; the trip-cost guide works through that math.

The shuttle solves the day. YARTS solves the trip. Neither one solves the other, and buying the wrong one is how people end up disappointed in a bus.

### When the bus actually beats driving

This is where most transit writing goes soft, so here is the honest version, including the cases where the answer is no.

YARTS wins outright if you are one or two people on a Valley-focused trip. A Merced round trip runs in the mid-forties for an adult at current summer rates, with one-way fares starting around fifteen dollars depending on where you board. Against that, a car costs you fuel, the entrance fee, and the eleven o'clock parking problem. Two people ride, arrive rested, and skip the part of the day everyone else spends circling.

YARTS wins outright if you are arriving by train or plane. Amtrak to Merced and YARTS into the Valley is a real, scheduled, year-round itinerary, and for anyone coming from the Bay, the day-trip piece weighs it against the drive. There is no rental car, no chain requirement in winter, and no need to be the person who drives four hours and then hikes.

Driving usually wins for a family of four. Per-person fares add up fast against a single vehicle entrance fee, and four round-trip adult fares from Merced cost several times what the gate charges a car. If the group is large and the budget is tight, the car is the cheaper answer and there is no point pretending otherwise. Park it once and use the free shuttle, which gets you most of the benefit anyway.

Driving wins if your day starts before the buses do. Dawn trailhead starts, sunrise photography, a Half Dome day: none of these fit a schedule whose first Valley arrival is mid-morning. Anyone chasing first light needs their own vehicle or a bed inside the park.

Driving wins if you are spreading out. YARTS serves a corridor, not the park. If your trip is Glacier Point on Tuesday, Tuolumne on Wednesday, and Hetch Hetchy on Thursday, you need a car. The bus is a Valley tool.

### The short version

- The Valley shuttle is free, runs 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., and comes every 18 to 32 minutes depending on route. No ticket, no reservation.
- Take the East Valley Shuttle for the Mist Trail, Mirror Lake, and the Pines. Take the Valleywide for everything else.
- The Mariposa Grove shuttle is effectively required in season, unless you have a disability placard.
- Confirm the Tuolumne buses are actually running before planning a day around them.
- YARTS runs year-round from Merced and seasonally from Fresno, Sonora, and Mammoth. It drops you in the Valley on the shuttle line.
- Budget for the entrance fee on YARTS, because the two official sources currently disagree about whether the fare covers it.
- One or two people, Valley trip, no car: take the bus. Family of four, multiple districts, dawn starts: drive, and park once.

The park's transportation problem is not that there are too many visitors. It is that there are too many vehicles carrying too few people each, into a valley with a fixed amount of floor. Both of these buses are the response to that, and one of them is free. Using them well is the cheapest upgrade available to a Yosemite trip.

---

## Walk-Up and Day-Of Permits: What You Can Still Get Today

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-walk-up-and-day-of-permits
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-08-04. Last updated: 2026-08-04.
Summary: Walk-up and same-day Yosemite permits: what needs no permit, the last-minute wilderness release, the Half Dome daily lottery, and day-of camping options.

Almost everything written about Yosemite permits is written for someone sitting at home in March with a calendar open. This is written for the other person: the one already inside the park, or checking into a motel in Mariposa tonight, holding nothing. Every guide they find tells them what they should have done twenty-four weeks ago. The useful question is different and nobody answers it. What can I still get today?

The honest answer has three parts. A great deal of Yosemite requires no permit and never did. One important thing has a genuine day-of path that most visitors never use. And one famous thing is simply closed to you, and no amount of showing up early changes that. Knowing which is which saves a day.

### First: most of this park needs no permit at all

Start here, because the permit anxiety around Yosemite is wildly out of proportion to the permit reality.

Getting in. There is no day-use or peak-hours entry reservation for 2026. The systems that ran from 2020 through 2025 are gone, including the February weekend requirement for Horsetail Fall. You pay at the gate and drive in. What is rationing your visit now is not paperwork, it is the number of parking spaces in Yosemite Valley, which is a harder problem than a reservation and one you solve by arriving before nine or after five.

Day hiking. Every trail in this park is open to you today without a permit, with exactly one exception, which has its own section below. The Mist Trail, Yosemite Falls, the Four Mile, Cathedral Lakes, Clouds Rest, the Valley Loop, Taft Point, Sentinel Dome: walk up and go.

Ranger programs. Free, no reservation, no permit. Walks, talks, and evening programs run daily in season and are the single most underused thing in Yosemite. The Park Bulletin carries the current schedule, and the programs guide explains which ones are worth rearranging a day for.

The big set pieces. Mariposa Grove, Glacier Point when the road is open, Tunnel View, the waterfalls, the museum, the Ansel Adams gallery. None of it is ticketed.

Day climbing. A climb you start and finish the same day needs no permit. Overnight big-wall climbs need a wilderness climbing permit, but that one is free, unlimited, and self-issued at a kiosk near the food lockers by El Capitan Bridge, twenty-four hours a day, either the day before or the day you start. It is the least bureaucratic permit in the National Park System.

Fishing. No park permit, but a California fishing license is required for anyone sixteen and older, and non-resident short-term licenses exist. Buy it in the park stores or in a gateway town.

### The wilderness permit, and where the internet stops helping

If you want to sleep out in the backcountry, you need a wilderness permit, and this is where the day-of picture gets specific. Yosemite splits every trailhead's daily quota in two. Sixty percent is awarded in advance through the lottery that opens twenty-four weeks out. The other forty percent is held back and released on Recreation.gov at 7 a.m. Pacific, seven days before the entry date, first come first served. The full permit guide covers how to play that release properly.

Here is the part that matters if you are already here, and it is the detail that catches people. Those last-minute permits stay bookable until they sell out, but not right up to the start date. The park's published reservation window stops taking online bookings a few days out, three by its own reckoning, and whatever the exact cutoff is on the day you look, the practical rule does not move: there is no booking tonight for a walk that starts tomorrow morning. Once you are inside that window, the counter at a wilderness center is the only door left.

After that, one door remains, and it is a narrow one. Whatever quota went unclaimed can be issued in person at a wilderness center on the start date of the trip. The Park Service's own language about this is worth quoting almost exactly, because it is unusually blunt for a government website: while unreserved permits will be available in person on the start date, few, if any, unused permits will be available. That is not discouragement for its own sake. In July, at Happy Isles or Cathedral Lakes, the honest number is zero. Two drainages over, on a Tuesday, at a trailhead nobody has heard of, it is sometimes not zero, and the rangers behind the desk know exactly which ones those are. Ask the question that way. Do not ask whether they have anything for the John Muir Trail; ask what they have at all, and then decide whether you want it.

### Where to stand, and by when

Permits are issued at the wilderness centers: Yosemite Valley, Tuolumne Meadows, Wawona, Big Oak Flat, and the Hetch Hetchy entrance station. Most run roughly 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. in season, and the outlying ones close for the winter entirely, so the Valley center is the reliable year-round door. Two rules ride along with them. A reservation is not a permit; someone in your party has to collect the paper, either the day before or by 10 a.m. on the start date, and an uncollected permit is cancelled and given away. And if you are hoping to catch released quota, be at the counter when it opens, not at lunchtime.

Come with a bear canister or plan to rent one there, and come with an alternate trailhead in mind. Flexibility about where you start is the only currency that works at that desk.

Photo: Cam DiCecca / Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

### Off-season, the whole system relaxes

Roughly November through April, the quota season ends and Yosemite wilderness permits become free, unlimited, and self-issued at trailhead registers. No lottery, no Recreation.gov, no counter. It is the single largest gap between how hard this park looks to get into and how easy it actually is at the right time of year, and almost nobody takes it, because the same weather that opens the door makes the walking serious. Winter in Yosemite covers what you are signing up for.

### Half Dome: the daily lottery is the day-of answer

The cables are the one thing you cannot talk your way onto. Permits are required every day the cables are up, rangers check them at a checkpoint below the subdome, and hiking past it without one is a citation, not a warning. There is no walk-up window, no standby line, and no ranger who will make an exception. You can hike to the base of the subdome without a permit, and many people do, and the view from there is genuinely worth the walk.

But there is a real day-of path, and it is badly publicized. Alongside the March preseason lottery, Yosemite runs a daily lottery every day the cables are up. You apply on Recreation.gov two days before you want to hike, in a window that runs from midnight to 4 p.m. Pacific, and results come by email that evening. Apply Thursday, hike Saturday. It costs ten dollars per application plus ten dollars per person if you win.

The strategic point, for someone already in the park: each day's application is an independent shot, so a week-long trip is several attempts rather than one. Midweek dates in the late season carry the best odds of the entire year. Our Half Dome lottery guide has the success rates broken down by weekday and weekend, which is the number that should decide which day you apply for.

The other route onto the cables is a wilderness permit. Backpackers hold a share of each day's Half Dome allocation, requested and paid for in person when the permit is picked up rather than through the day-hiker lottery, and it applies only from trailheads whose routes plausibly pass the dome. If you were already trying to get a backcountry permit, ask about this at the counter.

### A bed tonight

Camping is the hardest same-day problem in Yosemite and the one with the least satisfying answer, so here is the honest state of it rather than a list that will be wrong by next season.

Camp 4 is the Valley's walk-in campground and the closest thing to a short-notice option here, but it is no longer a queue at a kiosk during the reservation season. Sites release on Recreation.gov on a rolling seven-day window, at 7 a.m. Pacific, and they go fast. That is the shortest booking horizon of any campground in the park, which makes it the one worth setting an alarm for if your trip is long enough to reach seven days out. Outside the reservation season it reverts to first come, first served, which is one of the quiet arguments for a winter trip. The park has changed how it allocates Camp 4 more than once, so check the campground's own page the day you need it rather than trusting anything written in advance, including this.

Cancellations are the real inventory. Recreation.gov releases cancelled sites continuously, and people cancel Yosemite constantly. Refreshing the campground pages in the evening, when the next day's no-shows get released, is a better use of twenty minutes than driving between campground entrances hoping for a sign. The park's own "camping without a reservation" page is the place to start, and the camping guide covers the booking windows in detail.

Outside the park is not a failure. National forest campgrounds line every approach highway, several are first come first served, and dispersed camping is legal in much of the Stanislaus and Sierra national forests. The gateway towns also carry the last-minute motel inventory, and a room in Mariposa tonight beats three hours of driving to campground entrances that are already full.

### The day-of playbook

- Before 8 a.m. If you want any chance at released wilderness quota, be at a wilderness center when it opens with an alternate trailhead written down. If you want to hike anything else, this is also when you should be parking.
- Any time before 4 p.m. Enter the Half Dome daily lottery for the day after tomorrow. It costs ten dollars and takes four minutes, and there is no reason not to do it on your first day in the park.
- Midday. Ask a ranger at the visitor center what is actually available today. This is what the desk exists for and it is a better information source than any website, including this one.
- Evening. Refresh Recreation.gov for campground cancellations. Check your lottery email. Look at tomorrow's ranger program schedule, which costs nothing and requires nothing.
- Tomorrow. The 7 a.m. Pacific wilderness release for the date seven days out is the best permit you can still get. If your trip is long enough to reach that date, take it.

### The short version

- Entry, day hiking, ranger programs, Mariposa Grove, Glacier Point, and day climbing need no permit today.
- Wilderness permits: forty percent releases at 7 a.m. Pacific seven days out, and online booking closes a few days before your entry date, not on it.
- Past that cutoff it is in-person unclaimed quota only, and the Park Service warns there will be few if any. Ask what exists, not what you wanted.
- November through April, wilderness permits are free and self-issued at the trailhead.
- Half Dome has a daily lottery: apply two days ahead, midnight to 4 p.m. Pacific. There is no walk-up and the checkpoint is staffed.
- Same-day camping means Recreation.gov cancellations, Camp 4's short-notice allocation, or a national forest campground outside the park.

The pattern under all of it is the same one that governs this park generally. Yosemite meters the few places everyone has heard of, and leaves the rest wide open. A visitor who arrives with nothing booked and insists on the famous thing will have a bad day. A visitor who arrives with nothing booked and asks what is available will get a permit, a trail, and a campsite, and will probably end up somewhere quieter than the plan they failed to make.

---

## Yosemite in Fall: What Closes, When, and What You Get Instead

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-fall
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-08-02. Last updated: 2026-08-02.
Summary: Yosemite in fall: how September, October and November compare, when fall color peaks, when the Half Dome cables and Tioga Road close, and which week to pick.

Every year around the second week of September, something happens in El Portal that I have come to use as a calendar. The traffic on Highway 140 thins out in the middle of the day. Not at 6 a.m., which is always quiet, and not at 8 p.m., but at 1 in the afternoon, the hour that in July is a slow-moving line of rental cars looking for parking two thousand feet above me. The park does not announce this. It just stops being crowded, the way a restaurant empties after the lunch rush, and for the next eight weeks Yosemite is a place you can walk around in.

Fall is the season I recommend most often and the season people book least. The reason for both is the same: the waterfalls are gone. If your mental image of Yosemite came from a photograph, that photograph was taken in May, and September will look wrong to you. What I want to do here is make the trade explicit, because it is a good trade and almost nobody lays it out honestly. You are giving up water. You are getting back everything else, and you are getting it on a schedule that closes down one door at a time until the park is in winter.

### The trade, stated plainly

Start with the crowds, because the numbers are stark and they are the whole argument. Averaged across 2010 to 2024, July brings about 625,000 people through Yosemite and August about 607,000. September drops to roughly 511,000. October falls to about 389,000, which is a little over 60 percent of a July. November collapses to around 196,000, under a third of the summer peak.

That October figure is the one to sit with. It is not a marginal improvement. It is a different park operating under the same name, on the same roads, with the same granite, and with nearly four in ten of the summer visitors simply absent. Trailhead lots that require a pre-dawn arrival in July have midmorning parking in October. The Mist Trail, which in June is a queue, is a trail again. And with the day-use reservation system retired for 2026, the summer months are absorbing that demand without a throttle, which sharpens the contrast further. The crowd forecast has the week-by-week detail.

Against that, the honest cost. By September, Yosemite Falls is a stain on the cliff or nothing at all. Most of the water in it is snowmelt, and the snow is usually gone by the end of July, so the fall does what the snowpack does. It will not come back in any convincing way until the November storms arrive, and in a dry autumn not until December. If you are bringing someone to Yosemite for the first time and the falls are the reason, fall is the wrong season and no amount of good weather fixes it.

Fall is the best season in Yosemite for everything except the one thing most people come for.

### The calendar is a sequence of closing doors

This is the part that generic fall guides get wrong by treating autumn as a single block of time. It is not. Yosemite in fall is a series of dated and semi-dated closures, and which week you pick determines which park you get. Here they are in order.

Labor Day. The crowd cliff. Nothing closes, but the family-vacation season ends and midweek visitation drops immediately. The first two weeks of September are, in my opinion, the single best stretch of the year in Yosemite: summer access, summer weather, and autumn emptiness at the same time. Everything is still open. Nothing has shut down yet.

Mid to late September. The high country begins closing its services while the road is still open. Tuolumne Meadows Campground typically shuts for the season in late September, and the seasonal store, grill, and visitor services wind down on roughly the same schedule. Tioga Road itself stays open, so you can still drive to Tenaya Lake and Olmsted Point, but you should plan on the high country having no food service and nowhere to resupply. Bring what you need up with you, water included. This catches people who visited in August and assume the same infrastructure is there.

The day after the second Monday in October. The Half Dome cables come down. In 2026 that is Tuesday, October 13. The park targets this date every year rather than fixing it to a calendar day, and conditions can move it, but the rule is reliable enough to plan around. After the cables come down, Half Dome is a technical climb, not a hike, and the permit season is over. If Half Dome is on the list, your fall window closes on a Tuesday in mid-October. The permit lottery guide covers how to get one before then, and the honest assessment of the hike covers whether you want to.

Any storm from mid-October onward. Tioga Road closes when snow arrives, and this is the closure that ruins itineraries, because it has no date. The historical median is around November 3, and in most years the road survives October. But it is a judgment call made on a forecast, not a calendar, and it can happen early: Tioga closed on October 21 in 2021 and on October 29 in 2016. It can also run long, and in the 2011 season it did not close until the following January. Treat every high-country plan after roughly October 10 as conditional, and check the road before you commit a driving day to it. The rest of the park is unaffected, which is the saving grace: a Tioga closure costs you the high country, not the trip.

November. Glacier Point Road closes on roughly the same schedule as Tioga, and once both are shut you are in the winter park: Yosemite Valley, Wawona, Hetch Hetchy, and the plowed roads that reach them, all open, all year. That park has its own case, made in the winter guide. November is the seam between the two seasons and the least predictable month in Yosemite. It can hand you golden black oaks under blue sky or four inches of wet snow, sometimes in the same week.

### Fall color: the received wisdom is wrong

You will read, in more than one place, that Yosemite has no fall color because the trees are conifers. That is half a fact used badly. Most of the forest is evergreen, correct. But the Valley floor is not forest, it is meadow and oak woodland and riparian corridor, and those are exactly the places deciduous trees live.

Four species do the work. California black oak is the backbone, turning gold and then a deep bronze across the Valley meadows, and it is the tree that makes an October photograph of Cook's Meadow look nothing like a July one. Bigleaf maple goes clear yellow and stands out hard against the dark conifers behind it. Pacific dogwood, the same tree that produces the white flowers people drive up for in May, turns red and pink in October, and it is best where its branch structure frames something: El Capitan Meadow and the Cook's Meadow loop are the reliable spots. Black cottonwood lights up yellow along the Merced River, which is why the river corridor is the single best fall drive in the park.

Timing: the show generally starts in early October and runs until the first serious snowstorm ends it. On the Valley floor at 4,000 feet, peak is usually late October into mid-November. That is later than most visitors assume, and it is the source of a specific scheduling irony worth naming. The best fall color in Yosemite Valley arrives after the high country has already closed. Mid-October is the compromise date: decent color starting, Tioga usually still open. Late October and early November trade the high country away for the better color. There is no week that gives you both at their best, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something.

Wawona, at a slightly higher elevation with black oak, dogwood, and maple all mixed together, is the other place worth a deliberate stop, and it is close enough to the Mariposa Grove to make one trip out of two. For where to stand and when the light works, the photography guide has the specifics.

### The two animals that make fall different

This is the part of the season I care most about as a naturalist, and it is missing from nearly every fall guide I have read.

The bears are in hyperphagia. Starting in September, black bears shift into a physiological state of near-continuous eating to build the fat they will overwinter on. The numbers are genuinely difficult to believe: a bear in hyperphagia can take in up to 20,000 calories a day, forage as much as 20 hours out of 24, and put on two to three pounds daily. The park's own bear team has described the daily target in acorn terms, roughly eleven pounds of acorns, which is a useful image for understanding what a bear is doing in a black oak grove in October.

Two consequences for a visitor. First, fall is the best bear-viewing season of the year, better than spring, because the animals are out longer and less cautious. Second, and more important, the Valley bear population goes up in autumn. Large transient males that spend the summer in the backcountry come down to Yosemite Valley, Wawona, and El Portal specifically for the acorn crop. There are more bears near people in October than in July, they are more motivated, and a car with food in it is a more attractive target than at any other time of year. Food storage discipline is not a summer rule that relaxes in the shoulder season, it is a rule that matters most in the shoulder season. The bear guide has the full protocol, including why the bear spray you packed is illegal here.

The deer are in rut, and the deer are the dangerous ones. Mule deer injure more visitors in Yosemite than any other animal in the park, bears included. That fact surprises people every single time I say it out loud on a walk, and fall is when it becomes most relevant. Bucks enter the rut in late autumn, they carry hard antlers, they are running on hormones, and their tolerance for an approaching human collapses. A deer that stood still for a photograph in August will not in November.

The mechanism of nearly every injury is the same and entirely preventable: someone approaches, often someone who has seen other people feeding deer, and the animal defends itself with antlers or with front hooves. In November 2021 a girl approached a buck that visitors had been feeding, and the animal's antlers opened a deep cut on her arm and wounded her chest badly enough that she was moved from the park clinic to a hospital. Fifty yards is the rule, it is the same rule as for bears, and in fall it is the rule that actually gets broken because deer look harmless in a way bears do not. The wildlife guide covers where to watch from.

### Smoke, but the other kind

Autumn is prescribed fire season in Yosemite, and this genuinely surprises visitors who arrive expecting clear skies after wildfire season has ended. Once fall brings cooler temperatures and enough moisture to make burning controllable, park fire crews run planned burns in Yosemite Valley, around Crane Flat, and in the Studhorse units near Wawona. Smoke from those projects is routinely visible in the Valley, in Foresta, and in El Portal.

Two things to hold at once. This is good work, and it is the reason a fire in these units later will not be catastrophic. It also means your October photographs may have haze in them and your throat may be scratchy for a day, and it is not something you can forecast months out, because the burns are scheduled against weather windows and get postponed constantly. The practical move is to check conditions when you arrive rather than planning around it. Note that this is a different phenomenon from summer wildfire smoke, which behaves differently and is worth understanding separately: the smoke season guide covers the geography of how smoke sits in these canyons and the real-time tools for reading it.

### Weather, and the thing that catches people

Yosemite Valley in October averages a high near 71 and a low near 41. That is close to ideal hiking weather, warm enough for shirtsleeves in the afternoon and cold enough that you want a jacket at breakfast. November averages a high of 56 and a low of 33, which is a real change: freezing overnight, and dark early.

The thing that catches people is not the cold, it is the daylight. By late October, sunset in the Valley is early and the walls make it earlier still, because the sun drops behind a 3,000-foot cliff well before it reaches the horizon. A hike that was comfortable in September, started at the same hour, finishes in the dark in November. Carry a headlamp from October onward and treat it as required equipment rather than an optional one. The car kit covers the rest of the shoulder-season load, and the short version is: add layers, add the headlamp, and from late October keep chains in the trunk even if the forecast is clear, because the storm that closes Tioga is the same storm that puts chain control on your drive home.

### How I would actually build the trip

If you want the high country: go in September, ideally the two weeks after Labor Day. Tioga and Glacier Point Roads are open, the weather is stable, Tuolumne is empty in a way it never is in July, and the crowd drop has already happened. Accept that there is no fall color yet and no waterfall to speak of. This is the best week of the year in Yosemite and I will argue about it.

If you want fall color: go the third or fourth week of October. You get color coming on, a real chance the high roads are still open, and Valley crowds at roughly 60 percent of summer. This is the compromise pick and it is the one I recommend to most people. Book flexible lodging, because if a storm shuts Tioga mid-trip you want to be able to restructure rather than cancel.

If you want the park nearly to yourself: go the first two weeks of November. Peak color on the Valley floor, under 200,000 people for the whole month, and a genuine chance of the best photographic conditions of the year, which is fresh snow on the rims above autumn color on the floor. You are giving up the high country entirely and accepting that weather may reroute your days. Go anyway.

Two or three nights is the right length in any of those windows. The short-trip itinerary works in fall with one substitution: swap the waterfall stops for the Valley loop and the river corridor, which is where the season actually is.

### The takeaway

Fall in Yosemite is a season of subtraction. The water goes first, then the high-country services, then the cables, then the roads. What is left after all that subtracting is a park with granite, light, color, deer in rut, bears eating around the clock, and a fraction of the people. That is a fair trade and I would make it every year.

Pick your week by which door matters most to you. If it is Half Dome, you are hiking before October 13. If it is Tioga Road, you are gambling after mid-October. If it is the black oaks going gold in Cook's Meadow with the first snow on the rim behind them, you are coming in November and you are going to have the place almost to yourself. That's the trip.

#### Fall is when the rooms come back

September through November is the availability window that summer does not have. Rates ease after Labor Day and midweek October is a different market from midweek July. If the plan is flexible enough to move around a storm, search your dates both inside the park and in the gateway towns before committing to either.
