## The Bear Spray You Packed for Yosemite Is Illegal

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-bears-safety-guide
Section: Wildlife and Nature. Published: 2026-06-16. Last updated: 2026-06-16.
Summary: Bear spray is banned in Yosemite. So is most of what you think you know about bears. A naturalist's guide to six myths and what actually keeps you safe.

You packed bear spray. You saw it on every packing list for every national park trip you've ever planned. It's sitting in the side pocket of your pack right now, and when you get to the Yosemite entrance station, a ranger is going to confiscate it. Because bear spray is illegal in Yosemite. Not just discouraged. Illegal. Possession and use are both prohibited. It is classified as a weapon under National Park Service regulations, alongside pellet guns and crossbows. This surprises roughly half the visitors I talk to on any given day.

I've worked in this park for close to two decades. I see bears regularly. What I see even more regularly is visitors who have absorbed a set of bear facts from the internet that are confidently wrong, internally contradictory, and occasionally dangerous. People show up with a canister of capsaicin on their hip and a head full of grizzly bear survival tips for a park that has not had a grizzly bear in it since 1895. They've read the wrong guide for the wrong park and prepared for the wrong animal.

### Myth 1: Bear spray works in Yosemite

Bear spray is remarkably effective against grizzly bears. A landmark 2008 study by Tom Smith and Stephen Herrero, published in the Journal of Wildlife Management, analyzed 83 bear spray incidents in Alaska involving 175 people and found it stopped aggressive behavior 92% of the time. That's a better track record than firearms. It's also completely irrelevant here, because there are no grizzly bears in Yosemite. There have not been since around 1895, when the last one was shot near Crescent Lake. The California grizzly has been extinct for over a century.

Is bear spray legal in Yosemite? No. Not in any form, not under any circumstances. The full answer, including the California-wide question, is its own piece.

Yosemite has only American black bears, Ursus americanus, somewhere between 300 and 500 of them. They are a fundamentally different animal in temperament, size, and behavior. An adult male black bear in Yosemite weighs between 250 and 350 pounds. An adult male grizzly can top 700. More importantly, the behavioral profile is different. Grizzlies are territorial and defensive. Black bears are opportunistic and, overwhelmingly, avoidant. The tools you need for each species are not the same.

The NPS ban on bear spray in Yosemite is laid out in the Superintendent's Compendium, which classifies it alongside "pellet guns, BB guns, bows and arrows, crossbows, blowguns, spearguns, spear-fishing equipment, and nets." Possession is prohibited. Use is prohibited. It is a weapon, and weapons are not permitted. The reasons are practical, not bureaucratic. Bear spray is not needed for black bears. The encounters that would theoretically justify it simply do not happen here. A USGS study found that capsaicin residue left on surfaces actually attracts bears. You are not repelling bears; you are seasoning the landscape.

In a park that sees over 3.5 million visitors a year, the risk of bear spray being deployed against humans, intentionally or accidentally, is not theoretical. And the Bear Team will tell you the biggest problem: visitors mis-deploy spray in situations that are not remotely threatening, causing unnecessary harm and stress to bears that were doing nothing wrong.

What works instead is your voice. The Bear Team says it plainly: "Your voice is your most effective tool." The specifics are below.

If you're heading to Yellowstone, Glacier, Grand Teton, or Denali, absolutely bring bear spray. Those parks have grizzlies, and in grizzly country, bear spray is the single most effective deterrent available to a hiker. That fact gets repeated so often and so universally that it has bled into advice for parks where it does not apply. Yosemite is one of those parks. This one does not have grizzlies, does not need bear spray, and does not allow it.

### Myth 2: Playing dead works with black bears

This is grizzly advice applied to the wrong species, and it is the most dangerous myth for Yosemite visitors because people confuse species-specific guidance all the time. With a grizzly, playing dead can work because the majority of grizzly attacks are defensive. The bear perceives a threat, charges, makes contact, and once the threat is neutralized (you, lying still and not fighting), the bear often disengages. The attack is about eliminating a threat, not acquiring food.

With a black bear, playing dead makes you easier to investigate. A black bear that is pushing past avoidance behavior and making contact is almost never being defensive. It is being curious or, in extremely rare cases, predatory. Lying motionless on the ground does not signal "I am not a threat." It signals "I am available."

The correct response to a black bear that will not leave is the opposite of playing dead. Make yourself as large as possible. Yell aggressively. If the bear makes contact, fight back. The NPS official guidance could not be more direct: "If you are attacked by a black bear, DO NOT PLAY DEAD. Try to escape to a secure place. If escape is not possible, try to fight back using any object available. Concentrate your kicks and blows on the bear's face and muzzle."

This distinction matters because people Google "what to do if you see a bear" and get advice written for grizzly country, then apply it in black bear country. There are no qualifiers in the search results. There's just "play dead," floating around the internet without species context, waiting to become a very bad decision.

### Myth 3: Hanging food from a tree works

Yosemite's bears defeated every hanging method decades ago, and the story of how they did it is one of the more entertaining arms races in wildlife management history.

The park first tried the classic rope-over-a-branch technique. Bears chewed through the ropes. Then came the counterbalance system, where you'd hang two equal-weight bags over a high branch so neither could be pulled down from the ground. Bears climbed to the branch and dropped onto the bags from above, tearing them free on the way down. Then the park installed metal food-storage poles in backcountry campsites. An avalanche knocked them down. Rachel Mazur, Yosemite's wildlife branch chief, documented this entire arms race in her book Speaking of Bears, and the progression has a certain comic inevitability to it. Every solution the park tried, the bears solved within a season or two.

The breakthrough came from an unexpected place. Behavioral ecologist Barrie Gilbert was watching a nature documentary one evening and saw a lion pawing uselessly at an ostrich egg on smooth ground. The egg just rolled away. The shape defeated the claws. Gilbert realized a smooth, hard-shelled container could do the same thing for bear-proofing food, and the portable bear canister was born. Bears cannot open them. They try. They roll them around, they chew them, they throw them off cliffs. The canisters hold.

The current regulation is absolute: bear bagging is prohibited in Yosemite. Bear canisters are required for all overnight wilderness trips. You can rent one at any wilderness center in the park for $5 per week. In frontcountry campgrounds, every site has a metal bear box. Use it. These are not suggestions. They are enforceable regulations, and they work.

### Myth 4: Black bears are dangerous to humans

Zero fatal bear attacks in Yosemite's recorded history, going back to the park's establishment in 1890. None.

Across all of North America, the continent's approximately 750,000 black bears kill fewer than one person per year. Dr. Lynn Rogers, who has spent over 50 years conducting field research on black bears, puts the risk in perspective: your chances of being murdered by another human are 60,000 times greater than being killed by a black bear. Since 1900, black bears have killed roughly 60 people across the entire continent. No mother black bear has ever killed anyone defending her cubs. That last point directly contradicts one of the most deeply held pieces of bear mythology, but it is true. Mother black bears bluff-charge, huff, jaw-pop, and retreat. They do not attack.

California did not record its first-ever fatal black bear attack until 2023, and it happened in Downieville, roughly 200 miles from Yosemite, involving a food-conditioned bear that had been drawn to cat food left on a porch. The circumstances were specific and tragic, but they were not analogous to a bear encounter on a trail or in a campground.

What I tell visitors, and I tell them this constantly, is that the river is more dangerous than the bears. The granite is more dangerous than the bears. Your own car, driving tired on Highway 140 at 10 PM after a long day of hiking, is more dangerous than the bears. Yosemite's bears are not trying to hurt you. They are trying to eat acorns and berries and occasionally whatever you left in your cooler. The fear is disproportionate to the risk by orders of magnitude. If you want to worry about something in this park, worry about the heat.

### Myth 5: That brown bear is a grizzly

Are there grizzly bears in Yosemite? No. There have not been for over a century. I hear this question every week during the summer season. A visitor comes up to me, excited and a little scared, and says they saw a brown bear. What they mean is they saw a grizzly. What they actually saw is a black bear that happens to be brown.

American black bears come in black, brown, cinnamon, blonde, and even blue-gray. The name refers to the species, not the color. In the western United States, over half of all black bears are some shade of brown. The variation is genetic, driven by a recessive gene that affects melanin production, and it varies geographically. In the eastern states, most black bears are black. In the West, anything goes.

There are no grizzlies in Yosemite. The last one in the park was shot near Crescent Lake around 1895. The last grizzly in the entire state of California was killed in 1922. The California grizzly has been extinct for over a century. It survives only on the state flag, which is a peculiar kind of memorial.

That cinnamon-colored bear you saw grazing near the meadow at dusk is a black bear. If you want to confirm this, look at the profile. Black bears have a straight facial profile, tall ears relative to their head, and no shoulder hump. Grizzlies have a dished face, smaller ears, and a prominent muscular hump above the shoulders. But you do not need to memorize those field marks for Yosemite. There is only one species here.

A California bill, SB 1305, would fund a roadmap for grizzly reintroduction by 2028. Even if it moves forward, actual reintroduction would be years or decades away.

### Myth 6: Bears hibernate all winter

At Yosemite's elevation, this is not quite right. Black bears enter torpor, which is physiologically distinct from true hibernation. A true hibernator, like a ground squirrel, drops its body temperature to near freezing and cannot be easily roused. A black bear in torpor drops from a normal body temperature of about 100 degrees Fahrenheit to roughly 88 degrees. Its metabolism decreases by about 75%. Its heart rate slows. But it can wake up. It does wake up, sometimes for days at a time.

At Yosemite's mid-elevations, where the Valley floor sits at about 4,000 feet and most campgrounds cluster between 4,000 and 8,000 feet, bears are sometimes active during warm winter periods. Food availability is the primary driver, not temperature alone. A stretch of warm days in January can bring bears out of their dens to forage. They have been documented digging under snow for cached acorns.

This matters practically because it means food storage rules apply year-round, not just during the summer season. If you're camping in Yosemite in November or March, the bear boxes are not decorative. Use them. I have spoken with visitors in late October who assumed the bears were "asleep" and left food on their picnic table overnight. The bears were not asleep. A bear that finds food in winter learns a lesson it carries into the next season and the one after that. Food conditioning is cumulative. Every easy meal makes the next car window look more worth breaking.

### What to do if you see a bear in Yosemite

Here is what actually happens when you encounter a bear, step by step, from someone who has been through it.

Stand up. If you're sitting at a picnic table or crouched by your tent, get vertical. Face the bear. Do not turn your back. Raise your arms above your head to make yourself look larger. Then yell. Not a polite "hey there." Yell aggressively, and keep yelling. "HEY BEAR. GO BEAR. GET OUT OF HERE." Clap your hands. Keep yelling. Do not stop after three seconds because you feel awkward. Most bears leave quickly. The ones that don't, yell louder. Bang sticks on trees. Clap rocks together.

A bear standing on its hind legs is not threatening you. It is investigating. Ears forward and nose raised means curiosity. The bear is trying to smell you and see you better. This is not aggression. Woofing, jaw-popping, and ears pinned back are fear-based displays, and what they indicate, more than anything, is that the bear is scared of you. It is telling you to back off, and you should, slowly.

The NPS says this, and I agree with it completely: "Do you have time to snap a quick picture? No." Put the phone away. I cannot count the number of times I've watched someone stand their ground yelling at a bear with one hand while holding up their phone with the other. The phone is not helping you. It is splitting your attention and keeping you closer to the bear than you need to be. There are better ways to see wildlife in this park than cornering a stressed animal.

Never run from a bear. Black bears can hit 35 miles per hour over short distances. You cannot. Running also triggers a pursuit instinct that standing your ground does not. Never climb a tree. Black bears are arboreal. They climb better than you do, faster than you do, and they started climbing trees before they could walk.

Yosemite bear safety comes down to your voice and your behavior. Report every bear encounter to the park: 209-372-0322. Even if nothing happened. Even if the bear left immediately. The Bear Team tracks every sighting, and the data drives management decisions about where to station rangers, which campgrounds need additional bear boxes, and which individual bears are becoming habituated and need hazing. Your sighting report is not bureaucratic overhead. It is data, and the Bear Team uses every piece of it.

### Yosemite food storage rules nobody reads carefully enough

The Yosemite food storage regulations carry a $5,000 fine, and the definition of "food" is broader than you think.

"Food" means: all food, all coolers (including empty ones), all trash, all toiletries, sunscreen, lip balm, insect repellent, deodorant, medications, and feminine hygiene products. If you put it in your mouth or on your skin, it goes in the bear box. If it has a scent, it goes in the bear box. That is not an exaggeration. It is the regulation, verbatim.

The empty cooler provision is the one that trips everyone up. Bears recognize the shape. A cooler under a blanket in your trunk is still a cooler to a bear that has learned, through years of operant conditioning, that cooler shapes contain food. It does not matter that this particular cooler is empty. The bear doesn't know that, and the regulation doesn't care.

Car storage rules are strict. You cannot leave food visible in your vehicle even during the day. Overnight, everything with a scent must be in the bear box, no exceptions. A bag of trail mix in your glove compartment is a violation. A tube of toothpaste in your center console is a violation. If you're packing your car for Yosemite, plan for this.

Soft-sided vehicles get special rules, and they are not in your favor. You cannot store food in a pop-up camper, tent trailer, or any soft-sided vehicle. Bears can and do tear through canvas and vinyl. Hard-sided RVs and vehicles only, and everything must be closed: windows up, doors shut, roof vents sealed.

The violation fine runs up to $5,000, and it is enforced. Rangers write citations. They write them regularly. This is not a theoretical penalty.

For backcountry trips, bear canisters are required for all overnights. You can rent approved models at wilderness centers throughout the park. BearVault and Garcia are the two brands most commonly available and NPS-approved. Pack the canister at least 100 feet from your campsite, on flat ground, and do not try to secure it with rocks or rope. That just gives the bear something to grip. The smooth container on open ground is the design. Trust it. And pack your canister efficiently. Put dense, calorie-rich food in first. Crush packaging to save space. A well-packed BV500 holds about five days of food for one person if you are not bringing a week's worth of luxury items. If you are planning your first trip, factor canister space into your meal planning from the start.

### Yosemite bear incidents: the data from 1998 to 2026

This is a conservation success story, and I wish I could end it there. I cannot.

In 1998, Yosemite recorded 1,584 bear incidents. Bears were breaking into cars every night. Property damage topped $660,000 in a single year. The park was losing the battle decisively. Bears had learned that visitor cars and campgrounds were reliable food sources, and they had passed that knowledge to their cubs, creating generations of food-conditioned animals. It was a crisis.

The response was systematic and expensive. The park installed over 2,000 metal bear boxes at campsites and trailheads. In 2004, bear canisters became mandatory for all overnight wilderness trips. A massive education campaign reshaped how visitors understood food storage. Open garbage containers were replaced with bear-proof models throughout the park. The "Keep Bears Wild" messaging became pervasive, and rangers began writing citations with real teeth.

It worked. Slowly at first, then dramatically. Bear incidents dropped 95% and property damage dropped 99% from that 1998 peak. By 2019, the park recorded its lowest incident numbers in modern history. The bears that once tore car doors off their hinges were, within a generation, foraging naturally and avoiding developed areas. A UC Santa Cruz isotope study tracked the shift in bear diet and found that human food as a proportion of bear nutrition dropped from 35% during the 1975 to 1985 period back to 13% by 2007, roughly matching pre-tourism levels. The bears were eating bear food again.

But then there is the road.

In 2025, 28 bears were hit by cars in Yosemite. Six were killed. Beth Pratt's 11-year analysis of the data showed an 85.7% rise in vehicle-bear collisions correlating with a 44.9% increase in visitation after the park's reservation system was removed. More visitors meant more cars, more cars meant more miles driven on park roads, and more miles meant more dead bears. In 2026, through mid-year, there have been 5 incidents, with property damage up 316% over the same period in 2025.

The uncomfortable truth is that Yosemite won the food storage fight. Decisively. The bears stopped breaking into cars because visitors finally learned to lock up their food. But the park is now losing the traffic fight. The animals that learned to stay out of coolers are getting killed crossing the road. The Red Bear Dead Bear program has been running since 2007, placing red markers at every vehicle collision site as a visceral reminder to slow down. Wildlife Protection Zones enforce speed limits of 25 to 35 miles per hour. It is still not enough. If you're visiting Yosemite for the first time, drive slowly. That is not a platitude. It is the single most impactful thing a visitor can do for bear conservation in this park right now.

### The takeaway

The bears are not the danger. You, the visitor, are the danger. Your food storage, your driving speed, your willingness to surround a mother with cubs for a photograph.

I have watched people form a semicircle around a sow and two cubs in Cook's Meadow while she stress-huffed and jaw-popped and tried to find an exit. I have watched people sprint toward a bear in Upper Pines Campground with their phones out. I have watched a man chase a bear into the tree line for a better angle. These behaviors are not just reckless. They are the reason bears become habituated, then food-conditioned, then "problem bears," and then dead bears. That escalation is well-documented and entirely preventable.

The best thing you can do for Yosemite's bears is boring. Store your food properly. Drive slowly, especially at dawn and dusk when bears are most active on the roads. Give them space. Fifty yards, minimum. If a bear changes its behavior because of your presence, you are too close, and you are breaking the law.

The best bear encounter is the one where you see a cinnamon-colored bear in a meadow at dusk, watch it graze on grass for ten minutes from 50 yards away, and walk back to your campsite grinning. That's the wildlife encounter you came for. That's the one you will remember for the rest of your life. Not the one where you chased it for a photo and it bluff-charged you. Not the one where it tore into your car because you left a granola bar under the seat. The quiet one. The one where you let it be a bear.

## Yosemite Heat Safety: A Naturalist's Survival Guide

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-heat-safety-guide
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-06-16. Last updated: 2026-06-16.
Summary: How hot does Yosemite get in summer? A naturalist's guide to which trails to avoid, where to swim, and how to stay safe in Yosemite Valley heat.

There's a version of Yosemite that exists in the collective imagination where the weather is always perfect. Golden light, cool breezes, maybe a dramatic cloud or two for the photographs. I've been working as a naturalist in this park for close to two decades, and I can tell you that version exists for about six weeks a year, split between May and October. The rest of the summer, Yosemite Valley is hot. Not Phoenix hot, not Death Valley hot, but a specific kind of hot that catches people off guard precisely because they didn't plan for it.

Yosemite Valley sits at roughly 4,000 feet in elevation, which sounds like it should be cool. It isn't. The Valley is a granite box, roughly seven miles long and a mile wide, with walls that rise 3,000 to 4,000 feet on either side. In July and August, daytime highs reach 90 degrees Fahrenheit regularly and occasionally crack 100. The granite absorbs heat all morning, radiates it all afternoon, and doesn't let go until well after dark. There is no sea breeze. There is no lake effect. There is no relief until the sun drops behind the south rim somewhere around 7 PM. Heat is the thing that catches more visitors off guard than anything else, with the possible exception of the altitude. People pack for postcard Yosemite. They should pack for a stone oven. If you're planning your first trip, this is the piece most planning guides leave out.

Photo: Michael Hogarth / Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

### How hot Yosemite actually gets in summer

How hot is Yosemite in summer? The monthly averages tell part of the story.

Month | Yosemite Valley (4,000 ft) | Tuolumne Meadows (8,600 ft)

June | ~82°F | ~62°F
July | ~90°F | ~72°F
August | ~90°F | ~70°F
September | ~83°F | ~65°F

Those numbers are measured in the shade, at a weather station, which is not where you'll be standing on the Mist Trail staircase at 1 PM. Yosemite summer temperatures are average highs, meaning half the days are hotter.

The averages are misleading in another way, too. Valley floor granite surfaces can hit 140 to 160 degrees Fahrenheit in direct sun. Dark granite, the kind that makes up large sections of the north wall, runs 30 degrees hotter than light granite. When you're hiking a south-facing trail in July, you're not just dealing with air temperature. You're dealing with radiant heat bouncing off every surface around you. Granite walls reflect and radiate heat from three directions. The trail surface cooks from below. And there's nothing to cut it. No wind off a body of water, no altitude-driven cooling, nothing. One hundred degree days happen roughly once a year, usually in late July, but the days that hover at 95 and feel like 100 on exposed granite are the ones that actually fill up the clinic.

### Exposed trails that will cook you

If you're hiking Yosemite in summer, not all trails are equal in the heat, and the differences matter more than most people realize. Some trails that are perfectly reasonable in May become genuinely dangerous in July.

Four Mile Trail, the steep route from the Valley floor to Glacier Point, is the one the National Park Service has specifically called "very dangerous, exposed." It faces south. Long stretches have no shade whatsoever. It gains 3,200 feet in less than five miles. On a 90-degree day, the combination of sustained climbing, direct sun, and radiant heat off the granite makes this trail a heat casualty machine. I have personally helped evacuate people from this trail. Every time, they started too late.

Upper Yosemite Falls trail is the other big one. The first mile, up to Columbia Rock, has some shade and is manageable early in the day. Above Columbia Rock, the switchbacks become fully exposed. You're climbing granite slabs with the Valley wall reflecting heat directly onto you. It's relentless, and there's no water source on the trail.

The Mist Trail above Vernal Fall footbridge is deceptive. Below the footbridge, you get the famous mist from the waterfall, which feels incredible on a hot day. Above it, you get a granite staircase in direct sun. The mist is gone. The shade is gone. You're climbing 600 stone steps with nothing between you and the sky. People don't expect the transition because the lower section felt so refreshing.

Half Dome's subdome and cables sit at 8,800 feet, which should be cooler, and the air temperature is. But the sun at that elevation is unrelenting, the granite reflects it from every angle, and there is nowhere to stop in shade on the subdome or the cables. You're completely committed once you start. Add the physical intensity of the cable climb and the fact that most people have already hiked 8 miles to get there, and you have a serious heat exposure problem even at elevation.

The Panorama Trail, an 8-mile descent from Glacier Point to the Valley, is the one people underestimate most. It sounds easy because it's "all downhill." It's 8 miles of exposed granite with limited shade, and the descent hammers your knees, which makes you drink more water, which you may not have brought enough of.

Here's something most visitors don't know: the heat actually causes rockfalls. A USGS study found that roughly 15 percent of unexplained rockfalls in Yosemite occur between noon and 6 PM from July through September. Thermal expansion of the granite. The rock quite literally swells in the heat and pieces break away. So the trails aren't just hot. They're dropping rocks.

The best strategy is simple and inflexible. The best time to hike Yosemite in summer is before 7 AM. Be done with exposed sections by 10 or 11 in the morning. I know that's early. I know you're on vacation. The window is real, and it doesn't negotiate. Check the best hikes guide for trails that work well with an early start.

### The water math

The NPS guidance says to carry one quart of water per hour of hiking in the heat. That's the official number, and it's fine as a baseline. My real guidance, from someone who has worked here through every July since the mid-2000s, is to carry more than you think you need. A full day on an exposed trail in July means 4 to 6 liters per person. That's heavy. A liter of water weighs 2.2 pounds. Six liters is over 13 pounds of water alone. You carry it anyway.

There's a counterbalancing danger that doesn't get enough attention. Hyponatremia, low blood sodium, happens when you drink too much plain water without replacing electrolytes. Your body dilutes its own sodium levels. The symptoms look a lot like heat exhaustion: nausea, headache, confusion. Which means people sometimes respond by drinking more water, which makes it worse. Carry electrolyte tablets or salty snacks. Trail mix exists for a reason. Pretzels are genuinely good trail food in the heat.

You should know the difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke because one is a bad afternoon and the other is a medical emergency. Heat exhaustion means heavy sweating, nausea, dizziness, pale and clammy skin. You feel terrible. You get into shade, you rest, you drink water with electrolytes, and you recover. Heat stroke means sweating stops. Skin goes red and dry. Confusion sets in, sometimes aggressiveness or slurred speech. This is a 911 call. This is a person whose body has lost the ability to cool itself. Cool them aggressively. Wet clothing, shade, fanning. Get medical help immediately. By some estimates, roughly a quarter of nontraumatic search and rescue missions in Yosemite are dehydration or heat related. That's nearly one in four. You don't want to be in that statistic.

### What to wear on the trail

A quick note on clothing, because what you wear matters as much as what you carry. Light-colored, loose-fitting clothing reflects heat better than dark clothes. A wide-brim hat is not optional. UPF-rated sun hoodies have become standard gear for anyone who works outside in the Sierra, and there's a reason for that: they cover more skin than sunscreen and don't wear off. Speaking of sunscreen, reapply every two hours, and know that the UV at 4,000 feet is already stronger than at sea level, and at 8,000 feet it's meaningfully more intense. The granite reflects UV from below, the thin air filters less of it from above, and the combination will burn you faster than you expect. A bandana or cooling towel soaked in cold creek water and draped around your neck is the single cheapest piece of heat management gear you can carry.

### The escape uphill

The single best heat strategy in Yosemite is also the simplest: go higher. Temperature drops roughly 3.5 degrees Fahrenheit per thousand feet of elevation gain. The math works in your favor quickly.

Tuolumne Meadows sits at 8,600 feet and runs 18 to 20 degrees cooler than the Valley. When it's 90 in Yosemite Valley, Tuolumne is 72. The hiking is better than anything in the Valley, the crowds are a fraction, and the temperature is the kind of summer weather you actually imagined when you booked the trip. Glacier Point at 7,200 feet is meaningfully cooler than the Valley floor, and the views compete with anything you'll see from below. Crane Flat and White Wolf are intermediate options if you want to get out of the Valley heat without driving all the way to Tuolumne.

Tioga Road is the heat escape that matters most. The corridor from Crane Flat at 6,200 feet to Tioga Pass at 9,945 feet drops temperatures dramatically. You can leave the Valley at 95 degrees and be in a light jacket at Olmsted Point an hour later. It's open roughly late May through early November, depending on snow, and in July and August there is no reason not to use it if the heat is getting to you.

Tenaya Lake, at 8,150 feet along Tioga Road, deserves special mention. Cold water, a sandy beach on the east end, and a 20-degree temperature drop from the Valley. It's one of the best places in the park on a hot day. More on swimming spots below.

### Yosemite thunderstorms and lightning safety

Here's where the heat escape gets complicated. The high country that saves you from the heat also has the most dangerous weather in the park.

Sierra Nevada afternoon thunderstorms are one of the most predictable weather patterns in the American West. The mechanism is straightforward. Summer sun heats the granite, the granite heats the air, warm air rises, hits moisture at altitude, and builds into thunderheads. In July and August, you can watch this happen like clockwork. By 11 AM it's common to see cumulus clouds building over the peaks. By early afternoon, those clouds have gone vertical and dark. By 1 PM, lightning.

The rule is simple. Be off exposed ridges, peaks, and open granite by noon. I don't say this as conservative advice. I don't say it as a suggestion. This is the rule. I've watched lightning strike Cathedral Peak from Tuolumne Meadows on a day that started blue and cloudless. The buildup from "nice morning" to "violent electrical storm" can happen in under two hours.

Specific locations where you absolutely do not want to be when lightning starts: Half Dome cables, where you are standing on an exposed granite dome holding a metal cable. Cathedral Peak. Lembert Dome. Any high-country pass above treeline. The summit of Clouds Rest. If you are above treeline and you hear thunder, you are already within strike range.

Lightning safety is not complicated. Get below treeline. Get off water. Get low, not flat, but crouching with your feet together. Don't shelter under a lone tree; it's a lightning magnet. Don't huddle in a group. Spread out so a single strike can't hit everyone. The monsoon pattern typically runs from mid-July through September, with the most intense activity in late July and August. Check the seasonal guide for more on how weather patterns shift through the year.

### Where to swim in Yosemite

Swimming is the best thing about Yosemite in summer that most first-time visitors don't plan for. They come with hiking boots and trail maps. They should also bring a swimsuit and a towel. What follows is the heat-day summary; the full guide to swimming in the Merced covers the season, the flow, the places where swimming is prohibited outright, and what cold water actually does to a swimmer.

The realistic swimming season runs from about mid-July through mid-September. Before that, the Merced River is running too high, too fast, and too cold with Sierra snowmelt. This point is non-negotiable: do not swim in May or June. The river in spring is a powerful, cold, silty current that does not care how strong a swimmer you are. Most river fatalities in Yosemite occur during the high-water period. The water looks inviting. It isn't.

By mid to late July, the river drops to swimmable levels and the water warms enough that getting in is a pleasure rather than a shock.

In the Valley, Sentinel Beach is the most accessible swimming spot. Sandy bank, a picnic area right there, views of Half Dome from the water. It's family-friendly and usually calm by late summer. Cathedral Beach, just downstream, is wider and deeper, with El Capitan framed in the view upstream. Watch the downstream current here, especially earlier in the season. The Housekeeping Camp area has a wider, slower section of river behind Curry Village. Raft rentals are available at Curry Village for the float from Stoneman Bridge to Sentinel Beach, a mellow three-mile drift that may be the best way to experience the Valley on a 90-degree day. Swinging Bridge offers shallow sandy bottoms that are good for wading and casual cooling off, especially with kids.

Outside the Valley, Tenaya Lake is the best subalpine swimming in the park. Sandy beach, clear water, mountain backdrop. The water temperature runs 55 to 60 degrees, which is bracing but tolerable once you commit. Wawona, at lower elevation with a smaller drainage, has the warmest swimming in the park.

The safety rules for swimming in Yosemite are short and absolute. Never swim above a waterfall. Ever. The current accelerates toward the lip in ways you cannot feel until it's too late, and people die this way. Don't swim in May or June. Cold water shock is real; water at 50 to 60 degrees triggers an immediate involuntary gasp reflex on immersion, and the shock response can impair muscle control for up to 90 seconds. Don't swim alone in deep cold water.

### Shady trails along the river

On a hot day, the best hike in Yosemite might be no hike at all. Or rather, the best hike might be a flat, shaded walk along the river where the goal is not a destination but just being outside without suffering.

Sections of the Valley Loop Trail along the Merced River are shaded by black oaks, cottonwoods, and the Valley's dense riparian corridor. The temperature under that canopy can be 10 to 15 degrees cooler than the exposed meadows 200 yards away. The Mirror Lake and Tenaya Creek trail is one of the shadiest walks in the Valley, a flat meander through forest along a creek bed. In late summer, Mirror Lake itself is mostly a sandy flat, but the walk to get there is cool and quiet. The path from Swinging Bridge to Sentinel Beach along the south bank of the Merced is another good one, flat and shaded and never far from water you can wade into.

The Lower Yosemite Fall loop is short, partially shaded, and runs close to Yosemite Creek. In July the waterfall itself is usually reduced to a trickle or gone entirely, but the walk is still pleasant and the creek still has some flow.

The key insight, and this is something it took me years of watching overheated, miserable visitors to fully appreciate, is that the park is not going anywhere. You don't have to summit something every day. On a 95-degree afternoon, a walk along the river in the shade, a swim, a nap under a black oak while staring up at granite walls, that is not wasting your time in Yosemite. That is Yosemite. The wildlife guide has more on what you might spot along the river corridor in summer, mule deer in the meadows at dusk, dippers working the riffles, the occasional coyote. The shade trails are where the animals are, too, because they're not stupid about heat either.

### Your car is also a problem

One more thing that people don't think about until they're living it. Your car, parked in a trailhead lot in full sun for six hours while you hike, will be nearly uninhabitable when you return. Car interiors can reach 130 degrees within an hour on a 90-degree day, and climb past 140 within a couple of hours. The steering wheel will burn your hands. The seatbelt buckle will brand your skin.

Don't leave pets in the car. Don't leave kids in the car. Don't leave medications in the car. Most medications degrade at those temperatures, including insulin, inhalers, and epinephrine. Trailhead parking lots in Yosemite are almost universally fully exposed. There are no covered parking structures. There are very few shaded spots, and they fill first.

Leave a towel draped over the steering wheel. Leave windows cracked if you feel safe doing so. Bring a second shirt to change into, because the dry one will feel transformative after a sweaty hike. And carry an extra liter of water in the car for the drive out. You will be thirstier than you expect.

### The takeaway

The heat in Yosemite is manageable with planning and dangerous without it. That's the whole thing. It's not complicated. Start early. Carry more water than you think you need. Know which trails are exposed and plan your day around that exposure. Know the difference between heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Go uphill when the Valley is a furnace. Watch the sky when you do.

And consider that some of the best summer days in this park have nothing to do with trails at all. A riverside afternoon in the shade. A cold swim at Cathedral Beach with El Capitan turning gold above you. A drive up to Tenaya Lake where it's 70 degrees and the water is clear and the granite slabs are warm enough to lie on but not hot enough to burn. That's Yosemite in the heat, done right. Plan for it and you'll have a story about the best swim of your life. Don't plan for it and you might end up in the back of an ambulance wondering what happened. I've seen both outcomes more times than I can count.

### Sources

- Heat Safety, NPS Yosemite
- Water Safety, NPS Yosemite
- Water Activities, NPS Yosemite
- Weather, NPS Yosemite
- Swimming in Yosemite, Yosemite Conservancy
- Lightning Safety, NPS

## When to Visit Yosemite in 2026: What the Traffic Data Says

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/when-to-visit-yosemite-2026-crowd-forecast
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-06-11. Last updated: 2026-06-11.
Summary: Yosemite has no reservation system in 2026 and is pacing toward its second-busiest year ever. NPS data, a month-by-month forecast, and the best days to visit.

In March, 225,817 people visited Yosemite. That is 45 percent more than the March before it and the busiest March this park has seen since 2016. Nobody who lives here was surprised. The National Park Service announced in late December that the entrance reservation system would not return in 2026, and the visiting public heard it as an open gate. Through April, the park has logged 836,458 visits against 739,313 over the same months last year. Then Memorial Day arrived and gave us the preview: 90-minute entrance lines, the Curry Village lot full by 8:30 in the morning, cars parked on the meadow edges because there was nowhere else to put them.

I made my argument about whether this was a good idea after that weekend. This piece is not that argument. This is the practical question that lands in my inbox every week now: with no reservation system and visitation climbing, when should you actually come?

To answer it properly I went through the National Park Service's visitor use statistics: monthly visitation for the past decade, the year-to-date numbers for 2026, and the gate-by-gate traffic reporting the park publishes in its press releases. Then I built a month-by-month forecast for the rest of 2026. The numbers, the method, and the charts are all below, and so are the specific days I would pick.

### The throttle is gone

Some history, because the data makes no sense without it. Yosemite has spent six years running an accidental experiment in demand management:

- 2020: Covid day-use limits. Visitation collapsed to 2.3 million.
- 2021: Day-use reservations all summer. 3.3 million.
- 2022: Peak-hours reservations, late May through September. 3.7 million.
- 2023: No reservations at all, a record Sierra snowpack notwithstanding. 3.9 million.
- 2024: The broadest system yet: reservations 5 a.m. to 4 p.m. on at least some days from mid-April through late October. 4.12 million.
- 2025: A scaled-back version, 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. from June 15 through August 15 plus the Memorial Day and Labor Day weekends. 4.28 million, the fourth-busiest year ever recorded here.
- 2026: Nothing. No reservation for the gates, and for the first time in years, none for the Horsetail Fall firefall crowds in February either.

Notice the direction of that visitation column. Even with throttles in place, demand has climbed every single year since 2020. The reservation systems never reduced the desire to be here. They moved it, spread it, and metered it. What 2026 removes is the metering, in a year when the underlying demand is the highest it has been since the 2016 record of just over 5 million visits.

### What 2026 looks like so far

Here is the year so far, with my projection for the months ahead, plotted against what 2025 actually did.

Yosemite monthly recreation visits, 2026 actual and projected, in thousands. The line is 2025. Source: NPS Visitor Use Statistics; 2026 figures preliminary. Months without a published figure are estimated from NPS period totals and rounded. Projection: The Talus Field.

The year-to-date math is simple and striking. Through April, 2026 is running 13 percent ahead of 2025. The growth is not evenly spread. January and February ran modestly ahead of last year. March, the first full month after the no-reservation announcement made national news, exploded: up 45 percent, although that comparison flatters 2026 a little because storms held down March 2025. April landed in line with a strong 2025 April. The lesson of the spring is that headlines move visitation, and the headline this year is that Yosemite is open, no ticket required.

My projection for the rest of the year puts 2026 at roughly 4.6 to 4.7 million total visits. If that holds, 2026 becomes the second-busiest year in the park's recorded history, behind only 2016 and ahead of 2019 and 2017. July alone projects to about 665,000 visits, which would be the biggest single month here in nearly a decade.

### What the reservation years actually did

To see why I expect summer to set near-records, look at what the throttles did to the shape of the last two summers.

Monthly recreation visits in thousands: 2024 under the broadest reservation system, 2025 under the scaled-back one, 2026 with none. The 2026 dashed segment is projected. Source: NPS Visitor Use Statistics; 2026 figures preliminary. Months without a published figure are estimated from NPS period totals and rounded. Projection: The Talus Field.

In 2024, with reservations covering 5 a.m. to 4 p.m. across most of the season, July topped out at 596,711. In 2025, with the requirement trimmed to 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. and only eight weeks of coverage, July rose to 628,400 and June to 607,410. Every loosening of the valve has produced more volume, immediately. The park's own August 2025 reporting showed the surge arriving on every road: visitation through the Highway 140 gate at El Portal and the Highway 41 gate at Wawona up about 8 percent year over year, and up more than 10 percent on Highway 120 from the west.

2026 removes the valve entirely in a year that was already pacing at record demand. That is the basis of the dashed line above, and it is why the people who study this park's traffic were not surprised by Memorial Day weekend. The only force left to cap a July Saturday is the road network itself: when the Valley loop saturates, the line simply backs up outside the gates, which is exactly what the two-to-three-hour afternoon delays the park now warns about look like in practice.

### How I built the forecast

The method is deliberately simple, and I would rather show it to you than hide it. I took 2025's monthly actuals as the base. For each remaining month of 2026, I applied a growth rate anchored to what 2026 has already demonstrated: the 13 percent year-to-date pace, damped hard in June, July, and August. The damping matters. March can absorb a 45 percent jump because March has empty road. July cannot, because July was already operating near the ceiling of what the park's entrances, lots, and Valley loop can physically process in a day. For the peak months I assumed 6 to 7 percent growth, which is roughly what the system demonstrated it could swallow when the 2025 restrictions came off in mid-August. Shoulder months got 10 to 15 percent, because that is where the headroom is and where displaced summer visitors tend to land.

Honest caveats: the 2026 figures are preliminary and the Park Service revises them. A bad smoke season can erase an August. A government shutdown, a Merced River flood, a midsummer policy reversal would all bend the curve. This is a forecast built on five months of data, not a promise. But the direction is not in doubt, and the direction is up.

### The crowd calendar

The forecast turns into a usable plan when you break it into days. The grid below is my crowd-pressure index for 2026: projected visits per day, split by weekday and weekend, scaled so that 100 equals a peak July weekend.

Weekday

Weekend

Jan

Crowd pressure, 0 to 100. 100 = a projected July 2026 weekend day. ▲ marks a holiday spike above the bar's value: firefall weekends in February, Memorial Day in May, July 4, Labor Day in September, Thanksgiving week in November, and the holiday week in December.

Crowd pressure by month and day type, 2026. Index derived from actual and projected monthly visitation; weekend days in Yosemite run roughly 45 percent busier than weekdays. Source: NPS Visitor Use Statistics; 2026 figures preliminary. Months without a published figure are estimated from NPS period totals and rounded. Projection: The Talus Field.

Read it month by month, with the second half of the year in mind:

- June: Peak season arrived early this year. Low snowpack pushed the waterfall peak into May, so the falls are already past their best while the crowds are at theirs. A June weekday scores 68; a weekend, 100. Come midweek or not at all.
- July: The projected biggest month in a decade, and July 4 lands on a Saturday, the single worst arrival day of 2026. The week after the holiday, midweek, is merely very busy rather than impossible.
- August: Slightly softer than July, with two asterisks: smoke season is real here in late August, and the falls will be near dry.
- September: The split month. Labor Day weekend (September 5 to 7) behaves like July. The Tuesday after it is a different park: summer weather, open high country, and weekday pressure that drops by a third.
- October: The sleeper, and my answer when people ask for the best remaining window of 2026. Weekday pressure falls to 46, Tioga Road usually stays open most of the month, and the light gets good.
- November: Quiet except for Thanksgiving week, which fills lodging months out. A weekday score of 28 means empty trails by summer standards.
- December through February: The quietest quarter, with two spikes: the holiday week, and the firefall window in mid-to-late February, which now runs without reservations and concentrates thousands of photographers on Northside Drive at sunset.
- March through May (for 2027 planners): Spring is the value play, waterfalls at full volume against half-of-summer crowds, but this year proved spring is where the new growth lands first. Expect next March to look like this year's April.

### The clock beats the calendar

Here is the part the monthly numbers hide: the difference between a miserable Yosemite day and a great one is mostly the hour you reach the gate. The park's traffic guidance is blunt about the shape of the day, and it matches what I see on Highway 140 every morning.

Relative inbound vehicle volume by hour on a busy summer day, stylized from NPS traffic guidance. The busiest entry window runs roughly 9 a.m. to 2 p.m.; afternoon delays can reach two to three hours on peak weekends. Source: NPS Visitor Use Statistics; 2026 figures preliminary. Months without a published figure are estimated from NPS period totals and rounded. Projection: The Talus Field.

It is no accident that every reservation system this park has run gated the same hours. The 2024 system covered 5 a.m. to 4 p.m.; 2025 covered 6 a.m. to 2 p.m. The Park Service has effectively published its own definition of when Yosemite is over capacity, twice. With no system in 2026, you enforce it on yourself:

- Be through the gate before 8 a.m. Before 7 is better on summer weekends. Lots in the Valley fill by mid-morning; on Memorial Day weekend the Curry Village lot was full at 8:30 a.m.
- Or arrive after 4 p.m. Summer light lasts past 8. An evening Valley visit with dinner outside the park beats a noon arrival in every measurable way.
- Never plan to arrive between 9 a.m. and 2 p.m. on a summer weekend. That is the window where the two-to-three-hour entrance delays live.
- Once parked, stay parked. Use the shuttles and bikes; a parking spot in the Valley on a July Saturday is not a thing to gamble twice.
- Text ynptraffic to 333111 for the park's live parking and traffic updates, and check road and lot status before you commit to the drive.

### The days I would pick

If I were planning a 2026 trip from outside the area, in order of preference:

- Tuesday through Thursday, September 8 to 30. The best all-around window left this year. Summer conditions, the full park open, crowd pressure down a third from July, and the falls do not matter because you came for granite and high country.
- Midweek in October. Nearly as good, cooler, quieter, with fall color in the Valley by the back half of the month. Watch for the first Tioga-closing storm, usually November but occasionally late October.
- Midweek in early November, before Thanksgiving. The Valley to yourself at the price of short days.
- Summer, if summer is what you have: any Tuesday or Wednesday, through the gate before 7:30 a.m. A well-executed July weekday beats a badly executed September Saturday. My no-reservations strategy piece covers the full playbook, and if it is your first visit, start here instead.
- The days to avoid entirely: July 3 to 5, every summer Saturday arriving after 8:30 a.m., Labor Day weekend, and the holiday week in December if you are not staying in the park.

### What could bend the curve

Forecasts age badly in public, so let me say what would change this one. If the early-season chaos keeps producing national coverage, some fraction of casual visitors will self-select out and the summer numbers come in under my line. If smoke closes the air in August, that month craters. And if the gridlock gets bad enough, the park retains the authority to manage entries again; the Park Service has said it will manage 2026 with staffed intersections, parking management, and real-time traffic monitoring instead, but that toolkit has limits a busy Saturday will find quickly.

None of that changes the planning logic. Demand for this park rises every year the gate is open, the gate is wide open in 2026, and the only variables you control are the month, the day, and the hour. Choose all three on purpose. The park at 6:45 on a September morning is still the same park that made the record books, minus the line to get in.

## What a Yosemite Trip Actually Costs in 2026

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-trip-cost-budget-2026
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-06-07. Last updated: 2026-08-01.
Summary: What a Yosemite trip costs in 2026: entrance fees, lodging, food, gas, and gear, with real budget, mid-range, and splurge totals.

People ask me what a Yosemite trip costs and I always give the same answer: it depends entirely on how you want to do it. Which is true but unhelpful. So here's the actually helpful version.

I've worked in this park for years. I've watched people do Yosemite for $50 a day and I've watched people do it for $800 a day. Both groups had great trips. The difference isn't quality. It's choices. And the choices are more straightforward than the internet makes them seem.

Let me walk through every cost category, give you real 2026 numbers, and then show you what three very different Yosemite trips actually add up to.

### Entrance fees

The big one that everyone knows about: $35 per vehicle for a seven-day pass. That's per car, not per person. A family of five pays the same $35 as a solo traveler.

If you're visiting more than one national park this year, or if you'll visit Yosemite more than twice, buy the America the Beautiful annual pass for $80. It covers every national park and federal recreation area in the country for a full year. One of the best deals in the federal government.

If you're entering on foot, bicycle, or horse, the fee is $20 per person. Motorcycles are $30 (valid for up to two motorcycles and four people).

New for 2026, and it changes the math for visitors from abroad: since January 1, international visitors pay a $100 surcharge per person age 16 and older, on top of the standard entrance fee. A car of four foreign visitors pays the $35 vehicle fee plus $400. For a group like that, the $250 nonresident America the Beautiful annual pass can pay for itself in a single visit. The surcharge does not apply to U.S. residents.

One thing that simplifies planning: Yosemite is not requiring timed-entry reservations in 2026. In previous years, a reservation was needed to drive in during peak hours. That system is not in effect this year, so the entrance fee is all you pay to get in. Check the current status before your trip, since the policy can change year to year.

### Lodging: the biggest variable

This is where trips diverge. Here's the real range:

Camping (cheapest): $24–$36 per night for a campsite. Valley campgrounds (Upper Pines, Lower Pines, North Pines) are $36. The more remote Tioga Road campgrounds (Tamarack Flat, Yosemite Creek, Porcupine Flat) are $24. Camp 4, the walk-in Valley campground, is $10 per person per night. For a couple, that's $20.

In-park cabins and tent cabins: Half Dome Village tent cabins run $170–$200 per night. You're getting a canvas roof and a cot, but you're sleeping in Yosemite Valley. Hard-walled cabins with bathrooms are $220–$300.

In-park lodges: Yosemite Valley Lodge rooms run $300–$500 per night depending on room type and season (summer rates are highest). The Ahwahnee starts around $580 for a standard room and climbs past $1,400 for suites. (The Wawona Hotel, normally $200–$300, is closed indefinitely for repairs as of 2026.)

Gateway towns: Motels and hotels in Mariposa, Oakhurst, Groveland, and El Portal range from $120 to $300 per night depending on the town and the season. Vacation rentals (Airbnb, VRBO) can be a deal for groups. A cabin that sleeps six for $250 per night is under $42 per person. Rates move with the season and the day of the week, so for real numbers on your dates, a live availability search around the park beats any table of averages, including this one.

The lodging decision is covered in detail in my guide to the gateway towns, but for budgeting purposes: camping saves you hundreds of dollars, and gateway towns save you a hundred or more compared to in-park hotels.

### Food: bring your own or eat in the park

Park food is fine but expensive. Here's what you're looking at:

Casual dining in the park: A deli sandwich and a drink at Degnan's, or a hot plate at Base Camp Eatery in the Valley Lodge, runs $18–$25 per person. Pizza from the Pizza Deck at Half Dome Village is $27–$35 for a pie (medium to large). A decent sit-down dinner at the Mountain Room at Yosemite Valley Lodge is $35–$55 per person.

The Ahwahnee Dining Room: Breakfast is $25–$35 (the buffet runs about $32). As of April 2026, dinner is prix fixe only: $95 for five courses or $125 for seven courses ($135/$165 with wine pairings). Reservations are required; walk-ins are no longer accepted. It's a memorable experience and worth doing once if the budget allows, but it's not an everyday meal.

Camp cooking: If you're camping or staying somewhere with a kitchen, bringing your own food is the single biggest money-saver on a Yosemite trip. A cooler stocked at a Mariposa or Oakhurst grocery store before you enter the park will cost $15–$25 per person per day for three meals plus snacks. I've seen families of four eat well for a full week on $400 of groceries.

The Village Store: There's a general store in Yosemite Village that sells groceries, but prices are 30–50% higher than a regular supermarket. Use it for things you forgot, not as your primary shopping.

My advice: bring a cooler, stock it before you arrive, and plan to eat one meal per day at a park restaurant if you want the experience. Trail lunches of sandwiches, fruit, and trail mix are better than anything you'll buy in the park anyway.

### Gas and driving

The drive to Yosemite is not trivial, and gas costs add up.

From San Francisco / Bay Area: About 170 miles each way. At current gas prices (~$4.75/gallon in California) and average fuel economy (28 mpg), that's roughly $25–$30 each way, or $55–$65 round trip. If you're making a day trip from the city, that's your floor just for fuel.

From Los Angeles: About 280 miles each way. Figure $45–$50 each way, $90–$100 round trip.

From Sacramento / Central Valley: About 170 miles, $25–$30 each way.

Once you're in the park: Gas is available at Wawona and at Crane Flat (both have 24-hour pay-at-the-pump with credit card). There's also a station in El Portal, just outside the Arch Rock entrance. All are expensive, typically $0.50 to $1.00 more per gallon than in gateway towns like Mariposa or Oakhurst. Fill up before you enter. The driving and parking logistics inside the park are their own adventure, but you won't burn much gas on the Valley shuttle loop.

Don't forget parking: Parking in Yosemite is free but competitive. There's no paid parking anywhere in the park. The cost isn't money. It's time.

### Gear: what you actually need

The outdoor industry wants you to believe you need $2,000 of gear to visit a national park. You don't.

Photo: Cory Goehring

Shoes: Sturdy, broken-in shoes with good tread. If you own hiking boots, great. If you don't, a pair of trail runners ($80–$150) will handle every trail in Yosemite except Half Dome. Running shoes and fashion sneakers are genuinely not safe on the steep, wet granite of the park's most popular hikes. This is the one gear purchase I'd say is non-negotiable.

Layers: Yosemite's temperature swings are dramatic. A summer day can go from 40°F at dawn to 95°F by noon to 55°F after sunset. Bring a warm layer (fleece or puffy jacket) and a rain layer even in summer. You probably already own these.

Day pack: Something to carry water, snacks, sunscreen, and a layer. A school backpack works. If you want to buy one, $30–$60 gets a perfectly good pack.

Water bottles: Bring them. The park has water refill stations. Don't buy single-use plastic bottles in the park. It's wasteful and expensive.

What you don't need: Trekking poles (unless you're doing Half Dome or have knee issues), a GPS device (your phone works fine), bear spray (prohibited in Yosemite; the bears here are black bears, not grizzlies), specialized hiking pants, or a $200 headlamp.

Total gear cost for someone starting from scratch: $100–$200 if you're buying shoes and a pack. $0 if you already own reasonable outdoor clothing and a backpack.

### Guided programs and activities

Yosemite Conservancy runs guided programs in the park, including naturalist walks, stargazing programs, and custom adventures, that range from $15 to several hundred dollars depending on the program type and duration.

Free programs: Ranger talks and evening programs are completely free. Yosemite Conservancy naturalist walks and stargazing programs are affordable: sunset walks are $15 per person and stargazing programs are $25 per person. The stargazing programs are some of the best things happening in the park.

Paid guided programs: Yosemite Conservancy custom adventures start at $500 for a half-day (up to four people) and $850 for a full day, with $50 per additional person. Multi-day and specialty programs cost more.

For budgeting, guided programs are optional but genuinely good. If you're a first-time visitor and can fit one into the budget, a guided program with a naturalist who knows the park will change what you see and understand about Yosemite.

### The three budget tiers

Here's what three different four-day, three-night trips look like for two people.

#### Shoestring: ~$400–$550 total ($200–$275 per person)

- Lodging: Campground, $36/night x 3 = $108
- Food: Cooler of groceries from home or a gateway-town grocery stop, ~$25/person/day x 3 days = $150
- Gas: Round trip from Bay Area, ~$60
- Entrance fee: $35
- Gear: $0 (using what you own)
- Dining out: One meal at a park restaurant, ~$50
- Total: ~$403

This is a real trip. A great trip. You eat well, you see everything, and you wake up in the park. Camping in Yosemite is not a compromise. It's the best way to be here.

#### Comfortable mid-range: ~$1,400–$1,800 total ($700–$900 per person)

- Lodging: Yosemite Valley Lodge or gateway-town hotel, $350/night x 3 = $1,050
- Food: Mix of camp-style lunches and park dining, ~$50/person/day x 3 = $300
- Gas: Round trip from Bay Area, ~$60
- Entrance fee: $35
- Gear: Trail shoes if needed, $80
- Guided program: One stargazing program, ~$50 for two
- Total: ~$1,575

This is the trip most people end up doing. Private room, some good meals, a mix of self-guided and guided activities. It's comfortable without being extravagant, and you don't feel like you're pinching pennies the whole time.

#### Splurge: ~$3,500–$5,000+ total ($1,750–$2,500 per person)

- Lodging: The Ahwahnee, $650/night x 3 = $1,950
- Food: Ahwahnee dining room dinners (prix fixe from $95/person) plus nice park lunches, ~$150/person/day x 3 = $900
- Gas: Round trip from Bay Area, ~$60
- Entrance fee: $35
- Guided program: Full-day custom adventure, ~$850 for two
- Extras: Souvenirs, specialty gear, etc. ~$200
- Total: ~$3,995

This is the trip where everything is dialed. You're sleeping in a historic lodge, eating well, and getting the VIP version of the park. It's a special-occasion trip and it's worth every dollar for the right celebration.

### Hidden costs people forget

Bear canisters: If you're backpacking, you need a bear canister. Rent one in the park for $5/week from any staffed wilderness permit station (plus a $95 refundable deposit). Car campers use the bear lockers at every campsite (free).

Tips: Guided programs and sit-down dining. Budget 18–20% on top of listed prices.

The gift shop purchase: Everyone says they won't. Everyone does. Budget $20 for the mug or the patch or the sticker.

### The bottom line

Yosemite can be done cheaply. That's the thing that surprises people most. The park itself doesn't cost much. Thirty-five dollars to get in, free shuttles, free trails, free ranger programs. The expensive part is lodging, and even that is manageable if you camp or stay in a gateway town.

Don't let the cost keep you from going. The people having the best time in this park are not always the ones spending the most money. They're the ones who showed up, planned well, and spent their time outside instead of in a hotel room. If you're starting from scratch, my first-timer's guide to Yosemite ties it all together.

#### The one number this article cannot give you

Every figure above is a range, and lodging is the line item that moves the most: the same room is a different price in October than in July, and midweek is not weekend. Pricing your actual dates takes about as long as reading this paragraph.

Price Mariposa lodging on your dates →
Where to stay: every option compared
