## Yosemite in September 2026: What Closes, and What Gets Better

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-september-2026
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-08-25. Last updated: 2026-08-25.
Summary: Yosemite in September 2026: dry waterfalls, closure dates for the pools, stores and shuttles, Mist Trail weekday closures, and the year's best Half Dome odds.

A man stopped me on the Valley loop in the first week of September last year, holding his phone up with a photograph of Yosemite Falls at full flood, and asked which trail got him to that. The honest answer was a time machine. The fall had been dry for six weeks. He had booked the trip in February off a photograph taken in May, which is the single most common way a Yosemite trip disappoints someone, and it is entirely avoidable.

September is the month the park is quietly at its best and looks, on paper, like it is running out. The waterfalls are down to their bones. The concessions start closing in the first two weeks. The shuttles stop. And underneath all of that, the high country is in the finest condition it reaches all year, the crowds thin out after Labor Day, and the light gets better every week.

Here is what the month actually offers, and what it takes away.

### The waterfalls are done, and that is not a reason to skip it

Yosemite Falls is dry. Not thin: dry. It runs on snowmelt from a shallow basin above the rim, and by September there is no snow left to melt. Mirror Lake is a meadow, which is what it is for most of the year and what surprises people who saw the spring photograph. Bridalveil, Vernal and Nevada still run, because their creeks drain bigger and higher ground, but they run thin.

Go for the walls, not the water. September is the month the Valley stops being about waterfalls and becomes about granite: El Capitan in low afternoon light, the Cathedral Rocks across the meadow, Half Dome catching the last of it. If waterfalls are the reason for the trip, the trip belongs in May, and the waterfalls guide has the month-by-month version of that argument.

### The high country is the reason to come

Tioga Road is open, the whole 39 miles of it, and the high country in September is better than the high country in July: the mosquitoes are gone, the afternoon thunderstorms are less reliable, the meadows have turned, and the crowds have gone back to school. Tuolumne Meadows, Olmsted Point, Tenaya Lake and the Cathedral Lakes trail are all at their best.

With two caveats that catch people out this year. The Tuolumne store and grill close on September 20, which removes the only food and the only reliable indoor shelter along the entire road, and the Tuolumne shuttle and the hikers bus both stop on September 13, after which the high country is drive-yourself. There has never been gas at Tuolumne. Fill up at Crane Flat on the way in and carry lunch, and the month is a gift. The Tuolumne day covers the drive properly, and Cathedral Lakes is the hike to spend a September day on.

### What closes, and when

This is the month the park contracts, and it does it in the first three weeks rather than at the end. The dates worth knowing: Jennie's Ice Cream and the Wawona stable finish on September 6; the Curry Village and Yosemite Valley Lodge pools on September 7; the Tuolumne store and grill on September 20. Of the High Sierra Camps, Glen Aulin and Sunrise close on September 6 and May Lake on September 9, with Vogelsang and Merced Lake shut for the whole season.

Two longer closures run through the month and are not seasonal: the Wawona Hotel and its dining room are closed for renovation, and White Wolf, its lodge, store and dining room, is closed for the season. If either was in the plan, it needs replacing rather than rescheduling. Raft rentals on the Merced are finished for the year.

The practical version: by the last week of September, the Valley still has food and beds and the high country has neither. Plan meals accordingly, and see where to eat for what stays open.

### The Mist Trail is closed four days a week

The most popular hike in the park is closed Monday through Thursday, 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., for repairs running through the end of October. The John Muir Trail detour is signed and adds distance and climbing. If Vernal and Nevada Falls are on the list, plan them for a Friday, Saturday or Sunday, or start very early and be through before seven.

This is the kind of thing that turns a planned day into an improvised one, and it is worth checking again the week you travel: the Park Bulletin carries the current edition's version. The Mist Trail guide covers the hike itself and the detour.

### Half Dome, and the best permit odds of the year

The cables are still up in September and come down the day after the second Monday in October, which makes this the last full month of the season. It is also the best month to apply. Weekday odds in the daily lottery run meaningfully better than weekend odds, and late-season weekdays are the strongest draw of the year: fewer applicants, cooler air, and the same cables. The lottery page has the published numbers and the strategy.

If the permit does not come through, September is also the best month for the alternative. Clouds Rest is higher than Half Dome, needs no permit, and is reachable from Tioga Road while the road is open.

### Fire season, and the air

September sits in the worst stretch of California's fire season, and smoke is the variable that no amount of planning controls. It can turn a clear week hazy in a day and clear again just as fast. Check air quality the morning you drive in rather than the night before, and treat a smoky forecast as a reason to shift a hard hike rather than cancel a trip. Visiting during smoke season covers how to read it and what to do.

Fire restrictions are usually still in force this month: fires only in portable stoves, grills and established rings, never unattended, and out cold before you leave. The restrictions piece has the current rules and how to check them.

### Crowds, and the Labor Day line

The month splits cleanly. Before Labor Day the Valley behaves like August: busy by mid-morning, worse at weekends, and parking gone in the three hubs by nine. After Labor Day it thins noticeably, and by the last week of the month a weekday morning in the Valley is genuinely quiet.

If the dates are flexible at all, take the second half. Same roads, same cables, better light, a fraction of the traffic. That is the whole argument of the crowd forecast, and September is where it pays best.

### What is on in the evenings

The Conservation Heritage Center runs a free evening series through the month: poetry from Tahoe to Yosemite on the 11th, the legacy of the old Yosemite Village on the 12th, the park's mountain lions on the 18th and its bats on the 19th, all at 7:30 p.m. The Moonlight Tour runs its last trip of the season on September 22, ticketed through the concessioner. Tom Killion's woodblocks are up at the Ansel Adams Gallery through September 26, free to walk through.

Ranger programs continue through the month and thin as the seasonal staff leave. The programs piece explains how to find the current schedule, and the Bulletin carries this edition's clock.

### Two Septembers

There is the September people book by accident, chasing a waterfall photograph into a month with no waterfalls, arriving to find the pool closed and the shuttle finished and the Mist Trail shut on a Tuesday. And there is the September people come back for: Tioga Road wide open, the meadows gold, the Valley emptying out after Labor Day, and the best Half Dome odds of the year.

They are the same month. The difference is entirely in what you expected. Start with the basics if this is your first visit, and plan the trip end to end if you want the full framework.

---

## Yosemite in June 2026: Two Junes, One Month

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-in-june-2026
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-06-02. Last updated: 2026-08-06.
Summary: A Yosemite naturalist breaks down June 2026 conditions: low snowpack, no reservations, early waterfall peak, Tioga Road open, and how to plan around all of it.

Every June, I watch the same thing happen. A family pulls into Yosemite Valley at 11 a.m. on a Saturday, spends forty minutes looking for parking, finds a spot at the overflow lot near the stables, walks to Lower Yosemite Fall, takes a photo, and leaves. They drove five hours for ninety minutes in a crowd. They didn't know the waterfalls were already fading. They didn't know the high country was open. They didn't know that two hours north of where they were standing, there were alpine lakes with nobody at them.

June is the month when the Valley is at its most crowded and, in a good year, at its most spectacular. Waterfalls hit their peak. The high country opens. The days are the longest of the year. Everything the park is famous for is happening at once. But with historically low snowpack and no reservation system, this June is shaping up to be the month that separates the visits that work from the ones that don't.

Here is how to be on the right side of that line.

### The waterfalls

The Sierra Nevada snowpack on April 1, 2026 was measured at roughly 18 percent of average, the second-lowest figure in recorded history. I covered what low snowpack means for the park this year in detail. Snowpack is the bank account that funds Yosemite's waterfalls, and this year the account is nearly empty.

In a normal year, warm June days melt the snowpack and send torrents of water over the Valley's granite walls. Yosemite Falls, Bridalveil Fall, Vernal and Nevada Falls all run at or near their peak. This is not a normal year. With so little snow to melt, the waterfalls peaked early. By late May, flows that would normally build through June were already declining. Yosemite Falls typically peaks in late May and can run strong into mid-June in an average snowpack year. In 2026, expect it to weaken noticeably by mid-June and reduce to a trickle by early July. Bridalveil Fall, which has a smaller watershed, will thin out sooner.

If seeing waterfalls at full power is a priority, the first two weeks of June are your window. After that, you are watching the decline. They will still be worth seeing. But the roaring, mist-soaking experience visitors imagine when they picture Yosemite Falls is a narrow window this year, and it is closing fast.

For waterfall-specific hiking, the Mist Trail is still the best way to experience Vernal and Nevada Falls up close. One complication: the National Park Service has announced weekday closures of the Mist Trail corridor beginning June 30 for a rehabilitation project. If you are visiting in late June or July, plan your Mist Trail hike for a weekend day or go before the closures begin.

### Tioga Road and the high country

Tioga Road opened on May 15, 2026, the earliest opening since 2015. In a typical year, it opens in late May or early June, and sometimes not until July. The low snowpack that is shortchanging the waterfalls gave us something in return: early access to the high country.

This matters more than usual in 2026. With no reservation system managing Valley crowds, the high country is the single best pressure valve available to you. Tuolumne Meadows, Cathedral Lakes, Tenaya Lake, the Dana Fork, Lembert Dome: these places are two hours from the Valley floor and they are a different park entirely. I drove up on the opening weekend and counted eight cars at the Cathedral Lakes trailhead at 9 a.m. on a Saturday. That same morning, the Valley had been full since 7:30. If your trip overlaps with a Valley gridlock day, Tuolumne is the answer.

Cathedral Lakes is the signature Tuolumne day hike and one of the best in the park. The trail to Lower Cathedral Lake is about 3.5 miles one way with roughly 1,000 feet of gain, ending at a granite-rimmed alpine lake beneath Cathedral Peak. In early June it may still have snow patches on the upper trail. Bring traction devices if you are hiking before mid-month.

Tuolumne Meadows Lodge opens June 5. The Tuolumne Meadows Store and Grill opens on the same timeline. This is also prime wildflower season: the meadows should be blooming by mid-June, though the compressed snowmelt may push the peak earlier and shorter than usual.

Entering through Tioga Pass from the east side is also in play now. If you come over the pass from the Eastern Sierra, you can spend a full day in the high country without ever touching the Valley.

### Glacier Point Road

Glacier Point Road opened on May 9, another early opening. This gives you access to Glacier Point itself, Sentinel Dome and Taft Point, and the full Glacier Point Road experience.

It also opens the option I recommend to almost every June visitor: hike Four Mile Trail up and Panorama Trail down. This is the single best day hike in Yosemite, and in June you get waterfalls at every turn. Vernal and Nevada Falls are both visible from the Panorama Trail, and Illilouette Fall, which most visitors never see, is at its best in early June. Start by 7 a.m. to beat the heat on the Four Mile ascent.

### Crowds in June 2026

There is no way to sugarcoat this. June 2026 is shaping up to be the most crowded month in the park in years. The reservation system is gone, and the numbers reflect it. More than 836,000 visits were recorded through late May, roughly 100,000 more than the same period last year. On Memorial Day weekend, Valley parking lots were full by mid-morning and entrance waits exceeded ninety minutes.

I wrote about why the park needs a reservation system. For planning your June trip, here is what you need to know:

Arrive before 7 a.m. On any Friday through Sunday, and especially on holidays, Valley parking lots will fill early. If you arrive at 10 a.m. on a Saturday, you will not find parking at any major trailhead. This is not an exaggeration. I watched it happen every weekend in May.

Park once and use the shuttle. The free Valley shuttle runs two routes, the Valleywide about every 22 to 32 minutes and the shorter East Valley about every 18 to 22, and between them they stop at every major trailhead, the Visitor Center, Curry Village, and the Ahwahnee. Getting around the Valley without moving your car is a skill worth learning before you arrive.

Visit midweek. Tuesday through Thursday, the park is a fundamentally different place. If you have flexibility, this is the single biggest quality-of-life improvement you can make. If you are still deciding where to stay in or near Yosemite, booking midweek dates also opens up more lodging options.

Go outside the Valley. The Valley floor absorbs roughly 90 percent of Yosemite's visitors. Hetch Hetchy is fifteen minutes from the Big Oak Flat entrance and rarely crowded. Wawona and the Mariposa Grove are on the south end. The Merced Grove has almost no one in it. And with Tioga open, the entire high country is available. Plan at least one full day outside the Valley.

If you arrive in the afternoon, the day is not wasted. The golden hour in Yosemite Valley in June starts around 6:30 p.m. and lasts until sunset around 8:25. Some of the best light and thinnest crowds of the day happen between 6 and 8 p.m.

### Bears in June 2026

Bear-related property damage in Yosemite increased 316 percent year over year according to recent park reporting. Drought years make wild food scarcer. When natural berry and nut crops are thin, bears look for alternatives. Your cooler in the back seat is an alternative.

Bear-proof food storage is not optional. Every campsite in the park has a bear box. Use it. Every piece of food, every scented item (toothpaste, sunscreen, lip balm), and every cooler goes in the box when you are not actively holding it. If you are day-hiking, do not leave food visible in your car. Not in a bag. Not under a blanket. Not in the trunk of a sedan, which a bear can pry open in under a minute.

A bear that learns to associate cars with food is a bear that eventually gets killed. I do not say that to be dramatic. I say it because it happens every year in this park, and every year it starts with someone who thought the rules were suggestions.

### What to pack

June in Yosemite Valley means daytime highs typically between 80 and 90 degrees Fahrenheit. The high country runs 15 to 20 degrees cooler. Mornings in the Valley start around 50 to 55 degrees and warm fast.

Your day pack for a June hike needs at minimum two liters of water per person for any hike over four miles, sun protection (the granite reflects everything), and a layer for elevation. If you are spending a full day in the high country, bring a real jacket. Afternoon thunderstorms are possible in Tuolumne by late June, and they move in fast at 8,600 feet.

The Merced River will be swimmable in some sections by mid to late June. In a low snowpack year, it warms up earlier. Check current conditions before wading in. Early June flows can still be fast enough to be dangerous even in a drought year.

### Two Junes

June 2026 in Yosemite is a compression event. Low snowpack pushed everything earlier: the waterfalls, the road openings, the wildflower bloom, the bear activity. No reservations pushed everything more crowded. The result is a month where the park is both more accessible and more strained than in recent memory.

If you are visiting in the first two weeks, you will see waterfalls and wildflowers and the high country waking up and the Valley at its most alive. If you are visiting in the last two weeks, the waterfalls will be fading, the Mist Trail may be partially closed, and the heat will be climbing. Both versions of June are worth the trip. But they are different trips, and planning for the one you are actually getting is the difference between a great visit and a frustrating one.

Start with the basics if this is your first time. Plan your trip end to end if you want the full framework.

The people who have the best June trips are not the ones who see the most. They are the ones who showed up knowing what kind of June they were walking into. This year, that matters more than it usually does.

Plan accordingly.

---

## Cathedral Lakes: the high-country day hike worth driving up for

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/cathedral-lakes-day-hike
Section: Trails and Hikes. Published: 2026-06-02. Last updated: 2026-06-02.
Summary: Cathedral Lakes is the best day hike in Tuolumne Meadows. Trail distance, elevation, best months, and how to hike Lower and Upper Cathedral Lakes in Yosemite.

The first time I sat on the granite shelf above Lower Cathedral Lake, late July, midday, I watched a yellow-bellied marmot sun itself on a rock for forty minutes while a chickaree complained from a hemlock about thirty feet behind me. Cathedral Peak rose straight out of the lake on the opposite side. There were maybe nine other people in sight, spread across a hundred acres of granite shoreline. The water was 55 degrees, glacially clear, the inverted reflection of Cathedral so sharp on a windless day that the picture you take with your phone looks like one of those puzzles where you can't tell which side is up.

This is not a hike that will surprise the people who already know it. Cathedral Lakes has been one of Yosemite's standard high-country day hikes since John Muir camped on the shoulder of Cathedral Peak in 1869 and described it in My First Summer in the Sierra as "one of Nature's cathedrals, hewn from the living rock." It is on every best hikes in Yosemite list. It still earns the listing.

What follows is how to do it well, what to actually look at, and the parts of it that almost nobody mentions.

### Cathedral Lakes trail distance, elevation, and trailhead

The Cathedral Lakes trail starts at the new Cathedral Lakes trailhead parking adjacent to the Tuolumne Meadows Visitor Center. The old trailhead at the side of Tioga Road was retired during the Tuolumne Meadows redevelopment, so the trail distances in older guidebooks read about three-quarters of a mile shorter than the current reality. For a broader look at the trailheads and routes in this area, and for the shorter walks that suit a day when this hike is too much, see Tuolumne Meadows in a day.

Current numbers, from the new trailhead:

- Total distance: roughly 9 to 10.5 miles round trip, depending on whether you visit Lower Cathedral Lake only, Upper Cathedral Lake only, or both.
- Elevation gain: about 1,000 to 1,400 feet of cumulative gain.
- Trailhead elevation: about 8,500 feet.
- Lower Cathedral Lake elevation: 9,288 feet.
- Upper Cathedral Lake elevation: 9,585 feet.

The trail begins flat through the meadow approach, then climbs steadily through lodgepole pine forest for about three miles, gaining most of its elevation in this stretch. It crests on a forested bench where a signed junction points right to the lakes and continues straight along the John Muir Trail toward Sunrise. The Lower Cathedral Lake spur descends about a half-mile through forest to the lake's outlet stream. Upper Cathedral Lake sits in a granite bowl a few hundred yards past the junction, directly below Cathedral Peak.

Plan five to seven hours for the round trip, including real time at the lakes. This is a hike where the lakes are the destination, not waypoints.

### Best time to hike Cathedral Lakes

Tioga Road has to be open, which means you're working with a window that runs roughly late May or early June through October or early November, depending on snow. In 2026, Tioga Road opened May 15, well ahead of the long-term average.

The Cathedral Lakes trail itself is not fully accessible the moment Tioga Road opens. The upper portions of the trail and the lake basins hold snow into late June or early July in normal years and into mid-July in heavy-snow years. If you're hiking before the second week of July, expect significant snow on parts of the trail and at the lakes. Bring a map. Be willing to turn around.

The best hiking conditions are typically mid-July through mid-September. Wildflowers in the meadows and forest understory peak in late July. The lake water reaches its warmest temperature (still cold) in early August. Fall light starts to change the character of the basin in mid-September.

This is one of the busier high-country day hikes. On summer weekends, the trail at peak hours can feel like a parade. The lakes themselves are large enough to absorb the crowd, and you can almost always find a granite shelf to yourself along the shore. But if you want solitude, weekday hikes or early starts (trailhead by 7 a.m.) are dramatically better. If you're basing yourself in the Valley or a gateway town, the drive to the trailhead takes roughly 90 minutes from Yosemite Village via Tioga Road. For getting around Yosemite by car, this is one of the drives that's worth it.

### What to see on the Cathedral Lakes trail

The trail itself is more interesting than most guidebooks make it sound. Here's what to notice, in the order you'll encounter it.

The first half-mile through the meadow. The approach crosses the edge of Tuolumne Meadows. In July, this stretch is one of the better wildflower walks you'll get all day. Look for shooting star, paintbrush, columbine, lupine, and the yellow Sierra wallflower in the open patches. Sandhill cranes have been documented on the meadow floor in spring. Mule deer and the occasional black bear are regular.

The forest climb. Three miles through dense lodgepole pine, with mountain hemlock mixing in at higher elevations. This is the unglamorous middle of the hike, but it's where most of the bird life is. Western tanagers, Cassin's finches, mountain chickadees, and several warbler species all use this forest. The chickarees (Douglas's squirrels) will let you know when you're close to their cone caches. Stop walking for thirty seconds and listen. The forest is louder than you think.

The lodgepole bark beetles. Look at the trunks of the lodgepoles as you climb. Many have the characteristic exit holes and pitch tubes of mountain pine beetle activity. The Sierra has been losing significant lodgepole stands to beetle outbreaks driven by warmer winters and drought-stressed trees, and the Cathedral approach is part of that larger pattern. The standing dead trees you walk past are not scenery. They're an ecological transition still playing out.

The Cathedral Peak view. About two miles in, the trail breaks out of forest and gives you the first clear view of Cathedral Peak. Stop. Cathedral Peak is one of the most distinctively shaped peaks in the Sierra, a slender granite spire with two main summits, and the reason for 150 years of religious-architecture metaphors that no one can seem to resist.

The trail junction. At about three miles, the spur trail to Lower Cathedral Lake branches right while the John Muir Trail continues toward Sunrise. The junction is signed. Take Lower Cathedral first if you're doing both lakes. The descent and re-ascent is real, and you don't want it on tired legs at the end of the day.

Lower Cathedral Lake. The outlet stream is on your right as you descend. The lake opens up suddenly, and the south shore, approached via a granite ramp, is the vantage point you've seen in photographs: Cathedral Peak rising directly across the water. The lake is deep enough to swim, cold enough to shock, and large enough that even with twenty other people scattered around the shoreline you can find a quiet shelf.

The granite slabs above the lake. Scramble up the slabs west of the outlet and you get a higher perspective with almost guaranteed solitude. This is where the marmots tend to sun themselves. The view extends across the basin and down toward Tenaya Canyon.

Upper Cathedral Lake. Smaller, with Cathedral Peak even closer overhead. The setting is more enclosed, the water colder, the mood different. Many hikers visit only the Lower. Doing both gives you two readings of the same basin, and the Upper is the quieter one.

Cathedral Peak itself. The rock you're looking at is a particular granodiorite called Cathedral Peak Granodiorite, named for this peak. Geologists know it for having unusually large potassium feldspar crystals, commonly 2 to 3 inches long, embedded throughout the rock. Walk up to the slabs and look closely. The feldspar phenocrysts show up as off-white blocky crystals studding the gray-pink groundmass. This is the same rock that makes up much of Tuolumne's high country. You've been walking on it all day.

The peak is climbable. The standard route is a fifth-class climb of about 700 vertical feet from the base, often done as a long day from Tuolumne. Muir made the first recorded ascent in 1869 in work boots, alone. The Park Service does not encourage casual visitors to attempt it. If you have climbing experience and want to try, get current beta from the Yosemite climber community before going.

### The Muir connection

John Muir camped here in late summer 1869 during his first season as a sheep tender in the high country. His journal entries from those weeks became the basis of My First Summer in the Sierra, published forty-two years later. The book includes the description of Cathedral Peak as "one of Nature's cathedrals, hewn from the living rock," and his solitary first ascent. He climbed it in work boots, carrying nothing.

Muir returned to this basin repeatedly over the next few decades. He wrote about it in multiple books. The Cathedral region became a touchstone in his evolving argument for wildland protection, an argument that eventually reached a president and reshaped the boundaries of what became Yosemite National Park.

Sitting on the granite at Lower Cathedral Lake, you are sitting in roughly the same place Muir sat in 1869. The basin has not been logged. The lake has not been dammed. The peak has not been turned into a tourist attraction. That continuity is part of what makes this hike feel like more than a hike.

### What to bring on a Cathedral Lakes day hike

The day pack basics are covered elsewhere. The Cathedral-specific version: carry three liters of water minimum, because there's no reliable potable water between the trailhead and the basin. Bring layers. Late July at 9,500 feet can be 75 degrees and clear or 50 degrees with a thunderstorm building in the same afternoon, and the wind off the lake at midday can be sharp. A rain shell is not optional in July and August; afternoon thunderstorms are common and develop fast, so plan to be off exposed granite by early afternoon if storms are in the forecast. Sun protection matters at this altitude. UV at 9,500 feet is intense and the lake basins are exposed.

Bring a real lunch. Sitting at the lake for an hour is part of the trip. A sandwich is better than a bar.

Day hikers don't need a bear canister, but secure your food when you stop. Black bears occasionally work the trails near the lakes, especially in the food-conditioning patterns that develop when too many hikers leave snacks unattended.

### Common mistakes

The main John Muir Trail continues from the Cathedral Lakes junction up over Cathedral Pass and on toward Sunrise. It is tempting to keep going. Don't, unless you've planned for it. Most day hikers should stop at the lakes and be content with that. (If you do want to keep going, see the through-hike section below.)

If you're camping, know the rules: campfires are prohibited at Lower Cathedral Lake, all camping must be at least 100 feet from water and trails, and you need to be at least four trail miles from Tuolumne Meadows. A wilderness permit is required for any overnight stay. If you're planning an overnight, see packing for a Yosemite backpack.

Don't swim before July. The water is too cold and snow patches around the lake make the shore slippery and unstable. The lake does not fully ice out in many years until late June. And don't rely on the trail being clear of snow before mid-July. I've seen the upper switchbacks buried into early July in heavy-snow years. Bring traction devices if you're hiking before mid-July, and be willing to turn around at the snowline.

### Cathedral Pass to Sunrise: the through-hike option

If you have the legs and the logistics, the through-hike from Tuolumne Meadows over Cathedral Pass to Sunrise High Sierra Camp or the trailhead at Tenaya Lake is one of the great Yosemite point-to-points. Roughly 13 miles with significant elevation change, crossing the high meadows above Cathedral Lakes that almost no day hikers see. You need a shuttle or a very understanding friend with a car at the far end. It is a serious day, not casual. But the high meadows above the lakes, with Cathedral Peak behind you and the Clark Range opening to the south, are worth the commitment.

### Why Cathedral Lakes is worth the drive to Tuolumne

Cathedral Lakes is the standard high-country day hike from Tuolumne for a reason. The trail is good. The destination is real. The peak is one of the most photogenic and historically resonant in the Sierra. If you're still planning your Yosemite trip, this hike belongs on the short list.

Plan an early start, bring a real lunch, sit on the granite for an hour after you arrive, and look closely at the rock under your hands. The crystals you're sitting on were cooling underground when this part of California was still under shallow seas. The peak above you was first described to a wider world by a Scotsman with a notebook in 1869. You are sitting in good company.

### Sources

- Cathedral Lakes Trailhead, NPS Yosemite
- Tuolumne Meadows and Tioga Road, NPS
- Geology of the Yosemite Area, USGS
- My First Summer in the Sierra, by John Muir (1911)

## Yosemite needs a reservation system

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/yosemite-needs-a-reservation-system
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-05-26. Last updated: 2026-05-26.
Summary: Without a reservation system, Memorial Day 2026 left Yosemite Valley gridlocked and its meadows damaged. Why the park needs timed entry back.

I built this guide so people can enjoy their national park. I want them to see the Valley at sunrise, hear a hermit thrush at dusk, watch a bear graze a meadow edge in October. I want them to have an experience good enough that they go home and care about public lands for the rest of their lives. That is the whole point.

This Memorial Day weekend made it clear that without a reservation system, none of that is possible at Yosemite.

### The mission, in plain language

The National Park Service was created by the Organic Act of 1916. The mission statement is one sentence long, and it has governed every national park in the country for 110 years:

"...to conserve the scenery and the natural and historic objects and the wild life therein and to provide for the enjoyment of the same in such manner and by such means as will leave them unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations."

Read it again. There are two mandates in that sentence: conserve the resource, and provide for enjoyment. Not one or the other. Both. And the second mandate comes with a condition: enjoyment must happen in a way that leaves the park unimpaired for the people who come after us.

Yosemite without a reservation system is currently failing on both counts.

### Failure one: people cannot enjoy their park

On Sunday of Memorial Day weekend 2026, visitors received a text alert at 7:39 a.m. telling them that parking lots in Yosemite Valley were already full. By mid-morning, the entrance stations had wait times exceeding ninety minutes. By evening, as one visitor told ABC7, "the entire park, it was impossible to park there. There's nowhere to park for anybody."

This is not an exaggeration and it is not an isolated incident. Since the reservation system was dropped for the 2026 season, Yosemite has recorded more than 836,000 visits through late May, roughly 100,000 more than the same period last year. March 2026 visitation jumped nearly 45 percent over the previous year. On peak days throughout the spring, Valley parking lots have been filling by 7 a.m.

When the lots fill, access to the eastern half of the Valley, including the Mist Trail, Happy Isles, Mirror Lake, and the Ahwahnee, becomes limited or effectively impossible for anyone arriving by car. The free shuttle system helps, but only if you can find a parking spot to begin with.

Think about what that means for the family that drove three hours from the Central Valley on their one day off. They arrive at 10 a.m. because they didn't know the lots fill by seven. They circle for an hour looking for parking. They give up and drive home, or they park illegally and get towed. Either way, they did not recreate in their national park. The Organic Act's promise of enjoyment was a dead letter for them.

The reservation system, which Yosemite ran in various forms from 2020 through 2025 (every year except 2023), was not perfect. It required advance planning. It frustrated some spontaneous visitors. But it did something essential: it spread the demand across the day so that the people who showed up could actually use the park. Under reservations, the Valley felt, for the first time in decades, like a place where you could park your car, walk to a trailhead, and breathe. That was not a minor improvement. That was the park working the way it was designed to work.

### Failure two: the resource is being damaged

Memorial Day weekend 2026 was not just inconvenient. It was destructive.

Videos from the holiday weekend showed dozens of cars parked illegally on meadow edges and road shoulders throughout the Valley. Visitors, unable to find legal parking, drove off pavement and onto the ground. Three tow trucks were deployed simultaneously to clear illegally parked vehicles from shuttle routes. Beth Pratt, a conservationist and author who has worked on Yosemite wildlife issues for years, described the scene plainly: people were "pulling onto meadows, pulling off pavement, going off-road."

Yosemite's meadows are not grass fields. They are complex ecosystems, home to rare sedges, native grasses, and invertebrate communities that have evolved over millennia in the Sierra's specific hydrology. A car driven onto a wet meadow compresses the soil, destroys root systems, and creates channels that alter water flow. The damage from a single vehicle can take years to recover. Multiply that by dozens of cars across a holiday weekend, and the cost to the resource is not theoretical. It is visible.

This is the second failure. The Organic Act does not say "conserve the scenery unless the parking lot is full." It says conserve. Period. And the condition on enjoyment, that it must leave the park "unimpaired for the enjoyment of future generations," means that when overcrowding causes direct, physical damage to the resource, the park is violating its own founding mandate. Cars on meadows is not a parking problem. It is a conservation failure.

### The data we already had

None of this is surprising. We have data that tells us exactly what happens when reservation systems work, and exactly what parks lose when they are removed.

At Arches National Park, a Utah State University survey of more than 500 visitors during the 2022 timed-entry pilot found that 84 percent of respondents wanted the reservation system to continue. Fifty-seven percent said timed entry made their experience "somewhat or much better." Eighty-nine percent of visitors were able to get a ticket, 98 percent entered on their desired day, and 86 percent received their preferred time slot. By any measure, the system worked for visitors and for the park.

In Yosemite, a March 2026 survey by the employee union found that 85 percent of 135 verified staff responses did not approve of Superintendent Ray McPadden's decision to drop the reservation system. These are the people who work in the park every day. They saw the reservation system work across five seasons. They know what the alternative looks like.

The alternative is what we saw this weekend.

### Who made this decision

On February 18, 2026, Superintendent Ray McPadden announced that Yosemite would not require vehicle reservations for the 2026 season. He cited park data suggesting that "a season-wide reservation requirement is not the most effective approach for the coming season," pointing to weekday parking availability and manageable traffic flow on non-peak days.

That analysis is technically true and practically meaningless. Nobody was arguing that Tuesday mornings in April needed reservations. The problem has always been weekends from May through September, and especially holiday weekends. A season-wide evaluation that averages peak and off-peak days together will always dilute the severity of the peaks. It is an analytical choice that obscures the very problem it should be addressing.

The decision also did not happen in a vacuum. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum's Secretarial Order 3426, issued in April 2025, directed the National Park Service to keep parks "open and accessible" and required superintendent-level closures or service reductions to be reviewed by the NPS Director and the Assistant Secretary. The National Parks Conservation Association called the order "ill-conceived," warning that it "flies in the face of responsible management of national parks, risking both visitor safety and the very resources the Park Service was created and is mandated to protect." Four major parks dropped their reservation systems for 2026: Yosemite, Arches, Glacier, and Mount Rainier. Rocky Mountain National Park, notably, kept its timed entry in place.

Superintendent McPadden said the park would rely on "real-time traffic monitoring" and promotion of areas outside the Valley. Those are fine supplemental tools. They are not substitutes for managing the number of vehicles that enter the park on a given day. You cannot real-time-monitor your way out of a parking lot that filled three hours ago.

### Why this matters beyond Yosemite

I write this guide so that people can plan a visit that works. I tell them to arrive early. I tell them to pack their car right. I tell them where to go when the Valley is full. I do this because I believe that a good experience in a national park is the beginning of a lifetime of caring about public land.

But there is a limit to what planning can fix. When the infrastructure cannot support the number of people who show up, no amount of advice about arriving before sunrise will solve the problem. The family that got turned away, the couple that spent ninety minutes in an entrance line, the solo hiker who watched cars drive onto a meadow: those people did not have a good experience. Some of them will not come back. And a person who drives away from a national park angry is a person who stops caring about national parks.

The reservation system was imperfect. It needed refinement, not elimination. Dynamic pricing, better shoulder-season incentives, improved cancellation policies, expanded public transit: all of these were available paths forward. Dropping the system entirely was the wrong call.

The data supports reservations. The staff supports reservations. The visitors, when surveyed at parks that had them, overwhelmingly support reservations. The Organic Act demands that enjoyment and conservation happen together. Right now, Yosemite is delivering neither.

I will be back out in the Valley tomorrow morning. If it is anything like this weekend, the parking lots will be full by seven, the meadow edges will have tire tracks in them, and a family from Fresno will be circling Yosemite Village wondering why they came. That is what the absence of a reservation system looks like from inside the park.

---

## So you decided to come to Yosemite on Memorial Day. What are you thinking?

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/memorial-day-skip-the-valley-go-high-2026
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-05-20. Last updated: 2026-05-20.
Summary: Yosemite Valley will be gridlock on Memorial Day weekend 2026. Tioga Road and Glacier Point Road are open early. Skip the Valley, go to the high country.

So you booked Yosemite for Memorial Day weekend 2026. Bold. The first reservation-free Memorial Day since 2019, the unofficial start of summer, every Bay Area family with a long weekend and the same idea you had. Brave.

Here is the good news: you can still have a spectacular trip. Here is the short answer, the one thing almost nobody arriving this weekend will do: skip Yosemite Valley and go up to the high country instead. Both Glacier Point Road and Tioga Road are open early this year, so the best places to be on Yosemite's Memorial Day weekend are 4,000 feet above the crowded Valley floor. Pivot. Don't even think about the Valley.

I'm not being dramatic. Let me show you the shape of the problem, and then let me show you the way out, because this year the way out is better than usual.

### Yosemite Valley crowds on Memorial Day: a parking lot. Literally.

The National Park Service dropped the day-use reservation system for the 2026 season. No cap on cars, no gate to stop you. Sounds great until you remember that the parking lots are the same size they were in 2019 and the Valley is still seven miles long. The constraint didn't disappear. It just moved from the entrance gate to the parking lot.

We already got the preview. On Saturday, May 2, 2026, a normal early-May Saturday before the season had really started, every parking space in Yosemite Valley filled by 10:59 a.m. Memorial Day weekend will be three to four times busier than that. Saturday morning is the worst of it. The Park Service knows this; it's been bracing the public for an "extremely busy weekend" and openly telling people to go anywhere but the Valley floor: Tuolumne Meadows, Wawona, the high country.

That's the rare moment where the rangers and I agree completely. So listen to us both. Go up, not in.

### Why the Yosemite high country is the move this year

Most years, telling you to skip the Valley for the high country in late May would be a cruel joke, because the high country would still be under snow with the gates locked. Not this year.

It was a thin snow year, the roads got plowed early, and both of the great high routes are already open weeks ahead of schedule:

- Glacier Point Road opened May 9, 2026, one of its earliest openings in years.
- Tioga Road opened May 15, 2026, the earliest opening in sixteen years. (Tioga typically doesn't open until late May or even June.)

So while ten thousand people fight for a parking space 4,000 feet down in the Valley, you can be standing on a granite dome with Half Dome at eye level and almost nobody around you. That is not a consolation prize. On a holiday weekend, it's the better trip.

(One quick check before you commit: high-country roads can still close briefly in a late-season storm. Text "ynptraffic" to 333111 the morning you go, and don't trust whatever a stale web page tells you about road status.)

### Option 1: Glacier Point Road, the biggest view for the least effort

Turn off Highway 41 at Chinquapin and drive the road to its end. Glacier Point itself sits 3,200 feet directly above Curry Village. A paved, stroller-friendly path leads to an overlook with Half Dome at eye level, the whole Valley floor below you, and Vernal and Nevada Falls stair-stepping up the Merced canyon. It is the highest reward-per-step view in the entire park, and on an early-season weekend you may have the rail nearly to yourself.

Want to actually stretch your legs? Two of Yosemite's best short hikes share a trailhead a few miles before the end of the road:

- Sentinel Dome. About 2.2 miles round trip, roughly 400 feet of climbing, topping out at 8,122 feet on a bare granite summit with a true 360-degree panorama: Half Dome, El Capitan, the Cathedral Range, the Clark Range, the Sierra crest. Grandparents can do it. Six-year-olds can do it. Pick this one for the view and the photo.
- Taft Point. Also about 2.2 miles round trip, mostly easy, ending at a mostly unfenced clifftop and the Taft Point Fissures, deep granite cracks that drop away as much as 2,000 feet beneath your boots, with the viewpoint itself perched some 3,000 feet above the Valley floor. It is thrilling and it is genuinely dangerous: every accident here comes from someone stepping too close for a photo. The view from six feet back is identical to the view from one foot back. Stand back.

Can't decide between them? We wrote a whole piece on how to choose, and you can link the two into one quiet loop. Don't bother with the Four Mile Trail down to the Valley this year, by the way; it's closed for 2026.

A couple of honest notes: there's no drinking water at Glacier Point and the snack stand may not be open yet, so bring a full water bottle and a sandwich. And the tour bus up here doesn't start running until mid-June, so this is a drive-yourself trip for now.

More: Glacier Point Road just opened for 2026

### Option 2: Tioga Road (open 2026), the high country two months ahead of the Valley

If Glacier Point is the easy headliner, Tioga Road is the adventure. Highway 120 climbs east through the park to Tioga Pass at 9,945 feet, and right now it's a ribbon of pavement through a high country still pulling itself out of winter. You'll see country that's a solid two months behind the green Valley you drove away from. A few stops to build a day around:

- Olmsted Point (about 45 minutes in from the Valley side). The moment the high country opens up in front of you, and the only place you'll see the back of Half Dome, with Clouds Rest and Tenaya Canyon spread out below. Watch your footing; there can still be snow and ice near the point in late May.
- Tenaya Lake (8,150 feet). An alpine lake right off the road. It'll likely still be ice-rimmed this early, which is its own kind of beautiful. The east-end beach is a flat, easy stroll to the water, no real hike required.
- Tuolumne Meadows (8,600 feet). The vast subalpine heart of the high country at the foot of the Cathedral Range. Stand at the edge and let the mountains do the work. Two short legs are reliable this early: Pothole Dome at the west end (a one-mile scramble up polished granite to a meadow panorama) and the flat walk to Soda Springs and Parsons Lodge (about 1.5 miles round trip, naturally carbonated springs the kids will love). Stay on the paths. The meadow is soaked and fragile this time of year.

Save the big alpine hikes for your next trip. Cathedral Lakes and the other classic Tuolumne destinations are still snowbound and won't be reasonable until late June or July. Bookmark the Cathedral Lakes day hike for later.

The catch up here is self-sufficiency. The road is open, but Tuolumne Meadows itself is barely awake: the store, grill, and campground aren't open yet, there's no gas anywhere past Crane Flat, and no reliable drinking water along Tioga Road this early. Fill the tank, pack all your own food and water, and store it in a bear locker. Bring layers, including a packable insulated jacket. Sunny afternoons hit the low 60s, but nights drop to near freezing at this elevation, and an afternoon thunderstorm is possible.

More: what to expect on Tioga's opening weekend

### A few practical things

No day-use reservations are required to enter Yosemite in 2026. That's exactly why the Valley will be slammed, and exactly why a card-in-the-glovebox high-country plan beats the crowd. Your entrance pass is $35 per vehicle, good for seven days, and the park is cashless. Bring a card. One bonus: Memorial Day Monday, May 25, is a fee-free day, so if you can swing a Monday visit, it's both the cheapest and the lightest of the three days.

And if your plans go sideways anyway (lots full, weather turns, a road closes), don't fight the park. Flex. There's almost always a great option the crowd hasn't thought of. (The Valley's marquee hike, the Mist Trail, gets weekday afternoon restrictions starting June 30, but over Memorial Day weekend it is fully open and will be mobbed.)

### What I'd tell a friend

Skip the Valley on Saturday. Genuinely, skip it. Get up early, point the car uphill, and spend the morning on Glacier Point Road or Tioga Road while everyone else circles a full parking lot 4,000 feet below. You will not get the classic head-craning-up-at-the-falls Valley shot this trip. You'll get something better: a high granite view with room to breathe, on the one weekend of the year when that's the smartest thing you can possibly do.

Welcome to Yosemite. You made it harder than it had to be, but you can still get this right.

Some links in this piece are affiliate links. If you buy or book through one, The Talus Field may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. The recommendations do not change for it. Full disclosure.

---

## Where to Eat in Yosemite: Every Area, and What Closes When

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/where-to-eat-yosemite
Section: Planning. Published: 2026-05-19. Last updated: 2026-08-28.
Summary: Restaurants in Yosemite Valley, Wawona, Fish Camp and the gateway towns, plus every place open around Mariposa in August 2026. From a resident who eats in them.

Food is the part of a Yosemite trip that visitors plan least and complain about most. The Valley is not a culinary destination. Most of the gateway towns aren't either. But there are eight or nine places across the region worth driving to, a shorter list worth eating at when you are already nearby, and a set of facts about where food exists at all that nobody tells you until you are hungry at 8,600 feet with the nearest open kitchen an hour away.

I live in El Portal. I eat in these places. The recommendations are not affiliate links and they are not sponsored. If a restaurant is not recommended here, it does not mean it is bad; it means I have nothing useful to say about it. Chains exist. Chipotle exists in Oakhurst. If you need a Chipotle, you will find one. That is not what the recommendations are for. Separately, further down, there is a complete roster of what exists in the Mariposa area, which is a different thing and worth having.

### Is there food in Yosemite National Park?

Yes, but almost all of it is in one square mile. Yosemite Valley has the park's only real concentration of food service: eleven counters, decks and dining rooms clustered in Yosemite Village, at Yosemite Valley Lodge, and around Half Dome Village. Outside the Valley the park thins out fast. Wawona has a general store. Tuolumne Meadows, up on Tioga Road, has a seasonal store and grill and the dining tent at Tuolumne Meadows Lodge, all of which close in September. Crane Flat and El Portal have small markets. Yosemite West, despite the name and the vacation rentals, has no restaurant, no store, and no gas.

Two practical consequences. If you are staying anywhere other than the Valley, plan on either a drive or a cooler. And if you arrive after about 9 p.m., assume everything is shut: this is a national park, not a town, and the kitchens keep park hours.

### Where to eat in Yosemite Valley

Half Dome Village Pizza Deck. The Half Dome is the order: house pepperoni and ricotta with fennel and a chili oil drizzle. Eaten on the wooden deck under the granite face of Glacier Point Apron at the end of a long day, beer on tap, picnic tables, and a line of people who have been doing the same thing all summer. There is almost always a wait, and the wait is part of the experience. This is the only restaurant inside the park I would go out of my way to eat at. It is not the best pizza in California. It is the best pizza in Yosemite Valley by a wide margin, and on the right summer evening it is the best meal of the trip. The location is officially Half Dome Village; most people still call it Curry Village.

Base Camp Eatery, Yosemite Valley Lodge. The busiest room in the park and the one most visitors actually eat in, which is why leaving it off a list is a disservice even when nobody drives to it. It is a food court: order at touchscreen kiosks, collect at a counter, sit at a long communal table. Grill, pizza, a hot line, breakfast from early. The value in it is throughput and hours, not cooking. At 7 a.m. on a July morning it is the fastest hot breakfast on the Valley floor, and at 8 p.m. it is often the last kitchen still taking orders. Plan meals around that second fact more than the first.

Degnan's Kitchen, Yosemite Village. The only place inside the park to get a halfway decent lunch for under twenty dollars. Order a sandwich at the counter, take it outside, eat it on a bench. The bread is real, the meat is fine, the line moves. If you forgot to pack a cooler, Degnan's is the fallback that does not feel like a fallback. A coffee and a breakfast sandwich there at 7 a.m. is also one of the better moves in the Valley if you slept inside the park. Upstairs in the same building, the Loft at Degnan's is a seasonal sit-down room with a bar, a wood-fired oven and an actual roof, and it is the answer to the question people ask on the third rainy afternoon: where can we sit indoors, inside the park, that is not a hotel dining room.

The Half Dome Village cluster. Four separate operations share one compound and get treated as one place, which is why visitors think Curry Village has a pizza deck and nothing else. Meadow Grill Taqueria, at the Village Store, is counter-service tacos and burritos beside the deck, outdoor seating, and the shortest path from a trailhead to a hot meal on the Valley floor. Coffee Corner opens early and is the reason you do not have to drive to Yosemite Village for a coffee before a Mist Trail start. Bar 1899 is the small indoor bar. Seven Tents Pavilion is the big buffet hall, mostly serving the tent-cabin guests. All four are seasonal to some degree, and the taqueria is usually the first Valley kitchen to close when the summer ends.

The Mountain Room, Yosemite Valley Lodge. The Valley's sit-down dinner option short of The Ahwahnee: a proper dining room with a wall of glass pointed at Yosemite Falls. Reservations are worth having in summer, and the falls are worth timing: the view is the reason to book this room rather than the food.

The Ahwahnee Dining Room. The special-occasion meal that does not require driving to Oakhurst. As of April 2026 the Ahwahnee moved to prix fixe only, five courses at $95 a person or seven at $125, dinner service, reservations required. This is not a spontaneous stop. If the night calls for it, book ahead. The room itself, thirty-four-foot ceilings and granite piers, is most of what you are paying for, and it is worth it once.

There is also a Starbucks in Yosemite Village, attached to the Village Store, which arrived in 2018 and generated more correspondence than any other food decision the park has made. It is a Starbucks. It has the shortest line in the Valley when the Degnan's counter is twenty deep, and that is the entire case for it.

### Wawona, Fish Camp and the south end of the park

The south end is thin and getting thinner. The Wawona General Store is the reliable one: groceries, sandwiches, the sort of resupply that turns a day trip into a picnic, twenty minutes from the Mariposa Grove. The Wawona Hotel dining room has kept an intermittent schedule in recent seasons, so do not build an evening around it without checking that week.

Two miles south of the gate, Fish Camp covers what Wawona does not, and it is closer than most people staying at the south end realise. Embers at Tenaya Lodge is the sit-down dinner, the nearest real restaurant to the Mariposa Grove, and Jackalopes, the bar in the same building, takes the walk-ins when Embers is booked. The Pine Tree Market and the Fish Camp General Store handle groceries and a sandwich. Past that you are driving to Oakhurst, another fifteen minutes down Highway 41.

### Tuolumne Meadows and the high country

This is the section that strands people. Tuolumne Meadows has a seasonal store and grill and the dining tent at Tuolumne Meadows Lodge, a canvas room serving breakfast and a fixed dinner with reservations, and that is the entire food supply along thirty-nine miles of Tioga Road. All of it opens with the summer and closes in September, in the 2026 season on September 20, several weeks before the road itself closes for the winter. There is no gas at Tuolumne either: the Tuolumne day covers that trap in full.

Plan the high country as a cooler day. Buy food at Crane Flat on the way up or in Lee Vining on the way over, eat it on a granite slab, and treat anything you find open at 8,600 feet as a bonus rather than a plan.

### Yosemite West restaurants: there are none

Yosemite West is a residential subdivision inside the park boundary off Wawona Road, and it is almost entirely vacation rentals. It has no restaurant, no store, no gas station and no shuttle. Guests are frequently surprised by this, because the booking listings emphasize the location and not the logistics. From Yosemite West the nearest food is the Valley, roughly forty minutes down and back, or Wawona, roughly half an hour south. If you are staying there, shop before you arrive. A full kitchen and an empty valley are a good combination only if you brought groceries.

### Restaurants near Yosemite: the gateway towns

Mariposa is the western gateway with the most restaurants, the most parking, and a downtown you would walk after dinner. Three of them are worth planning around.

1850 Restaurant & Brewing Co., Mariposa. The sit-down dinner option in town. Wood-fired pizzas, a burger that is genuinely good, a short list of house-brewed beers, and a patio that fills on summer evenings. Closed Monday and Tuesday. Service can be slow when the dining room is full; the food is worth it.

Smokin Oak BBQ, Mariposa. Opened in late 2024; the adjacent Twisted Cedar Tap House followed in early 2025, pouring mead, beer and cider on draft. Brisket cooked the right number of hours, served on butcher paper. Sides are the usual lineup, all competent; the slaw is the one to get. Closed Monday and Tuesday. Lunch is the move. By 7 p.m. they are often sold out of brisket and the move shifts to the pulled pork, which is also fine.

Tacos Sonora, Mariposa. A taco truck permanently parked at 5034 Coakley Circle. Fast, cheap, and exactly what it should be. Two carne asada tacos and a horchata, no frills, no table to sit at. The post-hike, pre-drive, no-decisions-required option. Open weekdays until 7 p.m., Saturday until 4 p.m., closed Sunday.

El Portal is the last stop on Highway 140 before the Arch Rock entrance, and it has more than its size suggests: the Cedar House Restaurant and the Canyon Bar at the Yosemite View Lodge, the River Restaurant at the Cedar Lodge, and Parkside Pizza. None of them is a reason to drive out of the park, which is the only reason none is on the list above, but all four are open to the public and not just to lodge guests, and on a night when the Valley kitchens have shut they are twenty-five minutes closer than Mariposa. The market here is the one I shop at and the last fuel and groceries before the gate.

Oakhurst is the southern gateway and the largest gateway community by population. It also has more chain restaurants than any other gateway combined. Skip those.

South Gate Brewing Company, Oakhurst. The post-park dinner default for visitors based in Oakhurst, Bass Lake or Fish Camp. Wood-fired pizzas with dough stretched to order, Blonde Ale-battered fish and chips, a long list of their own beers, and a dining room with enough seating to absorb a Saturday night without a two-hour wait. Vegan and gluten-free options exist and are not afterthoughts. Closed Tuesdays. The default answer for "where should we eat" in Oakhurst.

The Elderberry House at Chateau du Sureau, Oakhurst. The fine-dining option, and the only restaurant in the region that is its own destination. Erna Kubin-Clanin opened the place in 1984 and the kitchen is still doing a rotating multi-course prix fixe that changes daily, with optional wine pairings out of a cellar that is taken seriously. Well over $100 a person before wine, and reservations are required well in advance. This is the anniversary dinner, the last-night splurge, the meal you build the rest of the day around.

Latte Da Cafe, Lee Vining. The east-side breakfast and coffee stop. Coming over Tioga Pass from Mammoth or Bishop or down from Lake Tahoe, this is the first real coffee on the route in either direction. The pastries are made in-house, the drip is honest, and the staff is the kind that remembers you the second time. Park behind the building, walk in, eat outside. Going east on a Tuesday in July, this is where the trip starts.

Groveland, on Highway 120, has a historic main street with the Iron Door Saloon on it and enough places to eat for a two-night stay. It is off the Mariposa roster below because it is in Tuolumne County, not because there is nothing there. Where to base yourself is a bigger question than where to eat, and the gateway towns comparison answers it properly.

### Everything that exists, by area

The recommendations above are opinions. This is not. The roster below is the August 2026 revision of the Mariposa eating-out list, a single sheet kept current locally and handed out at visitor desks and lodge counters. It records what exists and roughly where, nothing more: no hours, no prices, no judgment, and inclusion is not a recommendation from anybody, including me. It is useful for the thing a review list cannot do, which is tell you that a town of four hundred people has a cafe in it at all. Names are as the sheet prints them where a business's own styling is unclear.

One caveat before the list. It covers Mariposa County plus Fish Camp, which is why Oakhurst, Bass Lake, Groveland and Lee Vining are absent: those are Madera, Tuolumne and Mono counties. And it lists a few places that are not aimed at visitors, the Senior Center being the obvious one. Read it as a census, not a menu.

Mariposa. 1850, Alley, California Commissary, Castillo's, Charles Street, Cinnamon Roll Bakery, Don Rubens Mexican, Falaf-a-lot at Grove House, Fredrick's of Savourys, Gold Cup Creamery, Grove House, Happy Burger, Hideout, High Country Cafe, Jantz Bakery, Little Shop of Ramen, Local Grape, Miners Roadhouse 140, Nayos Mexican Food, Pizza Factory, Pony Expresso, the Senior Center, Smokin' Oak BBQ, Starbucks, Sticks Coffee House, Subway and Twisted Cedar, plus four that are mainly takeout: the Pioneer Market Deli, Short Stop Sandwich, the Stage Stop Deli and Take and Bake.

Highway 140, between Merced and the park. Catheys Valley has the Chevron and that is the whole list, which is worth knowing at 10 p.m. Midpines has the June Bug Cafe at the Yosemite Bug, the one stop on that stretch people drive to on purpose. Up Triangle Road in Bootjack: the Bootjack Market, Sierra Cider and Steve's Sportsman's Cafe.

Highway 132, the Coulterville route. Coulterville and Greeley Hill carry the Copperpot Cafe, the Coulter Cafe, the Main Street Deli, and Cerritos Goods for takeout. This is the road people take toward the Big Oak Flat entrance from the north, and four places across two villages is the entire supply on it.

El Portal. Canyon Bar, the Cedar House Restaurant, the River Restaurant and Parkside Pizza.

Yosemite Valley. Seven Tents Pavilion, Bar 1899, Coffee Corner, the pizza counter and the Taqueria at Meadow Grill, all at Half Dome Village; Degnan's Kitchen, the Loft at Degnan's and Starbucks in Yosemite Village; Base Camp Eatery and the Mountain Room at Yosemite Valley Lodge; and the Ahwahnee. Eleven, which is more than the Valley feels like it has when you are standing in a line at one of them.

Tuolumne Meadows and the south. Tuolumne Lodge on Tioga Road. Wawona General Store at the south end, and over the Madera County line in Fish Camp, Embers and Jackalopes at Tenaya Lodge, the Pine Tree Market and the Fish Camp General Store.

Trucks and pop-ups. Ten of them work the county, and they are the part of the food scene no visitor finds by searching: All About the Wurst, Birrieria El Campeon, Dixon's Fixin's, Fishworks, L & J Mexican Food, the Lemon Drop Trailer, Mariposa Sips & Sweets, Sal's Taco Truck, the Tacos Sonora truck and Yosemite Pizza. Trucks move, so a name is all this can give you. Check the county fairgrounds, the Saturday farmers market and the brewery patios, in that order.

The same sheet carries a catering column, fifteen operators working the county, which is the answer nobody has when a group trip turns into a dinner for twenty or a small wedding turns real. If that is the trip you are planning, the proposal guide covers the venue half of the problem.

### The short version, by area

Where | Area | Meal | Price | Season | Reservations

Base Camp Eatery | Yosemite Valley | All three | $$ | Year-round | No
Degnan's Kitchen | Yosemite Valley | Breakfast, lunch | $ | Year-round | No

Hours and closing days move with the season and with staffing, and the park's own concessioner hours change more than the towns' do. The Park Bulletin carries what is open in the current Yosemite Guide edition; treat the table as the shape of the thing, not as today's schedule.

### Can you bring your own food into Yosemite?

Yes, and for most trips you should. There is no restriction on bringing food into the park, no inspection at the gate, and no rule against a cooler. The rule that does exist is about storage, and it is federal law rather than advice: food stays within arm's reach during the day and goes into a bear locker at night, never left in a car overnight, never in a truck bed. To a bear, food means anything with a scent, which includes trash, sunscreen and toothpaste. The bear guide covers what happens when people get this wrong, and the packing piece covers the cooler.

The best lunch in Yosemite is a sandwich you made in a parking lot, eaten on a granite slab beside the Merced. It costs four dollars, it saves an hour of queueing, and it is the meal people describe afterwards.

### What closes, and when

This is the part almost no other list covers, and it is the part that ruins evenings. The park's food service contracts and shuts down through September, weeks before the roads do. In the 2026 season the Tuolumne store and grill closed on September 20 and Jennie's Ice Cream in Wawona on September 6. Valley service holds up longest and thins out anyway: the taqueria and the Loft go first, then the deck, then the hours shorten on everything left.

In winter the Valley keeps a genuine core open, Degnan's, Base Camp and the hotel dining rooms among them, but the high country has nothing at all, and Tioga Road is closed regardless. If you are visiting between October and May, check what is actually open before you plan a meal around it. The winter guide has the rest of that picture.

### The takeaway

Food in Yosemite is not the trip. The trip is the park. A meal that does not slow you down or empty your wallet is a meal that did its job. Pack a cooler, eat the pizza at Half Dome Village one night, eat the brisket in Mariposa one night, drink the coffee in Lee Vining one morning, and the rest of the time eat lunch on a granite slab next to the river. That is the part of the trip you will remember.

For where to base yourself, see Yosemite gateway towns compared and the lodging guide. For one-day and two-day itineraries, see One day or two in Yosemite. For what a trip actually costs, see the budget breakdown.
