## Tioga Road opens May 15: a plan for opening weekend

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/tioga-road-opening-weekend-2026
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-05-13. Last updated: 2026-05-13.
Summary: Tioga Road opens May 15, 2026. What's open in Tuolumne Meadows, road conditions, short hikes for mid-May, and a day east to Lee Vining and Mono Lake.

Tioga Road (Highway 120) in Yosemite National Park opens Friday, May 15, 2026. That is well ahead of the long-term average opening of May 28. Glacier Point Road already opened on May 9. No day-use reservations are required to enter Yosemite this year, just a standard entrance pass.

Tioga Pass status (May 13, 2026): plowed, gate scheduled to come up Friday morning. For live updates, text "ynptraffic" to 333111 or check nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/tioga.htm. If you just need the standing version, the window, what is actually open in week one, and what to bring, the Tioga opening page is the short version, kept current each season.

### What's open on Tioga Road opening weekend

There is a difference between "the road is open" and "Tuolumne Meadows is open for the season," and opening weekend lives entirely in the first one. On Friday the pavement is plowed, but most of what you might picture, the store, the grill, the lodge, the campground services, the wilderness center staff. All of that comes online over the following weeks.

What you get this weekend is the road itself. A ribbon of asphalt through twelve-foot snow walls, glassy half-frozen lakes, snowmelt creeks running hard, and a high country still pulling itself out of winter. That is a spectacular thing to drive through. It is also a spectacular thing to be unprepared for.

Snow conditions in mid-May still include big drifts at Olmsted Point, ice along Tenaya Lake's shaded shore, and lingering snowpack on most trails above 8,500 feet.

Here is the honest breakdown.

#### What's open

- Tioga Road and Tioga Pass entrance station
- Olmsted Point and the major pullouts
- Tenaya Lake parking (the lake itself may still hold ice along the shaded shores)
- Tuolumne Meadows pullouts
- Crane Flat gas station (24/7, pay at pump, credit and debit only)
- Vault toilets along the road

#### What's not open yet

- Tuolumne Meadows Campground: still closed; the rehabilitation is ongoing and no opening date has been announced
- Tuolumne Meadows Grill: opens May 30
- Tuolumne Meadows Lodge and dining room: opens June 5
- Tuolumne Meadows Store and Post Office: opens later in summer (currently scheduled for August)
- Tuolumne Meadows Visitor Center and Wilderness Center: limited or no staffing until late May
- White Wolf Lodge and campground: closed for the season due to sewer line damage
- Gas at Tuolumne Meadows: not in operation (offline for several years now)
- Potable water: not available anywhere along the road

Pack like you are heading into the backcountry, even if you are just driving up for the day.

### Tioga Road conditions and what to bring before you go

Gas up before you start climbing. Crane Flat is the only fuel inside the park on the western side, and it is pay-at-pump only. On the east side, your next gas is in Lee Vining, about 45 minutes past Tuolumne. Bring all your water (two liters per person minimum if you are walking anywhere), bring all your food (sandwiches, snacks, a thermos of coffee), and plan for vault toilets. There is nothing to buy along Tioga Road on opening weekend, and there is no potable water. Cell service is essentially zero from Crane Flat to Lee Vining, so download offline maps before you leave the Valley.

Carry chains, layers, and a full tank. Tioga Pass tops out at 9,945 feet. Morning temperatures will be in the 20s and 30s, even when the Valley is mild. Black ice at dawn and dusk is real, especially near Olmsted Point and the climb to the pass.

Arrive early. The Park Service recommends arriving before 8 a.m. to avoid congestion and full parking lots, especially on opening weekend. Sunrise at Olmsted is one of the best photographs you will ever take in Yosemite, and you will share it with almost no one.

### The best Tioga Road stops and short hikes for opening weekend

Here is how I would build the day, and how I do build the day, every single year that the road opens.

#### Stop one: Olmsted Point

You can see Half Dome from a lot of angles in Yosemite, but only from Olmsted Point do you see its back side, the broad northern face, with Clouds Rest rising to its left and Tenaya Canyon dropping away below. The half-mile nature trail south of the parking lot is usually walkable on opening weekend; the slickrock catches the sun and dries fast, even with snow patches in the shaded hollows. The glacial erratics scattered across the polished granite are doing a lot of teaching, if you let them. Each one was carried here by an ice sheet and left when the ice melted out from under it.

Wear shoes with grip. Bring sunglasses. Snow glare at altitude is fierce.

#### Stop two: Tenaya Lake

Ten minutes further east, Tenaya Lake will likely still be ice-rimmed on opening weekend, with open water in the middle reflecting Tenaya Peak. Park at the east beach pullout. The walk down to the sand is short and easy, and it is one of the few places where you can be at the edge of an alpine lake in mid-May without committing to a real hike.

The full Tenaya Lake Loop Trail crosses the inlet on a boardwalk that Yosemite Conservancy donors helped fund and then traces the south shore through forest. That south shore holds snow and mud longer than anywhere else in the area. If you want to attempt the full 2.5-mile loop, bring waterproof boots, expect slush, and stay on the trail. The revegetation work along the loop is fragile, and meadow soils take years to recover from a single boot print in the wrong place.

For most people, an unhurried hour along the east beach is exactly the right move.

#### Stop three: a short wander in Tuolumne Meadows

A few more miles east, the road drops into the great open of Tuolumne. The meadow itself will be a patchwork of last year's brown grass, the first hints of green, sheets of meltwater, and lingering drifts. Do not walk across the meadow. Pull off at one of the half-dozen designated pullouts, stand at the edge, and let the Cathedral Range do the work.

If you want to stretch your legs, two short options are reliable on opening weekend:

- Pothole Dome at the west end of the meadow. A one-mile round-trip scramble up polished granite with a panoramic view of Tuolumne, Lembert Dome, and the Sierra crest. The approach across the meadow edge will be wet, sometimes flooded, so stick to the established path. The granite itself dries fast.
- Soda Springs and Parsons Lodge from the Lembert Dome parking area, about 1.5 miles round-trip on a flat dirt road. The historic lodge building is closed until summer staffing arrives, but the exterior, the naturally carbonated springs bubbling up through iron-orange sediment, and the Tuolumne River running hard with snowmelt are all yours. Kids love the springs.

Skip Lukens Lake, May Lake, Cathedral Lakes, and Lembert Dome's summit. Those trails are snowbound at this point in May, and a few of them will not be reasonable until late June.

### Driving Tioga Pass east to Lee Vining and Mono Lake

This is the part that makes opening weekend a full trip rather than a day in the park. Once you cross Tioga Pass at 9,945 feet, the road drops more than 3,000 feet in twelve miles down to the Mono Basin, and the world changes underneath you. Granite gives way to volcanic landscape. The Sierra wall stands behind you, the Great Basin opens ahead, and Mono Lake spreads out below with its white tufa towers and a summer population of up to two million migratory birds.

Three pullouts are worth the brake-tap on the way down. Tioga Lake just below the pass, where Mount Dana sits in the reflection. Ellery Lake a mile farther. And the Mono Lake Vista Point before the canyon drops, where the Mono Basin opens up for the first time.

#### Where to eat in Lee Vining

Lee Vining has more lore than it has dining options, and not all of the lore is still earned.

Whoa Nellie Deli at the Tioga Gas Mart is the famous one. The fish tacos built its reputation in the late 1990s, and they are still on the menu. The original chef, Matt Toomey, left in 2012 to open his own place in Mammoth, and over the years the deli has slipped a little. Portions are still generous, the view of Mono Lake from the picnic tables is still wonderful, and the Thursday and Sunday evening live music is still a great scene. But prices have crept up, the food is more uneven than it used to be, and the "world famous" billing is doing a lot of heavy lifting now. Go for the experience and the view. Order the tacos and the fries. Manage your expectations.

Latte Da Coffee Café at the El Mono Motel, just down Highway 395 in town, is what I find myself recommending more often these days. It is small, family-run, and all-organic. There is a garden out back with a few tables, and the pace is exactly the opposite of the Mobil-station bustle. Pastries, espresso, an unhurried breakfast. The El Mono Motel itself is one of those quirky eleven-room places that the eastern Sierra still has a few of, every room decorated differently, and the café is folded right into it. If you are doing a full day on the road, Latte Da in the morning and a Whoa Nellie picnic in the afternoon is a nice way to honor both eras.

Other reliable options in town: Nicely's for a classic diner breakfast, Bodie Mike's for barbecue, the Lee Vining Market for picnic supplies.

#### Make a day of Mono Lake

If you have a few hours left in the afternoon, drive south of Lee Vining on Highway 395 to South Tufa at the Mono Lake Tufa State Natural Reserve (south on 395, then east on Highway 120, about ten miles all told). Three dollars per adult, free under 16, and your America the Beautiful pass covers it. A boardwalk and a one-mile loop carry you through a forest of calcium carbonate towers that grew underwater at freshwater springs, then emerged when the lake dropped after Los Angeles began diverting the basin's streams in 1941. The story of how the lake was saved is one of the great American conservation stories, and the Mono Lake Committee Information Center and Bookstore in downtown Lee Vining (open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. daily) is the right place to learn it. Their HD film, "The Mono Lake Story," is a roughly twenty-five-minute primer.

In mid-May the lake is filling with nesting California gulls (the eared grebes and phalaropes that make Mono Lake famous arrive later, in summer and fall). By August the shoreline is carpeted in dark, shifting bands of brine flies. If you have never seen a million birds eating a trillion flies, it is something to come back for.

### What to pack for Tioga Road in May

For the high country on opening weekend, the difference between a good day and a frustrating one is footwear.

- Waterproof hiking boots. Not optional. Every trail will have wet, muddy, or partially snow-covered sections.
- Microspikes (Kahtoola or equivalent) in the pack for any shaded snow patch.
- Trekking poles for slush, mud, and slick granite.
- Layers: a puffy jacket and a shell, even if the forecast looks mild. Temperatures swing 30 to 40 degrees between dawn and afternoon.
- Sunglasses and sunscreen. Snow glare and 9,000-foot UV are a combination.
- Plenty of water and food. There is no source for either on Tioga Road yet.
- A bear-aware approach to food even on a day hike. Black bears are out of dens, hungry, and active in meadows. Use the lockers at trailheads.

For my full lists, see the day pack and car trip kit.

### A note on visiting responsibly in the early season

Early-season Tioga Road is the most fragile version of Tioga Road. The meadow soils are saturated. The vegetation is just emerging. The trails are soft. A single off-trail boot print in the wrong place in May can leave a scar that will still be visible in August.

Stay on trails. Stay on boardwalks. Use the pullouts. Pack out everything you bring in. Give wildlife room (50 yards from black bears is the park standard). Bear spray is not permitted in Yosemite. Store all scented items in lockers or canisters, even snacks in your car at a trailhead.

The whole reason the high country is worth visiting is that someone in 1864, and 1890, and 1916, and 1984, and every year since, decided it was worth protecting. Treat it like the inheritance it is.

### Tioga Road 2026: frequently asked questions

#### When does Tioga Road open in 2026?

Friday, May 15, 2026. That is well ahead of Tioga's long-term average opening date of May 28.

#### Is Tioga Pass open right now?

As of May 13, 2026, the road is plowed and scheduled to open Friday. Text "ynptraffic" to 333111 for live updates, or check nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/tioga.htm.

#### Is Highway 120 through Yosemite open?

Yes. Highway 120 (Tioga Road) through Yosemite opens Friday, May 15, 2026. Highway 120 west of the park (Big Oak Flat to Crane Flat) is open year-round.

#### What is the elevation of Tioga Pass?

Tioga Pass sits at 9,945 feet (3,031 meters), the highest state highway pass in California. Tioga Road climbs from 6,200 feet at Crane Flat to the pass over roughly 39 miles.

#### Do I need a reservation to enter Yosemite in 2026?

No. The day-use reservation system is not in effect this year. A standard entrance pass is required.

#### Is the Tuolumne Meadows store open on opening weekend?

No. The grill opens May 30, the lodge June 5, and the store opens later in the summer (currently scheduled for August).

#### Can I camp at Tuolumne Meadows on opening weekend?

No. The Tuolumne Meadows Campground remains closed while its rehabilitation continues, and no opening date has been announced for 2026. Check Recreation.gov for updates.

#### How long does it take to drive Tioga Road?

Tioga Road runs about 39 miles from Crane Flat to the Tioga Pass entrance station. Allow roughly 90 minutes one-way without stops, or a full day with Olmsted Point, Tenaya Lake, and Tuolumne Meadows. With Lee Vining and Mono Lake added on, plan a long, perfect day.

For more on the early season up high, see Glacier Point Road is open. For 2026 strategy, see Yosemite without reservations in 2026. Once Tioga is open, the high country also becomes the best stargazing in the park.

---

## So you want to hike Half Dome

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/so-you-want-to-hike-half-dome
Section: Trails and Hikes. Published: 2026-05-12. Last updated: 2026-05-12.
Summary: The honest case for the Half Dome cables, and the better hike most miss: Clouds Rest, a thousand feet higher, with bigger views and no permit.

I get it. You want to hike Half Dome.

Everybody does. It's the silhouette on the license plate, the logo on the beer can, the thing your friend did last summer that they won't shut up about. And I'm not going to tell you you're wrong for wanting it. The cables are unlike anything I've ever done anywhere else in the national park system. You clip your hands onto those steel cables, lean into the granite at a 45-degree angle, and pull yourself up 400 vertical feet of rock with nothing between you and the Valley floor but air and gravity. Your arms burn. Your legs shake. The whole world drops away beneath you. And when you stand on top, at 8,839 feet, looking out at a panorama that stretches from the Clark Range to the Cathedral Peaks, it feels earned in a way that very few things in life feel earned.

It's worth doing once.

I mean that. If the stars align, if you get the permit, if you're in the shape, if the weather cooperates, do it. It's a genuine bucket-list hike. But I want to be honest with you about what "if the stars align" actually means, because for most people planning a Yosemite trip, the stars don't align. And that's where this article goes somewhere you might not expect.

### The hike itself

Let's start with what you're signing up for. The Half Dome day hike is a 14 to 16 mile round trip from Happy Isles in Yosemite Valley with about 4,800 feet of total elevation gain. The National Park Service says most hikers take 10 to 12 hours. Some take longer. You're leaving before sunrise and getting back after dark unless you're in serious shape and moving fast.

The route follows the Mist Trail or the John Muir Trail (or one up and the other down) past Vernal Fall and Nevada Fall, two of the most famous waterfalls in the world, and then up through Little Yosemite Valley to the base of the subdome. That's where the real drama begins.

The subdome is a steep granite staircase carved into the rock. It's exhausting after the miles you've already put in. And then you reach the cables.

Two steel cables, held up by metal poles, run 400 feet up the back of Half Dome at roughly a 45-degree grade. You grab the cables, you pull, you step, you repeat. There are wooden crossboards every few feet to brace your feet on. When it's crowded (and in July and August, it's crowded), you're doing this in a conga line, waiting for people above you to move, gripping cables that a hundred sweaty hands have already gripped that morning. When the rock is dry and the sky is clear, it's thrilling. When the rock is wet, it's dangerous. Nearly all fatal falls from the cable route have happened when the rock was wet.

The NPS doesn't sugarcoat it: rangers assist hundreds of people on the Half Dome trail every summer. Most of those emergencies could have been prevented with better preparation.

### The permit problem

Here's where the dream starts running into reality.

You need a permit to hike past the subdome, seven days a week, whenever the cables are up. The cables typically go up the Friday before Memorial Day and come down the day after Columbus Day. No permit means a ranger turns you around. No exceptions.

A maximum of 300 people per day are allowed past the base of the subdome: roughly 225 day hikers and 75 backpackers.

There are two ways to get a day-hiker permit, and both are lotteries.

The preseason lottery has its application window during the month of March, with results emailed in mid-April. You can request permits for up to six people and specify your preferred dates or a date range. Here's the catch: in 2024, 35,289 applications were submitted. The success rate was 22%. That means roughly four out of five people who applied didn't get a permit for any of their requested dates.

Saturdays are the most requested day, with about 21% of all applications targeting a Saturday. Mondays and Tuesdays are the least popular. If you have flexibility on dates, weekdays give you better odds, but "better" still means most people don't get in.

The daily lottery is a second chance. During cable season, additional permits are released two days before each hiking date. You apply by 4 PM Pacific time, and results come late that evening. In 2024, 35,561 daily lottery applications were submitted with a 19% success rate. Weekday odds run around 22%. Weekend odds drop to about 14%.

Both lotteries charge a $10 non-refundable application fee. If you win, there's an additional $10 per person permit fee. Permits are non-transferable and require photo ID at the subdome checkpoint.

For the full breakdown on how both lotteries work, including strategy tips, see the permit lottery guide.

The bottom line: If you're planning a Yosemite trip around specific dates, there's roughly a one-in-five chance you'll get a Half Dome permit. If your entire trip hinges on that permit, you're building a vacation on a coin flip. And if you don't get the permit, you might spend your best hiking day in Yosemite feeling like the trip was incomplete.

I don't want that for you.

### Here's what I actually want to tell you

If what you're after is the cables, the specific experience of pulling yourself up the back of Half Dome on steel cables, standing on that famous summit, looking down at the Valley from the place in every photograph, then yes, you need the permit, and you should go for it. Play both lotteries. I hope you get it.

But if what you're really after is an incredible full-day hike in Yosemite with a summit that makes your jaw drop and views that make you feel like you're standing on top of the Sierra Nevada, I want to tell you about Clouds Rest.

Because Clouds Rest is the better hike. And I don't say that lightly.

### Clouds Rest from Sunrise trailhead

Clouds Rest is a 9,926-foot peak on the north rim of Tenaya Canyon. Its summit is more than a thousand feet higher than Half Dome. From the top, you get a 360-degree panorama that includes Half Dome itself (looking down at it from above), Tenaya Canyon (one of the most dramatic canyons in the park), Yosemite Valley, the Cathedral Range, Mount Hoffmann, and the entire high country stretching to the Sierra crest. On a clear day, you can see from the foothills to the peaks of the Ritter Range.

The view is bigger than Half Dome's. In every direction.

And you don't need a permit.

The hike starts at the Sunrise Lakes trailhead on Tioga Road, about 1.4 miles east of Olmsted Point at the south end of Tenaya Lake. It's 13 miles round trip with roughly 2,000 feet of elevation gain in two separate pushes. The trailhead sits at 8,151 feet, which means you start high and stay high the entire day. No climbing 4,800 feet from the Valley floor. No Mist Trail staircase with a thousand other people. No heat radiating off the Valley walls in July.

That last point matters more than you think.

### Why this is better than Half Dome in July and August

Half Dome's cable season peaks in July and August. Those are also the hottest months in Yosemite Valley, where the trailhead sits at 4,000 feet. You wake up at 4 AM to beat the heat. You climb 4,800 feet on a trail that has no shade for long stretches. You share the Mist Trail with what feels like the entire state of California, and the Mist Trail can be genuinely dangerous when it's that crowded. By the time you reach the subdome, you've been hiking for five or six hours in conditions that punish anyone who didn't bring enough water or didn't train enough.

Clouds Rest from Sunrise trailhead starts at 8,150 feet. The air is cooler. The trail is shaded through lodgepole forest for most of the first several miles. You're sharing the trail with maybe a few dozen people all day, not hundreds. There's no permit lottery, no subdome checkpoint, no conga line. Just you, the granite, and the biggest views in the park.

As soon as Tioga Road opens, typically late May to early June depending on the snow year, this hike is available. In a low snow year, the trail can be clear by early June. You might encounter a few snow patches here and there in the first couple of weeks after Tioga opens, but the trail is well-defined and the route is intuitive. Bring trekking poles if you're hiking in early season, and gaiters if the snow is still melting. By late June or early July, the trail is fully clear.

### The trail, section by section

Miles 0 to 1.5: The flat approach. From the trailhead, cross Tenaya Creek (early season: expect wet feet; by July you can rock-hop) and follow signs toward Clouds Rest and Sunrise High Sierra Camp. The first mile and a half is gentle, rolling through forest over granite slabs. This is your warmup. Enjoy it.

Miles 1.5 to 2.5: The first climb. The trail gains about 1,000 feet through a series of switchbacks up to the ridgeline east of Tenaya Canyon. This is the hardest sustained climb of the day. Old stone trail work (steps, walls) marks the path, though some of it has crumbled with time. Take your time. You're at altitude and it's going to feel harder than 1,000 feet normally feels.

Miles 2.5 to 4.5: The descent and meadow. At the saddle, you'll pass the junction with the trail to Sunrise High Sierra Camp. Continue south as the trail drops about 400 feet into a forested meadow. Sunrise Mountain rises to the east. In early season, parts of this section can be marshy. A small pond sits in the meadow, and the surrounding area can be wet. This is the quiet middle of the hike. You'll likely see almost no one.

Miles 4.5 to 5.5: The second climb. The trail turns west and begins its second major ascent, another 1,000 feet up toward the Clouds Rest ridgeline. This one is steady but less steep than the first. As you climb, the trees thin and the views start opening up. You'll catch your first glimpses down into Tenaya Canyon, sheer granite walls dropping thousands of feet. This is the moment you realize what you're hiking toward.

Miles 5.5 to 6.5: The spine. And then the trees fall away entirely.

The final half-mile to the summit follows a narrow granite ridge, the spine of Clouds Rest. The ridge is maybe 10 to 20 feet wide in most places, with the north side dropping thousands of feet into Tenaya Canyon and the south side falling steeply toward the Merced River drainage. The trail uses the slightly less exposed south side of the ridge for most of the approach, but there's no hiding from the fact that you're walking along the top of a wall.

It's not technical. You don't need ropes or climbing experience. But if you're afraid of heights, this section will test you. The granite is solid underfoot (good traction when dry) and the trail is clear. But the exposure is real, and on a windy day, it's intense.

Take your time. Stop often. Look around. The views open in every direction and they only get better the higher you go.

The summit. The top of Clouds Rest is a broad granite platform. Not a point, not a knife-edge, a place where you can sit, eat lunch, lie on the warm rock, and take in a panorama that most people in Yosemite never see.

Half Dome rises to the south, and you're looking down at it. That's the thing that gets people. You spent your whole trip staring up at Half Dome from the Valley, and now you're above it. Tenaya Canyon drops away to the north in one of the most dramatic vertical landscapes in the Sierra. To the west, Yosemite Valley unfolds: El Capitan, Bridalveil Fall, the whole sweep of it. To the east, the Cathedral Range and the high country. To the south, the Clark Range and the Merced watershed.

It's one of the great summits in the national park system. And on a Tuesday in June, you might have it to yourself.

### Water and logistics

Water plan: The only reliable water on the trail is in the first couple of miles: Tenaya Creek at the trailhead, and a few seasonal streams and the marshy meadow in the middle section. After that, there's nothing until you return. Carry at least 3 liters. If it's a hot day or you're a heavy drinker, carry 4. A water filter is useful in early season for topping off at the meadow streams, but by late July those may be dry. For a full day-pack checklist, see the day pack guide.

Start time: Leave the trailhead by 7 AM at the latest in summer. Earlier is better. The hike takes 7 to 10 hours round trip for most people, and you want to be off the summit before afternoon thunderstorms build. Lightning on the spine of Clouds Rest is not a theoretical risk. It's the primary safety concern of this hike. If you see clouds building, turn around. The summit will be there tomorrow.

Parking: The Sunrise Lakes trailhead parking lot is small, roughly a dozen spots. On summer weekends, it fills by 7 AM. Additional parking is available along the shoulder of Tioga Road nearby, but check for "no parking" signs. On weekdays, parking is rarely an issue before 8 AM.

What to wear: Trail runners or hiking boots with good traction. The granite on the spine is grippy when dry but slick when wet, same as Half Dome's cables. Layers for the summit: at nearly 10,000 feet, it can be 15 to 20 degrees cooler than the Valley and windy even on a calm day below. Sun protection is critical at this elevation.

The trailhead creek crossing: Tenaya Creek crosses the trail within the first few hundred feet. In spring and early summer when snowmelt is heavy, this can be a real ford: knee-deep, cold, fast. By mid-July, it's usually a rock-hop. By late August, it might be dry. If you're hiking in early season, bring shoes you don't mind getting wet or carry sandals for the crossing.

### Safety

Clouds Rest is safer than Half Dome in most respects. No cables, no conga line, no permit-pressure pushing people to hike in conditions they shouldn't. But it has its own risks.

Lightning. This is the big one. The summit and spine are fully exposed at nearly 10,000 feet. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July and August. If you see dark clouds building or hear distant thunder, descend immediately. Do not wait to see if the storm passes. Get off the ridgeline and into the trees. The standard rule applies: summit before noon, descend by early afternoon.

The spine exposure. The narrow ridge is not dangerous if you're careful, but it demands respect. Stay on the trail, don't scramble onto side ledges for photos, and be honest with yourself about your comfort with heights. There's an old alternate trail that goes around the east side of the summit, avoiding the exposed ridgeline, though it's less maintained and can be hard to follow.

Distance and altitude. Thirteen miles at 8,000 to 10,000 feet is a serious day, especially if you're visiting from sea level. The altitude makes everything harder. Drink water before you're thirsty, eat before you're hungry, and take rest breaks in the shade. Altitude sickness symptoms include headache and nausea. If you feel them, descend.

Early season hazards. Snow patches on the trail can linger into late June, especially on north-facing slopes. Post-holing through soft snow is exhausting and disorienting. If you're hiking in the first two weeks after Tioga opens, check current conditions and be prepared to turn around if snow coverage is too heavy.

### Half Dome vs. Clouds Rest: the honest comparison

| Half Dome | Clouds Rest (from Sunrise)

Round trip distance | 14 to 16 miles | 13 miles
Elevation gain | 4,800 feet | ~2,000 feet
Summit elevation | 8,839 feet | 9,926 feet
Starting elevation | ~4,000 feet (Valley) | 8,151 feet (Tioga Road)
Permit required | Yes, lottery, ~20% odds | No
Typical time | 10 to 14 hours | 7 to 10 hours
Crowds on trail | Heavy (Mist Trail, cables) | Light to moderate
The cables | Unique, iconic, nothing like it | No cables, open granite ridge
Summit views | Spectacular, mostly south/west | 360-degree, higher elevation
Available | Cable season (late May to mid-October) | Whenever Tioga Road is open
Heat exposure | Significant (Valley start, low elevation) | Minimal (high elevation start)
Biggest risk | Wet cables, lightning, overcrowding | Lightning, exposure on spine

Half Dome gives you the cables. Nothing else in the park, nothing else in any park, gives you that experience. The cables are singular.

Clouds Rest gives you everything else. The bigger views, the higher summit, the quieter trail, the cooler temperatures, the freedom from lottery stress, and a ridgeline walk that is, in its own way, just as thrilling as the cables. Different, but equal.

### If you still want Half Dome

Do it. Seriously, if you have the permit, you're in shape, and the weather is good, go hike Half Dome. It's one of the great experiences in the American outdoors. Read the permit lottery guide for strategy on both lotteries, pack the right day pack, start before dawn, bring 4 liters of water and gloves for the cables, and check the weather forecast the night before. If there's any chance of rain, don't go. The cables are not worth your life when the rock is wet.

But if the permit doesn't come through, or if you're visiting in June before the cables go up, or if the idea of the Mist Trail in August makes you feel tired just thinking about it, go do Clouds Rest. Drive up Tioga Road, park at the Sunrise trailhead, walk 6.5 miles through some of the most beautiful high country in the Sierra Nevada, and stand on a summit that's higher than Half Dome, quieter than Half Dome, and (I'll say it) more beautiful than Half Dome.

You won't feel like you missed anything. You'll feel like you found something better.

---

## Glacier Point Road is open: a plan for the early season

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/glacier-point-road-open-2026
Section: Seasonal Guides. Published: 2026-05-11. Last updated: 2026-05-11.
Summary: Seventeen miles to a 7,200-foot viewpoint at eye level with Half Dome. What is open at the top, what is not, and how to plan early-season 2026.

Glacier Point Road is open for the 2026 season. The Park Service plowed it through the back end of winter, the gate at Chinquapin came up after seven months of closure, and cars are again climbing the seventeen miles to a viewpoint at 7,200 feet that puts you at eye level with Half Dome.

If you have been waiting for this, here is what to know about the road in the first weeks of the season. Not the road in general. Not the road in July. The road now, in this snowpack year, with what is and is not actually working at the top.

### What is open at the top

The road is open. The viewpoint is open. The vault toilets are open. The amphitheater is there.

Drinking water is not yet available at Glacier Point. Bring your own. A liter per person at the absolute minimum if you are walking out to Sentinel Dome or Taft Point, more if it is warm. The Glacier Point gift shop and snack stand are seasonal and may not be open in the first weeks. Check the Park Service's conditions page the night before you drive up. Do not assume you can buy a sandwich at the top.

The trailheads accessible from the road include Sentinel Dome and Taft Point (the two most-walked short hikes off Glacier Point Road), Pohono (the long rim trail), the top of the Panorama Trail, the top of the Four Mile Trail, Mono Meadow, and the Bridalveil Creek area. Most of these will have snow on the shaded north faces and patchy slush in the trees through May. Trekking poles are not optional this time of year if you are going beyond the immediate viewpoint. Microspikes are useful on the first half mile of any trail off the road that climbs.

A note worth saying plainly: the Park Service has flagged intermittent closures of the Panorama Trail between Nevada Fall and the Illilouette Creek junction for ongoing rockfall remediation. If your plan was to descend Panorama to the Mist Trail, check the conditions page before you start down. The Mist Trail itself has its own current closure (more on that elsewhere on the site).

### What the road actually feels like early in the season

The drive up Glacier Point Road in May is one of the most overlooked drives in the park, partly because most visitors are not yet thinking about it and partly because the road conditions in the first few weeks tend to filter casual drivers. The first half climbs through ponderosa pine and incense cedar with patches of black oak still leafing out. Around 6,500 feet you are in white fir country, and by the time you cross Bridalveil Creek the conifers have shifted to red fir and lodgepole. There will be snow in the woods. There will be snow in the meadows. There may be running water across the road at culvert sections where the meltwater is finding its early routes.

The road is paved, and the Park Service plows it well, but the corners are tight, the sun and shadow alternate quickly, and the asphalt at 6,000 feet on a sunny May morning is doing things differently than the asphalt in the Valley. Drive it like you have all day.

Traffic in these first weeks will be heavier than the off-season but lighter than what July will bring. The early hour helps. So does the fact that many visitors planning a Yosemite trip have not yet realized Glacier Point is back. The first stretch after the opening is, in my experience, the most pleasant time to drive this road. The locals know. The internet has not caught up yet.

### What I would do with the day

Pick one of two plans, depending on what you want.

The slow plan. Drive up for sunrise. In mid-May, that is somewhere around 5:55 a.m., so leave the Valley by 4:45. Park at Glacier Point itself. Walk the paved 0.3 miles out to the overlook in the pre-light. Watch the light hit the high peaks east of the Valley before it hits the Valley floor. Half Dome catches it first. Then the Clark Range. Then, finally, the inner Valley and the north walls. There is no faster way to learn how the light works in Yosemite than to watch it land in this order, from this vantage. Bring a thermos. Bring layers (it can be in the thirties at the rim even in May). Plan to stay an hour after sunrise, which is when most of the people who came up will leave and you will have the railing to yourself for ten minutes.

The hike plan. Drive up after breakfast, park at the Sentinel Dome and Taft Point trailhead (about a mile and a half before Glacier Point itself). Hike Sentinel first, Taft second, eat lunch on the rim somewhere quiet, then drive the last bit of road and walk out to Glacier Point with your legs already loose. The total walking is around five miles with modest elevation gain, and the experience of standing on Sentinel's bare granite cap (which is exfoliated granodiorite, not bare granite the way most people use the word) and then standing inches from the void at Taft is a study in what 2,500 feet of vertical can mean. There is a piece on the site about how to choose between those two hikes if you only have time for one.

If you are bringing kids, or visitors who can't hike, there is a third plan: Glacier Point itself only. The walk to the overlook is paved, short, and stroller-friendly. The view is the highest-bang-per-step view in the park. Eat your sandwiches on the wall, count peregrines, and drive back down. That is a complete day.

### What you will probably notice first

Two things. The first is the silence. Glacier Point in May is quieter than Glacier Point in July by an order of magnitude. The marmots are still mostly in their winter dens. The Clark's nutcrackers are loud but not constant. The wind, when it comes, comes in waves rather than all afternoon. Stand still for a minute and you will hear the Merced River from 3,000 feet down, sometimes the falls, almost always the wind moving through the lodgepoles behind you.

The second is the snow. Looking east from Glacier Point you see the Cathedral Range, Mount Hoffman, Mount Clark, and behind them the high peaks of the Clark Range. Even in this thin snowpack year (more on that later this week), the high country still looks like winter from up here. Tioga Road is still closed. The high lakes are still frozen. The Sentinel Range above Tenaya Canyon will hold snow for another six weeks. You are looking at country that is two months behind the Valley you just drove out of.

That contrast is the whole pitch for an early-season Glacier Point trip. From this one parking lot you can see both the Yosemite that is already in spring and the Yosemite that is still in winter. There are not many vantages in the country where you can hold both seasons in a single look.

### One small thing to bring

A pair of binoculars. Glacier Point is one of the best peregrine falcon viewpoints in California. The pair that nests below Glacier Point's east face usually has eggs by mid-May and chicks by late June. From the overlook you cannot see them, but you can sometimes hear them and almost always spot the adults working the cliff face for swifts. The white-throated swifts themselves, riding the air pouring up the south face, are worth ten minutes of focused attention.

Also: a wind layer. The temperature spread between the Valley and the rim on a clear May day can be twenty degrees. People underestimate this every year.

### The honest takeaway

The first weeks of the season are one of the few times in the year when Glacier Point feels like a place you discovered rather than a place everyone has already been to. The road will be dirty. The amenities will be skeletal. You may not be able to buy water. The Panorama Trail may be partly closed. The Mist Trail, if you were planning to combine, is currently closed.

Go anyway. Drive up early. Bring your own water. Walk the short trails before the lot fills. Stand on the overlook for longer than you think you should. Then leave by lunch. The rest of the season will fill this place up. The first few weeks never quite do.

The door is open. Walk through it.

---

## The Mist Trail: everything the internet isn't telling you

URL: https://thetalusfieldjournal.com/articles/mist-trail-the-real-guide
Section: Trails and Hikes. Published: 2026-05-11. Last updated: 2026-08-27.
Summary: The most hiked trail in any national park. The honest answers about shoes, water, when to go, and whether you can actually die out there.

The Mist Trail is the most hiked trail in Yosemite. It might be the most hiked trail in any national park. On a Saturday in June, a thousand people will walk some version of it. On Reddit, it generates more questions than every other Yosemite trail combined: Is it hard? How wet will I get? Can my kids do it? What shoes do I need? Is it worth it? Can I die?

The answers to those questions, in order: yes, soaked, probably, not sneakers, absolutely, and statistically unlikely but not impossible.

Here's the rest of what you need to know, from someone who has hiked it more times than he can count and has watched thousands of visitors attempt it in every condition from perfect sunshine to horizontal rain.

### What the Mist Trail actually is

The Mist Trail runs from Happy Isles at the east end of Yosemite Valley up alongside two waterfalls: Vernal Fall (317 feet) and Nevada Fall (594 feet). The full trail to the top of Nevada Fall is about 5.4 miles round trip with roughly 2,000 feet of elevation gain. The section to the Vernal Fall footbridge, the turnaround point for most families, is 1.6 miles round trip with about 400 feet of gain.

There are four logical stopping points, and each one is a complete hike on its own.

The Vernal Fall footbridge (0.8 miles from Happy Isles, 400 ft gain). Paved trail, moderate grade, excellent views of Vernal Fall from the bridge. This is where most families with young children turn around. It's worth the walk even if you go no further.

The top of Vernal Fall (1.3 miles from Happy Isles, 1,000 ft gain). This is where the "mist" in "Mist Trail" happens. The trail climbs a granite staircase directly alongside the fall, and when the waterfall is flowing at peak volume (May and June), you get drenched. Not sprinkled. Drenched. The granite steps are wet, steep, and uneven. A metal railing is bolted into the rock on the exposed side. At the top, an emerald pool sits above the fall with views down the canyon. This section is strenuous and exhilarating.

The top of Nevada Fall (2.7 miles from Happy Isles, 2,000 ft gain). Past the top of Vernal Fall, the trail continues through forest and along the Merced River canyon to the base and then the top of Nevada Fall. The views from the top, looking down 594 feet of whitewater with Liberty Cap and Half Dome towering behind you, are some of the most dramatic in the park.

The loop return via the John Muir Trail (total ~6.5 miles). From the top of Nevada Fall, you can return via the JMT, which switchbacks down more gently through forest. This makes a loop and saves your knees on the descent. Most experienced hikers go up the Mist Trail and down the JMT.

Past the top of Nevada Fall, this trail is also the standard approach to Half Dome. If that's your goal, read the permit lottery guide first, and the honest case for the cables before you commit.

### The wet granite reality

Between mid-April and late June, the granite staircase below Vernal Fall is a waterfall itself. Spray from the fall hits the trail continuously. The steps, hundreds of them, carved and placed by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s, are wet, mossy in places, and uneven. Some are a foot tall. Some are two feet tall. Some are angled in ways that make your feet slide.

This is where most Mist Trail injuries happen. Not from falling off the trail. From slipping on wet granite stairs while wearing the wrong shoes.

Shoes matter on this trail more than any other trail in Yosemite. Hiking boots or trail shoes with real tread are the minimum. Running shoes with worn-out soles are a slip waiting to happen. Flip-flops, sandals, and fashion sneakers are genuinely dangerous on wet granite, and I say that without exaggeration. I've watched people go down hard on these stairs in shoes that had no business being on a wet rock face.

If you don't own hiking shoes and you're doing this trail in peak waterfall season, buy a cheap pair with rubber lugs. It's a thirty-dollar investment in not spending your Yosemite trip in the medical clinic.

### You will get wet

This is not a gentle misting. In May and June, when the Merced River is running at full snowmelt volume, the spray zone below Vernal Fall is like standing in a rainstorm for twenty minutes. Your clothes will be soaked through. Your phone will get wet. Your camera will get wet. Your pack will get wet.

What to do about it.

Put your phone in a ziplock bag. You can still take photos through the bag. Better yet, bring a waterproof phone case.

Wear synthetic or wool clothing, not cotton. Cotton gets heavy and cold when wet and takes hours to dry. Synthetic dries in thirty minutes in the sun at the top of the fall.

A rain jacket helps but isn't necessary if the day is warm. In July and August, when the falls are lower, you might get misted rather than soaked. In May and June, the rain jacket keeps you warm on the way up but you'll be sweating under it.

Bring a dry shirt in a ziplock in your pack. Change at the top. This is the move that separates people who had a great time from people who spent the rest of the hike shivering.

### When to go

Peak waterfall (May through mid-June). The most dramatic experience. Vernal Fall is thundering, the mist zone is intense, the granite is soaked. Nevada Fall is at full power. This is the version that makes everyone's jaw drop. It's also the most crowded and the most slippery.

Mid-season (late June through July). Flow decreases. The mist zone shrinks. The stairs are drier and safer. Still beautiful. The crowds thin slightly on weekdays.

Late season (August through October). The falls slow to a trickle. The trail is completely dry and the stairs are easy. Different experience, more of a canyon hike than a waterfall hike, but still worth it for the granite scenery.

Time of day. Start early. The trailhead at Happy Isles fills by 8 a.m. on summer weekends. The closest parking is the trailhead lot at Curry Village, pinned on the site's map. The Mist Trail is in shade in the early morning, which means cooler hiking and better light on the falls. By afternoon, the trail is in full sun and the heat on the granite stairs is punishing.

2026 weekday restrictions. Starting June 30, 2026, the Mist Trail between Vernal Fall and Nevada Fall is closed Monday through Thursday, 7 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., for trail repairs, through the end of October. On weekdays, you'll either need to time your hike to reach that section after 3:30, or take the JMT bypass between the two falls. Weekends are unaffected. The bypass got more scenic this summer: the JMT's "Ice Cut" segment, between Clark Point and the Panorama Trail junction, reopened in late July 2026 after nearly three years closed for storm and ice damage, so the full Mist Trail-JMT loop is open again.

### The safety talk

I need to be direct here, because the internet makes this trail look like a walk in the park, and it isn't.

In 2025, roughly 30% of Yosemite's search-and-rescue operations originated on the Mist Trail corridor. Thirty percent, from one trail. The park averages close to one fatality per month on this trail and the falls above it. That's not a scare tactic. It's a number, and it's real.

Most fatalities on this trail are cardiac arrests, people who were not prepared for the strenuous nature of this hike. The exertion is real, the elevation gain is steady, and the heat in summer compounds both. If you have a heart condition, or if you don't hike regularly, take this seriously before you start.

The pools above both Vernal Fall and Nevada Fall look calm and inviting. They are not. The current is powerful, the granite is frictionless when wet, and the lip of the fall is just downstream. There is no second chance. If you go past the railing, you are in the kill zone. The NPS signs are not being dramatic. They are being accurate.

Stay behind the railings. Don't wade. Don't swim in the pools above the falls. Don't walk on the wet granite near the edge "for a photo." This is the single most important safety rule on this trail, and it's the rule that, when broken, has killed people. Swimming in the Emerald Pool and the Silver Apron is not merely a bad idea, it is prohibited; the swimming guide lays out where in this park you may and may not get in the water, and what the Park Service has documented happening here.

The trail itself is also a significant source of injuries, not fatalities, but twisted ankles, broken wrists, heat exhaustion, and falls on wet granite that require a ranger assist or a helicopter. That 30% SAR number isn't just about the falls. It's about people underestimating the trail, running out of water, wearing the wrong shoes, and getting in over their heads on steep, wet rock. This trail is beautiful and it is dangerous, and those two things are true at the same time.

Beyond the falls: the trail is steep and physical. People with heart conditions, serious knee issues, or no hiking experience should consider turning around at the footbridge. The staircase to the top of Vernal Fall gains 600 feet in half a mile on uneven wet stairs. It's a real workout.

Bring more water than you think you need. The trail starts at 4,000 feet and gains 2,000 feet in full sun on the upper sections. Two liters minimum. Three liters if you're going to the top of Nevada Fall. There is no water available on the trail. Water and restrooms are at Happy Isles at the start and at the top of Nevada Fall (seasonal).

### The crowd question

Yes, it's crowded. Especially on weekends in May through July. The Mist Trail is Yosemite's signature hike and it draws people from all over the world.

The crowd thins dramatically with elevation. The footbridge is packed. The staircase is busy. The top of Vernal Fall has people. The section between Vernal and Nevada Falls is noticeably quieter. The top of Nevada Fall, on a weekday, can feel almost empty.

If you want the Mist Trail experience without the crowd: go on a weekday, start before 7 a.m., and hike past Vernal Fall to Nevada Fall. Most people turn around at Vernal. The ones who keep going get rewarded with a bigger waterfall and a fraction of the people.

### Is it worth it

Yes. Without qualification. The Mist Trail in peak waterfall season is one of the great hiking experiences in the United States. The combination of the granite canyon, the thundering water, the physical challenge of the stairs, and the views from the top is something that doesn't exist anywhere else.

Just don't show up in flip-flops with one bottle of water and no idea what you're walking into. The internet makes this trail look like a casual stroll past a pretty waterfall. It's not. It's a real hike in a real mountain environment, and the people who prepare for it have a spectacular day. The people who don't are the ones writing the Reddit posts about how they slipped on the stairs, ran out of water, and wished they'd stayed at the hotel.

Come prepared. Read the day pack packing list, and pack the car the night before so the early start actually happens. Start early. Wear real shoes. Bring a ziplock for your phone and a dry shirt for the top.

Then get ready to get soaked, because the Mist Trail earned its name, and it's worth every wet, steep, breathless step.

Some links in this piece are affiliate links. If you buy or book through one, The Talus Field may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. The recommendations do not change for it. Full disclosure.
